50 per cent for five years, 100 per cent for the next five years and nil thereafter
50 per cent for the entire fifteen-year period
100 per cent for ten years followed by 25 per cent for five years
50.x: Section 10AA provides 100 per cent exemption for the first five years, 50 per cent for the next five years and 50 per cent of ploughed-back profit for another five years.
50.tq: Track the exemption sequence and distinguish the successive time periods.
xs: **Sec 10AA**: **100%** for **five years**, **50%** for the next five, and **50% of ploughed-back profit** for a further five — option **(1)** is correct.
The exemption is on **export income** of an eligible SEZ unit.
xa: Only units operational by **30 June 2020** get this (extended from **31 March 2020**).
The **SEZ Act, 2005** came into force on **10 February 2006**.
SEZs are **single-window**, export-oriented enclaves.

50.s: India's rank in the World Bank's Doing Business 2020 report was:
50.x: India rose from 142nd in 2014 to 63rd in DB 2020; the report was discontinued in 2021 over data irregularities.
xa: Doing Business was conceptualised by the **IFC** and published by the **World Bank Group**.
Its replacement is **B-READY**.

50.s: Of the 355 provisions amended by the Jan Vishwas 2.0 Bill, how many were decriminalised?
50.x: The Bill (introduced 18 August 2025, passed 2026) amended 355 provisions across 16 Acts and decriminalised 288 of them.
xa: It covers **16** Acts across **10** ministries.
**Jan Vishwas Act 2026**: an **Improvement Notice** for first-time Legal Metrology lapses.
DPIIT runs a **Reducing Compliance Burden** exercise.

50.s: District BRAP, or DBRAP, is intended primarily to:
o: Extend business reforms to district-level administration and Tier-II and Tier-III cities
Measure the competitiveness of Indian states against foreign countries
Rank only metropolitan cities on exports
50.x: DBRAP extends the reform process to districts and Tier-II and Tier-III cities.
50.tq: Apply the meaning of the district-level extension to the appropriate administrative scope.
xs: **DBRAP** takes business reforms to **district level** and **Tier-II and Tier-III cities** — option **(1)** is correct.
It does not replace state-level BRAP or compare states with foreign countries.
xa: State-level **BRAP** began in **2015** under **DIPP** with the **World Bank Group**.
DPIIT is preparing **BRAP 2026**.
AP has been **No. 1** consistently from **2016**.

50.s: Which of the following reforms have contributed to the improvement of the Ease of Doing Business in India?
o: Removal of all foreign ownership restrictions in * Indian companies
Expansion of public sector enterprises into new sectors
50.x: The rollout of GST in 2017 unified India's fragmented indirect tax structure into a single national tax regime, simplifying compliance for businesses across states and being one of the key reforms credited with improving India's Ease of Doing Business rankings. The other options describe the opposite of liberalizing, business-friendly reform.

50.s: India’s position in mobile phone manufacturing is best described as follows:
o: The second-largest mobile phone manufacturer in the world
The fifth-largest mobile phone manufacturer in the world
The largest mobile phone manufacturer in the world
The third-largest mobile phone manufacturer in the world
50.x: India is identified as the second-largest mobile phone manufacturer.
50.tq: Use the precise rank rather than assuming that the largest domestic market is the largest manufacturer.
xs: India is the world's **second-largest mobile phone manufacturer** — option **(1)** is correct.
Some **2026** notes say "**among the top 3** in volume".
xa: Mobile output rose from **₹18,900 crore (2014-15)** to **₹5.45 lakh crore (2024-25)**, CAGR ~**40%**.
**99.2%** of phones used in India are made domestically.
Smartphones were the **largest export category in 2025**.

50.s: The SPICe+ reform was introduced to improve which ease-of-doing-business area?
50.x: SPICe+ supports starting a business; online building-plan approvals target construction permits, IBC insolvency and GST taxes.
xa: **SPICe+** (**2020**) bundles **11 services** of **3 ministries**; also **MCA21 V3**.
**DILRMP**, **ULPIN**, **NGDRS** improved **registering property**.
**GST** as an EoDB reform was the APPSC-G2 **2025** key.

50.s: Invest India, established in 2009, is best described as:
o: A statutory regulator under the Reserve Bank of India for foreign exchange transactions
A World Bank Group index for ranking investment destinations
A not-for-profit joint venture involving DIPP, FICCI, CII, NASSCOM and the States, serving as the national investment promotion agency
A private company established exclusively by NASSCOM for software exports
50.x: Invest India was established in 2009 as a not-for-profit joint venture involving DIPP, FICCI, CII, NASSCOM and the States, and serves as the national investment promotion agency.
50.tq: Separate the investment-promotion agency from a regulator, index or private industry body.
xs: **Invest India** (**2009**) is a **not-for-profit JV of DIPP, FICCI, CII, NASSCOM and the States**, the **national investment promotion agency** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is not a regulator, an index or a NASSCOM-only company.
xa: It also acts as an **investment-facilitation SPV**.
**NSWS**: **686** central + **7,498** state approvals.
The **FIF** portal joined NSWS in **Aug 2022**.

50.s: Business Reform Action Plan, commonly abbreviated as BRAP, was first released in 2015 by:
o: DIPP, now DPIIT, in association with the World Bank Group
The Ministry of Finance and the IMF
50.x: BRAP was first released in 2015 by DIPP, now DPIIT, with the World Bank Group.
50.tq: Who-launched-what trap using neighbouring institutions as distractors.
xs: **BRAP** was first released in **2015** by **DIPP (now DPIIT)** with the **World Bank Group** — option **(1)** is correct.
NITI Aayog runs a separate **Investment Friendliness Index**.
xa: BRAP = **Business Reform Action Plan** (APPSC-GS **2019**).
AP was **2nd** in BRAP **2015** (Gujarat **1st**).
DPIIT is preparing **BRAP 2026**.

50.s: In BRAP 2016, Andhra Pradesh shared the No. 1 rank with:
50.x: Andhra Pradesh was jointly first with Telangana in BRAP 2016 and has been described as No. 1 consistently since.
xa: APPSC-GS **2023** key: AP **1st**.
BRAP **2024** was the **7th edition** with **435** reform points.
NITI Aayog's index (**Jul 2026**) put AP among **"Frontrunners"**.

50.s: The four principles associated with the 435 reform points in BRAP 2024 were:
50.x: The BRAP 2024 reform points were organised around Simplification, Elimination, Digitisation and Decriminalisation.
50.tq: Direct recall of a four-part policy framework.
xs: BRAP **2024**'s **435** points follow **Simplification, Elimination, Digitisation and Decriminalisation** — option **(4)** is correct.
These are **state-specific** reform points, aimed at cutting and digitising procedures, not adding inspections or penalties.
xa: BRAP **2024** was the **7th edition**.
**DBRAP** extends reforms to **Tier-II** and **Tier-III** cities.
**Jan Vishwas** laws also pursue **decriminalisation**.

50.s: Which strategy most directly reflects the central approach of Make in India?
o: Replacing digital services with traditional services
Restricting manufacturing to wholly state-owned enterprises
Attracting foreign direct investment and global firms to manufacture in India
Promoting only domestic consumption without export orientation
50.x: Attracting FDI and global firms to establish manufacturing in India is the strategy most typical of Make in India.
50.tq: Match the initiative with its characteristic strategy rather than its general developmental effects.
xs: The most typical Make in India strategy is **attracting FDI and global firms to manufacture in India** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is not about state-only manufacturing or domestic-only consumption.
xa: Slogan: "**Make in India for the World**".
**New Sectors** pillar opened **FDI** in defence, insurance, medical devices.
EoDB and PLI aim to join global value chains (**"China+1"**).

50.s: The World Bank's Doing Business rankings were meant mainly to guide which of the following?
50.x: Per the APPSC-GS 2019 key, the Doing Business rankings mainly guide foreign investors on the ease of doing business in a country. They are not meant for consumers, election bodies or monetary policy.
xs: Doing Business rankings mainly guided **foreign investors** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS **2019**).
They were not tools for consumers, election bodies or central banks.
xa: The report was conceptualised by the **IFC**, the World Bank Group's private-sector arm.
It had **10** parameters, from **starting a business** to **resolving insolvency**.
India's rank improved from **142** to **63**.

50.s: Which of the following is a reform credited with improving India's Ease of Doing Business?
o: Removal of all foreign ownership restrictions
50.x: Faceless assessment is a credited EoDB reform; removal of all foreign ownership restrictions, nationalisation and PSU expansion are not EoDB reforms.

50.s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Make in India — Manufacturing and investment hub
Digital India — Digital infrastructure, services and empowerment
50.x: Skill India aims at skilling youth for jobs, not real-time digital payments. Digital India, Make in India and Startup India are correctly matched with their respective objectives.
50.tq: Find the one objective wrongly transferred from a different digital initiative.
xs: **Skill India — Real-time digital payments** is wrongly matched — option **(1)** is the answer.
**Skill India** (**15 July 2015**) is about **skilling the workforce**.
**Digital India** = digital infrastructure, services, literacy; **Startup India** = start-up ecosystem; **Make in India** = manufacturing hub.
xa: ⚠ **Digital India** **1 July 2015** vs **Skill India** **15 July 2015**.
**Startup India**: **16 Jan 2016** (National Startup Day).
**Make in India**: **25 Sept 2014**.

50.s: Which of the following missions was launched first?
50.x: Make in India came on 25 September 2014, before Digital India (1 July 2015), Skill India (15 July 2015) and Startup India (16 January 2016).
xa: ⚠ Digital India precedes Skill India by two weeks — the classic trap.
**16 Jan** = **National Startup Day**.
DPIIT-recognised startups: **502** (2016) → **2.47 lakh** (**12 Aug 2026**).

50.s: When was the National Manufacturing Policy (NMP) released by the Government of India?
50.x: The Government of India has released the National Manufacturing Policy (NMP) on 4 November, 2011 with the objective of enhancing the share of manufacturing in GDP to 25% within a decade and creating 100 million jobs. NMP aims to increase manufacturing sector growth to 12-14% over the medium term and to enhance global competitiveness of Indian manufacturing through appropriate policy support. It also seeks to empower rural youth by imparting necessary skill sets to make them employable.

50.s:
Consider the objectives of National Manufacturing Policy, 2011 and select correct answer by using code given below :
1. To increase manufacturing sector growth to 12-14 percent over the medium turn.
2. To create 100 million additional jobs by 2025 in manufacturing sector.
3. To enhance global competitiveness of Indian manufacturing through appropriate policy support.
4. To increase manufacturing exports at the rate of 25 percent per annum during XII Plan period.
Which one of the following is NOT a pillar of Atmanirbhar Bharat?
50.x: The five pillars are Economy, Infrastructure, System, Vibrant Demography and Demand. Privatisation is not listed as one of these pillars.
50.tq: Find the odd policy term that does not belong to the stated five-pillar framework.
xs: **Privatisation** is not a pillar of Atmanirbhar Bharat — option **(2)** is the answer.
The five pillars: **Economy**, **Infrastructure**, **System**, **Vibrant Demography**, **Demand**.
xa: The **May 2020** package was ~**Rs 20 lakh crore** (~**10%** of GDP).
**Vocal for Local** is linked with Make in India.
Make in India links with '**Vocal for Local**' and "Make in India for the World".

50.s: Ease of Doing Business ranking for the States in India is released by :
o: Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal
50.x: The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India releases Ease of Doing Business (EoDB) rankings for States and Union Territories in India. These rankings are based on the implementation of the Business Reforms Action Plan (BRAP). The rankings are designed to measure and compare the progress of states in implementing business reforms aimed at streamlining processes, reducing compliance burdens, and promoting transparency. The rankings aim to encourage competition and improvement among States/UTs in creating a businessfriendly environment.

50.s: According to recent data released by Indian Cellular Association (ICA), India has acquired what position in the world in producing mobile phones?
50.x: According to data released by Indian Cellular Association (ICA) in April 2018, India became the second largest mobile phone producer in the world after China in 2017. As per the data of 2025-26, India has retained this position.

50.s: Recently, India's first 'National Investment and Manufacturing Zone' was proposed to be set up in
50.x: National Investment and Manufacturing Zones (NIMZs) are one of the important instruments of the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011. NIMZs are envisaged as large areas of developed land with the requisite eco-system for promoting world class manufacturing activity. NIMZs differ from SEZs in size, levels of infrastructure planning, governance structures governing regulatory procedures, and exit policies. India's first 'National Investment and Manufacturing Zone' was proposed for Prakasam (Andhra Pradesh).

50.s: Which two States have been jointly ranked first in the ease of doing business ranking issued by the World Bank and DIPP in October 2016?
50.x: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana has been jointly ranked first in the 2016 All-India State/Union Territory-wise ease of doing business rankings issued by the World Bank and DIPP (Now DPIIT) in October 2016, while 2015’s topper Gujarat slipped to the third spot. In 2018 rankings, Andhra Pradesh ranked highest while Telangana and Haryana stood at 2nd and 3rd place respectively. Andhra Pradesh has topped again in the Ease of doing business index in 2019, followed by Uttar Pradesh and Telangana. The Ministry of Commerce and Industry released the assessment of States/UTs based on implementation of Business Reforms Action Plan (BRAP) for the year 2020 on 30 June, 2022. In this assessment Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Punjab, Tamil Nadu and Telangana were the Top Achievers based on implementation of BRAP.

50.s: What is the position of India in manufacturing of mobile phones in 2023?
Recently, India’s first ‘National Investment and Manufacturing Zone’ was proposed to be set up in :
50.x: National Investment & Manufacturing Zones (NIMZs) are one of the important instruments of National Manufacturing Policy, 2011. NIMZs are envisaged as large areas of developed land with the requisite eco-system for promoting world class manufacturing activity. So far, four NIMZs (Upto February, 2023) namely Prakasam District (Andhra Pradesh), Sangareddy District (Telangana), Kalinganagar, Jajpur District (Odisha) and Hyderabad Pharma City NIMZ in Rangareddy District (Telangana) have been accorded final approval while total 24 NIMZs (including 8 NIMZs along the Delhi-Mumbai Industrial Corridor region) have been accorded in-principle approval.

50.s: Which one of the following is not an initiative for industrial development?
50.x: Make in India, Ease of Doing Business and Start-up India are initiatives to facilitate investment and development of manufacturing and industrial sector in India. While Digital India is not an initiative for industrial development. It is a flagship programme of the Government of India with a vision to transform India into a digitally empowered society and knowledge economy. Digital India consists of three core components : the development of secure and stable digital infrastructure, delivering government services digitally, and universal digital literacy.

50.s: Make in India was launched on:
50.x: Make in India was launched on 25 September 2014. Digital India came on 1 July 2015, Skill India on 15 July 2015 and Startup India on 16 January 2016.

50.s: The nodal ministry for Make in India is the:
50.x: Make in India is steered by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.

50.s: How many champion services sectors are there under Make in India 2.0?

50.x: The 15 manufacturing sectors are under DPIIT, while the 12 services sectors are under the Department of Commerce.

50.s: The National Manufacturing Policy, 2011 aimed to create how many jobs?
50.x: NMP 2011 targeted 100 million jobs; 143 million by 2035 is the National Manufacturing Mission target.

50.s: The annual manufacturing growth target of the National Manufacturing Policy, 2011 was:
50.x: NMP 2011 aimed at 12-14 per cent manufacturing growth along with a 25 per cent GDP share.

50.s: Which NIMZ in Andhra Pradesh received final approval in 2016?
50.x: Chittoor and Prakasam got in-principle approval in 2013, but only Prakasam got final approval in 2016.

o: Incentives limited to the electronics sector alone
A sector-, location- and technology-neutral approach

50.s: Which of the following was launched on 15 July 2015?
50.x: Skill India was launched on 15 July 2015; Digital India came two weeks earlier on 1 July 2015.

50.s: The National Logistics Policy was launched in:
50.x: The National Logistics Policy came in September 2022; October 2021 is PM GatiShakti and December 2021 the India Semiconductor Mission.

50.s: The National Policy on Electronics was announced in:
50.x: The National Policy on Electronics was announced on 20 February 2019.

50.s: The PLI scheme of 2020 covers how many sectors?
50.x: The PLI scheme covers 14 sectors with an outlay of ₹1.97 lakh crore.

50.s: PLI-Auto requires a minimum domestic value addition of:

50.x: PM E-DRIVE replaced FAME-II (2019-24); PLI-LSEM was replaced by the Mobile Phone Manufacturing Scheme.

Consider the following statements about the PLI scheme:

2. Coal mining equipment is one of its sectors.
3. Its incentive is paid on incremental sales of goods made in India.

50.s: The Tata OSAT unit approved under the India Semiconductor Mission is located at:

50.s: India's first semiconductor-fab SEZ is at:
50.x: The Tata Electronics-PSMC wafer fab at Dholera, Gujarat is India's first semiconductor-fab SEZ.

50.s: About what share of mobile phones used in India are made in India?
50.x: About 99.2 per cent of mobile phones used in India are made in India.

50.s: Under the sunset clause, Section 10AA benefits go only to SEZ units operational by:
50.x: Only SEZ units operational by 30 June 2020 get the Section 10AA tax benefits.

50.s: Under the SEZ Act, 2005, who can set up an SEZ?
o: Central Government, State Government or any person
50.x: An SEZ can be set up by the Central Government, a State Government or any person, including private, joint or foreign developers.

50.s: The Atmanirbhar Bharat package of May 2020 was worth about:
50.x: The May 2020 Atmanirbhar Bharat package was about ₹20 lakh crore, roughly 10 per cent of GDP.

50.s: India's logistics cost, which PM GatiShakti and the National Logistics Policy aim to cut, was historically about:
50.x: India's logistics cost was historically 13-14 per cent of GDP, which these policies seek to reduce.

50.s: The World Bank's Doing Business report was discontinued in:
50.x: Doing Business was discontinued in 2021 over data irregularities and ethics concerns; DB 2020 was the last edition.

50.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the 10 Doing Business parameters?
50.x: Getting electricity, resolving insolvency and protecting minority investors are among the 10 parameters; ease of living is not.

50.s: India's rank in the World Bank's Doing Business 2018 report was:
50.x: India rose to 100 in DB 2018, a jump of 30 places; it was 142 in DB 2015 and 63 in DB 2020.

50.s: The World Bank's Doing Business report was conceptualised with:
50.x: Doing Business was published by the World Bank Group and conceptualised with the IFC.

50.s: Which of the following was among India's weakest Doing Business indicators?
50.x: Enforcing contracts and registering property were India's weakest indicators.

50.s: B-READY, the successor of Doing Business, rests on how many pillars?
50.x: B-READY has 3 pillars; Doing Business had 10 parameters and the NITI Investment Friendliness Index has 8 pillars.

50.s: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 is credited with improving which EoDB area?
50.x: IBC 2016 is credited with improving resolving insolvency.

50.s: GST (2017) is credited with improving which EoDB area?
50.x: GST, faceless assessment and e-filing are credited for paying taxes and a unified market.

50.x: Jan Vishwas 2.0 covered 16 Acts and 355 provisions, of which 288 were decriminalised.

50.s: SPICe+ (2020), a reform for starting a business, integrates how many services?
50.x: SPICe+ integrates 11 services of 3 ministries.

50.s: Despite the four labour codes, about what share of India's workers remain informal?
50.x: Over 80 per cent of workers remain informal despite the four labour codes.

50.s: The AP Single Desk Portal was launched in:
50.x: The AP Single Desk Portal was launched in April 2015.

50.s: In 2024-25, what share of approvals on the AP Single Desk Portal was given within SLA?
50.x: 16,458 of 16,783 approvals (99.20 per cent) were given within SLA in 2024-25.

50.s: The Asian Competitiveness Institute, which ranks Indian States on ease of doing business, is based in:
50.x: The ACI is in Singapore and ranks States on three 'ABC' pillars.

50.s: In the ACI EDB Index 2018, which State ranked first?
50.x: Andhra Pradesh ranked first (up from 5th in 2016), Maharashtra second and Delhi third.

50.s: In BRAP 2019 (released September 2020), which State ranked second?
50.x: In BRAP 2019, AP was 1st, Uttar Pradesh 2nd (up from 12th) and Telangana 3rd.

50.s: How many States were Top Achievers in BRAP 2020?
50.x: BRAP 2020 had no numeric ranks; 7 States, including AP, were Top Achievers.

10.s: The first phase of liberalization was initiated in India under the regime of :
10.x: The first phase of liberalization was initiated in India in 1991 with the adoption of new economic policy under the regime of Prime Minister P.V. Narsimha Rao.

10.s: Which statement correctly relates Rajiv Gandhi's reforms to those of 1991?
o: Liberalisation began in the 1980s, but the 1991 reforms were far more comprehensive.
Rajiv Gandhi introduced the complete 1991 package.
The 1991 reforms merely continued an unchanged policy of the 1960s.
10.x: Some liberalisation began under Rajiv Gandhi in the 1980s, but the 1991 programme was much more comprehensive.
xa: 1980s growth broke the **Hindu rate** and touched **5.5%** — but it was **debt-fuelled**.
The 1991 PM was **P.V. Narasimha Rao** (took office **21 June 1991**).
⚠ **Rao** = father of reforms (PM); **Manmohan Singh** = architect of liberalisation (FM).

10.s: The expression 'Licence-Permit-Quota Raj', used to describe the pre-1991 regime of controls in India, was coined by:
10.x: C. Rajagopalachari coined 'Licence-Permit-Quota Raj' to criticise the control regime that was a long-term cause of the 1991 crisis. Nehru led the planned economy, Mahalanobis designed the Second Plan model, and Raja Chelliah headed the 1991 tax reform committee.
10.tq: Licence Raj term = Rajaji (C. Rajagopalachari).
xs: **C. Rajagopalachari** coined **Licence-Permit-Quota Raj** — option **(2)**.
**Raja Chelliah** headed the **tax** reform committee, not the term's author.
xa: The control regime (incl. **MRTP 1970**) was a long-term cause of the crisis.
1991 **Industrial Policy** abolished licensing for all but **5-6** industries.
MRTP **asset limits** were abolished in 1991.

10.s: Who is widely called the 'father of Indian economic reforms'?
10.x: P.V. Narasimha Rao is called the father of Indian economic reforms; Dr. Manmohan Singh is regarded as the architect of liberalisation.
xa: The era is called the "**Manmohan-Rao era**".
Rao took office on **21 June 1991**.
Some liberalisation had begun under **Rajiv Gandhi** in the **1980s**.

10.s: The Narasimham Committee of 1991 was primarily concerned with:
o: Industrial licensing and foreign trade quotas
Financial-sector reform, including interest deregulation and private banks
10.x: The Narasimham Committee focused on financial-sector reform, including interest deregulation and the development of private banks such as HDFC and ICICI.
10.tq: Distinguish the committee's sector from neighbouring reform committees.
xs: The **Narasimham Committee** (**1991**) dealt with **financial-sector reform** — interest deregulation and private banks — option **(3)**.
Private banks such as **HDFC** and **ICICI** were allowed.
**Insurance** reform was the **Malhotra Committee** (1993).
xa: ⚠ **Narasimham** = banking; **Chelliah** = tax; **Rangarajan** = disinvestment; **Malhotra** = insurance.
RBI shifted from **regulator to facilitator**.
**SEBI** became statutory in **1992**.

10.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: C. Rangarajan Committee – Disinvestment of PSUs
R.N. Malhotra Committee – Capital account convertibility
10.x: Rangarajan dealt with PSU disinvestment, Chelliah with tax reforms, Malhotra with insurance and Tarapore with capital account convertibility.
xa: **Narasimham Committee** (1991) = banking/financial sector.
⚠ **Full capital account convertibility** is still not adopted.
**100% FDI in insurance** is now in place (May 2026).

10.s: Which statement correctly relates liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation?
o: Globalisation is an outcome of liberalisation and privatisation, with outsourcing as a major feature.
Privatisation is the outcome of globalisation, and liberalisation means only export promotion.
Liberalisation and privatisation prohibit international technology flows.
Globalisation is independent of both, and outsourcing is unrelated to it.
10.x: Globalisation is described as the outcome of liberalisation and privatisation, and outsourcing is its major feature.
xa: Globalisation = integration with the world through **trade, capital, technology and labour** flows.
IT/outsourcing boom cushioned the CAD; **1,800+ GCCs** earned **$38.25 bn** of services exports (July 2026).
Indian MNCs: **Tata, Reliance, Infosys, Sun Pharma** went global.

10.s: After the financial-sector reforms, the RBI was expected to shift from being a regulator to being a:
10.x: The reforms envisaged the RBI moving from direct regulation towards facilitation of the financial system.
xa: **SEBI** became statutory in **1992**.
**Narasimham Committee**: interest deregulation, private banks (HDFC, ICICI).
Stabilisation used **tight monetary policy by RBI** to control inflation.

10.s: The sharp reduction in the list of industries reserved for the public sector in 1991 is known as
10.x: Dereservation means reducing the industries reserved for the public sector and opening them to private participation.
10.tq: Discriminate between similarly prefixed reform terms.
xs: Cutting industries reserved for the public sector is **dereservation** — option **(3)**.
It happened in **1991**, opening those industries to private players.
**Disinvestment** = sale of PSU equity — a different privatisation measure.
xa: Sick units: **BIFR** set up to revive them.
**New PSE Policy (2021)** made strategic disinvestment a major reform.

10.s: Reduction of tariffs and quantitative restrictions under the 1991 reforms is termed:
10.x: Import liberalisation cut tariffs and QRs; de-licensing ended licensing, disinvestment sold PSE equity, globalisation integrated India with the world.
n: De-licensing is associated with international trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Deregulation is associated with foreign investment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Import liberalisation is associated with multinational corporation participation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Liberalisation promotes greater market orientation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
xa: Average import tariff fell from **~125%** (late 1980s) to **~30%** (early 2000s).
Remaining **QRs removed April 2001**.
⚠ LERMS **1992** → unified rate **1993** → convertibility **1994** → WTO **1995**.

10.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
10.x: Liberalisation reduces domestic controls through industrial de-licensing, import deregulation and private-sector expansion.
n: Liberalisation removes or reduces domestic controls. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Liberalisation focuses on removing state controls. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Import deregulation is an instrument of Liberalisation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Private-sector expansion is an aspect of Liberalisation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]

10.s: LPG reforms were associated with which of the following?
10.x: The LPG reforms opened the door to multinational corporations. Licensing, the joint sector and public-sector dominance belong to the pre-1991 policies.
10.tq: Discriminate pre- and post-1991 features.
n: LPG reforms were associated with multinational corporations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
xs: **LPG reforms** were associated with **multinational corporations** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Globalisation facilitated **expanded entry and participation of MNCs**.
**Industrial licensing**, the **joint sector** and **public-sector** dominance belong to pre-1991 policy.
xa: Indian MNCs that went global: **Tata, Reliance, Infosys, Sun Pharma**.
Licensing abolished for all but **5-6** industries.
**Navratnas (1996)**: **9** PSUs; **Miniratnas**: **97** profit-making PSUs.

10.s: Which one of the following represents a long-term cause rather than an immediate trigger of the 1991 crisis?
o: Persistent fiscal profligacy and rising fiscal deficit
10.x: Persistent fiscal profligacy was a long-term domestic structural cause. The other three were immediate external-financing or geopolitical pressures.
10.tq: Find the structural domestic factor among short-term external shocks.
xs: **Persistent fiscal profligacy** is a **long-term cause** — option **(3)**.
**NRI deposit flight**, the **Gulf War** and **foreign banks stopping lending** were **immediate triggers**.
xa: Other long-term causes: **Licence-Permit-Quota Raj** (MRTP 1970), **PSU losses**, **weak exports**.
⚠ **9.4%** = Centre + States; **8.4%** = Centre's GFD.

10.s: The 1991 New Economic Policy was introduced primarily to address which of the following?
o: Dominance of the public and joint sectors
Decline in agriculture's share of GDP
10.x: The 1991 New Economic Policy was a response to a severe balance-of-payments crisis, when foreign reserves covered only about two weeks of imports.
10.tq: Recall the trigger for the 1991 reforms.
n: The 1991 New Economic Policy was introduced to address the severe 1991 Balance of Payments crisis. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
xs: The **1991 New Economic Policy** was introduced to address the **severe 1991 Balance of Payments crisis** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Forex reserves had fallen to **$975 million (June 1991)** — about **two weeks** of imports.
SEZs, joint-sector dominance and agriculture's share were not its trigger.
xa: Crisis indicators: **high inflation**, **low forex reserves**, **large fiscal deficit** (APPSC 2025).
Triggers: **Gulf War (Aug 1990)**, political instability, **NRI deposit flight**.
**67 tonnes of gold** were pledged to the **Bank of England and UBS**.

10.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the causes of India's 1991 balance of payments crisis?
o: The Gulf War led to a doubling of oil prices.
Current account deficits had been financed by foreign borrowing since the 1980s.
Remittances from the Gulf region rose sharply.
10.x: Gulf remittances dried up rather than rising; the other three were causes of the crisis.
xa: Other trigger: **collapse of the Soviet Union** (**Dec 1991**) — a lost trading partner.
Political instability: **two changes of government** Dec 1989 - June 1991.
Long-term cause: **fiscal profligacy** — GFD **5.4%** (1981-82) to **8.0%** (1989-90).

10.s: The foreign exchange reserves of India in June 1991 were approximately
o: $975 million, sufficient for about two weeks of imports
$69.3 billion, sufficient for about one year of imports
$22.8 billion, sufficient for about three months of imports
$9.75 billion, sufficient for about six months of imports
10.x: India's foreign exchange reserves stood at approximately $975 million in June 1991, covering only about two weeks of imports.
10.tq: Match the crisis-year figure with its associated coverage period.
xs: Reserves were **$975 million** in **June 1991** — enough for about **two weeks** of imports — option **(1)**.
**$69.3 bn** was external debt; **$22.8 bn** was external debt in **1983-84**.
xa: Reserves later rose to **$701.4 bn** (~**11 months** of import cover).
⚠ Forex cover: **2 weeks (1991)** vs **over 11 months** now.
In **May 2026** the PM urged citizens to cut fuel, gold and foreign-travel spending — a step not taken even in **1991**.

10.s: The gross fiscal deficit of the Centre in 1990-91 was approximately
10.x: The Centre's gross fiscal deficit was 8.4 per cent of GDP in 1990-91, compared with 6.1 per cent in 1980-81. The 9.4 per cent figure refers to the combined Centre and States figure.
10.tq: Distinguish the Centre-only figure from the combined Centre and States figure.
xs: The Centre's GFD in 1990-91 was **8.4 per cent** of GDP — option **(4)**.
⚠ **9.4%** is the **combined Centre + States** figure; **3.2%** is the trade deficit/CAD share.
xa: Inflation about **12%**; GDP growth **1.1%**.
Govt internal debt reached **53%** of GDP (1990-91).

10.s: The Indian rupee became convertible on the current account in:
10.x: The rupee became market-determined in 1993 and current-account convertible in 1994; capital-account convertibility stayed partial.
xa: ⚠ Devaluation **1991** → market rate **1993** → convertibility **1994**.
**LERMS (March 1992)**: dual rate — **60%** at market rate, **40%** at official rate.
**WTO** founding member **1995**; **FERA → FEMA** in **1999**.

10.s: Which of the following was NOT a fiscal policy measure of 1991?
10.x: The tax net was widened, not contracted; expenditure control, subsidy cuts and better tax collection were part of the package.
xa: Also included: discipline in managing **Centre and State funds**.
Lower peak income/corporate tax rates (**Chelliah**).
Fiscal deficit (Centre + States) had reached **9.4%** of GDP.

10.s: Under the post-1991 liberalisation measures, tax rates were ____ and the tax base was ____.
10.x: Tax rates were cut and the base widened, alongside scrapping MRTP asset limits, deregulating interest rates and allowing private banks.
xa: **SEBI** became statutory in **1992**.
Industrial licensing abolished except for a few (**5-6**) industries.
Liberalisation = **reduction of state control**.

10.s: After the 1991 delicensing, delicensed firms got:
o: Freedom in pricing but curbs on expansion
Price controls and curbs on expansion
Price controls but no curbs on expansion
Freedom in pricing and no curbs on expansion
10.x: Delicensed firms gained pricing freedom and faced no expansion curbs; licensing stayed only for a few (5-6) industries.
xa: MRTP asset limits, pre-entry restrictions and merger controls were abolished.
Telecom, banking and civil aviation were **reshaped** by reforms.
**Dereservation**: public-sector-reserved industries cut sharply in **1991**.

10.s: Under the Industrial Policy of 1991, the MRTP asset limits were:
10.x: The 1991 policy abolished MRTP asset limits, pre-entry restrictions and merger/expansion controls.

10.s: How many public sector undertakings were given Navratna status when the scheme was introduced?
10.x: The Navratna scheme initially covered nine PSUs, distinct from the 97 Miniratnas.
10.fixed: Navratna scheme (9 PSUs) was introduced in 1997, not 1996

10.s: India removed its remaining quantitative restrictions on imports in:
10.x: The remaining QRs went in April 2001; average tariffs fell from about 125% to about 30% and general customs duty was later cut to 10%.
xa: Import licensing was dismantled; **EXIM scrips** and quotas removed.
**DGFT** changed from controller of trade to "**facilitator**".
Strategy shifted from **import substitution to export promotion**.

10.s: Disinvestment of PSU equity under the 1991 reforms was first undertaken mainly to:
10.x: Disinvestment was first used to bridge the fiscal deficit and only later for efficiency; nationalisation was not part of the NEP.
xa: **Dereservation** (1991) opened public-sector-reserved industries to private players.
**New PSE Policy (2021)** for **Atmanirbhar Bharat**.

10.s: After globalisation, India's imports:
10.x: Globalisation expanded trade and technology access, but imports grew faster than exports.
xa: India's world trade share had fallen from **1.78%** (1950) to **0.6%** (1995).
IT/outsourcing boom **cushioned the CAD**.
CAD peaked at **4.8%** of GDP (**FY13**).

10.s:
Assertion (A): Civil aviation saw the entry of private airlines after the 1991 reforms.
Reason (R): Power distribution underwent complete and uncontested privatisation.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
10.x: Private airlines did enter civil aviation, but power-distribution privatisation remained debated, so R is false.
xa: **Telecom** and **banking** were also reshaped.
**Railways** remained a state monopoly.
Source of the slow-sector notes: **LENS, May 2026**.

10.s: Which of the following was NOT an element of the Washington Consensus?
10.x: Privatisation, deregulation and property rights were among the ten Washington Consensus rules; expanding import quotas was not.
xa: It is blamed for the **1997** and **2008** crises.
It is now seen as **obsolete** (14 Mar 2026).
SAP conditions also included **currency devaluation** and **austerity**.

10.s: About how many tonnes of gold in all did India pledge during the 1991 BoP crisis?
10.x: About 67 tonnes were pledged to the Bank of England and UBS, along with an IMF loan and devaluation.

10.s: The principal immediate purpose of the 1991 rupee devaluation was to:
o: Increase the price of Indian exports in foreign markets
Make Indian exports cheaper and help correct the balance of payments
Finance the fiscal deficit through currency expansion
10.x: Devaluation makes domestic goods relatively cheaper for foreign buyers and was undertaken to help address the balance of payments crisis.
10.tq: Apply the economic effect of devaluation rather than recall only its date.
xs: Devaluation aimed to **make Indian exports cheaper** and **correct the balance of payments** — option **(3)**.
This was the **APPSC 2024** key.
Option (1) is the opposite effect; capital account convertibility is still **not** full.
xa: Devaluation: about **20%**, in two steps on **1 and 3 July 1991**.
**Currency devaluation** is a standard **SAP** conditionality.
Strategy shift: **import substitution → export promotion**.

10.s: Stabilisation measures under the New Economic Policy are essentially:
10.x: Stabilisation corrects short-term imbalances (fiscal deficit, inflation, BoP) through demand management; structural adjustment is the supply side.
xa: Lead institutions: **IMF** (stabilisation) and **World Bank (IBRD)** (structural adjustment).
Stabilisation tools: subsidy cuts, **tight monetary policy** by RBI, **rupee devaluation**.
Some UPSC notes also list trade liberalisation under stabilisation.

10.s: Structural Adjustment Programmes are best described as
o: short-term central-bank operations for controlling currency circulation
domestic programmes confined to agricultural subsidies
WTO agreements dealing exclusively with customs valuation
IMF and World Bank loan packages intended to reduce fiscal imbalances and adjust economies for long-term growth
10.x: SAPs are IMF and World Bank loan packages designed to reduce fiscal imbalances and promote long-term economic adjustment and growth.
10.tq: Identify the defining combination of institutions, loans and long-term objectives.
xs: SAPs are **IMF/World Bank loan packages** to **reduce fiscal imbalances** and **adjust economies for long-term growth** — option **(4)**.
This is the **APPSC 2018** definition.
xa: Conditions: **austerity, privatisation, deregulation**, **currency devaluation**, better tax collection.
SAP outcomes raised poverty in the Global South — growth fell from **3.2% to 0.7%** a year.
The **Washington Consensus** (**10** rules) is now seen as obsolete.

10.s: Which plan began immediately after the phase of structural adjustment and macroeconomic stabilisation?
10.x: The Eighth Plan, covering 1992–97, began after structural adjustment and macroeconomic stabilisation.
10.tq: Link the plan period with the reform transition rather than with the preceding Annual Plans.
xs: The **Eighth Plan (1992-97)** began right after structural adjustment and macro-stabilisation — option **(2)**.
The **Sixth** and **Seventh** Plans saw rising deficits — average GFD **6.3%** and **8.2%**.
xa: Average growth **6.8%** from **1993-94**.

10.s: Which one of the following pairs correctly identifies the lead institutions associated with stabilisation and structural adjustment respectively?
10.x: Stabilisation is linked with the IMF, whereas structural adjustment is linked with the World Bank, particularly the IBRD.
10.tq: Test the institutional pairing by keeping the order of the two reform components fixed.
xs: **IMF** leads stabilisation; **World Bank (IBRD)** leads structural adjustment — option **(3)**.
Option (4) reverses them; the **WTO** (1995) is a trade body.
xa: Stabilisation = **short-term, demand side**; structural adjustment = **long-term, supply side**.
India received an **IMF loan** of about **$7 bn** in 1991.
India was a **WTO** founding member in **1995** (successor to **GATT, 1948**).

10.s: Structural adjustment under the 1991 reforms is:
10.x: Structural adjustment is long-term and supply-side, while stabilisation is short-term and demand-side.
n: Stabilisation is short-term in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
Stabilisation is demand-side in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
Structural adjustment is long-term in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
Structural adjustment is supply-side in nature. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
xa: Lead institution: stabilisation = **IMF**; structural adjustment = **World Bank (IBRD)**.
Stabilisation comes **first**; structural adjustment follows or runs alongside.
The **Eighth Plan (1992-97)** began right after structural adjustment and stabilisation.

10.s: Which of the following best describes free trade?
o: Reduction or removal of trade barriers
Provision of an internationally competitive environment
Creation of a level playing field for exports
10.x: Free trade means reducing or removing trade barriers such as tariffs and quotas. The other options are SEZ objectives.
10.tq: Discriminate free trade from SEZ aims.
n: Free trade involves the reduction or removal of trade barriers. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
xs: **Free trade** = the **reduction or removal of trade barriers** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The other options describe aims such as attracting investment and competitiveness, not the meaning of free trade.
xa: **Globalisation** involves the **reduction of import duties** on capital goods.
**Import substitution** gave way to **export promotion** after **1991**.
**WTO** founding member, **1995** — successor to **GATT** (**1948**, **23** countries).

10.s: Integration of the domestic economy with the world economy, with greater participation of MNCs, is called:

n: Globalisation integrates the domestic economy with the world economy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation integrates the domestic economy with the world economy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation facilitates expanded participation of Multinational Corporations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation occurs through trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation occurs through foreign direct investment capital. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation occurs through cross-border technology. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation facilitates technology flows. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation promotes greater global integration. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Globalisation facilitates expanded entry of Multinational Corporations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
xa: Globalisation also involves the **reduction of import duties on capital goods**.
**Liberalisation** and **privatisation** are strategies; **globalisation** is their outcome, with **outsourcing** a major feature.
**FERA → FEMA** (**1999**) was a globalisation measure.

10.s:
Arrange the following measures in the order in which they occurred during the initial 1991 reform sequence:
A. Industrial delicensing
B. Devaluation of the rupee
C. Removal of import quotas and EXIM scrips
D. Market-determined exchange rate

xs: Order: **B, A, C, D** — devaluation, delicensing, import quota removal, market rate — option **(1)**.
**Devaluation (July 1991)** came first; then **industrial delicensing**.
Then **MRTP** limits abolished and **EXIM scrips** and quotas removed; market rate in **1993**.
xa: ⚠ Devaluation **1991** → market rate **1993** → convertibility **1994**.
**LERMS** (March 1992) was the dual-rate bridge.
Remaining **QRs** were removed only in **April 2001**.

10.s: The Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS) was introduced in:
10.x: LERMS came in March 1992 (60% at market rate, 40% at official rate); a unified market rate followed in March 1993.
xa: ⚠ LERMS **1992** → unified rate **1993** → convertibility **1994** → WTO **1995** → FEMA **1999** → QRs removed **2001**.
The rupee was devalued about **20%** on **1 and 3 July 1991**.
Capital account is only **partly** convertible.

10.s: SEBI was given statutory status in:
10.x: SEBI received statutory status in 1992; FEMA replaced FERA in 1999.
xa: **LERMS** came in **March 1992**.
Current account convertibility: **1994**.
WTO founding member: **1995**.

10.s: The growth of India's IT and outsourcing exports after 1991 helped to:
10.x: IT and outsourcing generated services exports that helped cushion India's current account deficit.
xa: **1,800+ Global Capability Centres** earned **$38.25 bn** of services exports in **July 2026**.
CAD was **0.8%** of GDP in **H1 FY26**; peak **4.8%** (FY13).
**ES 2025-26**: persistent CAD = structural cause of India's **high cost of capital**.

10.s: India became a founding member of the WTO in:
10.x: India was a founding member of the WTO in 1995; the WTO succeeded GATT (1948).

10.s: Which of the following was a feature of the economic groundwork laid during the 1980s?
o: Complete abolition of all industrial licensing
Broad-banding of licences and easier imports of capital goods

10.tq: Distinguish preparatory 1980s measures from post-1991 reforms.
xs: The 1980s saw **broad-banding of licences** and **easier imports of capital goods** — option **(2)**.
Other 1980s steps: MRTP limit raised to **₹100 crore**; **FERA** eased.
Licensing was abolished (for all but **5-6** industries) only in **1991**; **FERA → FEMA** came in **1999**.
xa: This groundwork was under **Indira and Rajiv Gandhi** (**1984-89**).
Growth touched **5.5%**, breaking the Hindu rate, but was **debt-fuelled**.
⚠ **Full capital account convertibility** has still not been adopted.

10.s: Which of the following sets contains only structural adjustment measures?
o: Delicensing, tariff reduction and public-sector disinvestment
Subsidy cuts, tight money and devaluation
Inflation control, deficit reduction and tight money
Demand management, exchange control and subsidy expansion

xs: **Delicensing, tariff reduction and PSU disinvestment** are structural adjustment measures — option **(1)**.

Subsidy cuts, **tight money**, **devaluation** and deficit reduction are **stabilisation** tools.
xa: Structural tools also include **MRTP relaxation**, **FDI opening**, **QR removal**, export promotion.

The **Eighth Plan (1992-97)** began right after structural adjustment and stabilisation.

10.s: Which one of the following was NOT a feature of the 1991 New Economic Policy?
10.x: Nationalisation was not a feature of the 1991 New Economic Policy. The policy instead promoted delicensing, disinvestment and greater foreign investment.

xs: **Nationalisation** was NOT a 1991 NEP feature — option **(2)**.
It was the **odd one out** in **APPSC 2018**.
**Disinvestment**, **FDI liberalisation** and **delicensing** were NEP features.
xa: Also NOT NEP: strengthening the **License Raj/MRTP**, import substitution, more SSI reservation.
The economy was opened to foreign and private investment in **1991** (APPSC 2018).
FDI up to **100%** via automatic route in high-priority industries.

10.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the 1991 New Economic Policy?
o: Full capital-account convertibility was not adopted.
Devaluation, tariff cuts and removal of import quotas were external-sector measures.
FDI was liberalised through an automatic route in high-priority industries.
Demonetisation formed part of the 1991 reform package.
10.x: Demonetisation was not part of the 1991 package; India's demonetisations were in 1978 and 2016.
xa: ⚠ **FDI in retail and defence** opened only much later.
**100% FDI in insurance** is now in place (May 2026).
**Nationalisation** was the odd one out (APPSC 2018).

10.s: Which of the following reflects the post-1991 reform direction?
o: Raising tariffs to protect domestic producers
Expanding the list of industries reserved for the public sector
Inviting FDI and FPI, with IT and services exports acting as a cushion
Restricting foreign investment to joint ventures with PSUs

xa: Direction: **import substitution → export promotion**.
Economy moved to **enhanced global integration** (**PYQ 2025**).
**1,800+ GCCs** earned **$38.25 bn** of services exports in July 2026.

10.s: A persistent current account deficit has been identified as a structural cause of India's:
10.x: Persistent CAD has been identified as a structural cause of India's high cost of capital.
xa: CAD was **0.8%** of GDP in **H1 FY26**; peaked at **4.8%** (FY13).
In 1991 the CAD was **3.1-3.2%** of GDP.
IT/services exports help **cushion the CAD**.

10.s: Which adverse outcome was associated with the pattern of growth after economic reforms?

Agriculture received all investment and labour-intensive sectors disappeared.
Capital-intensive sectors generated more jobs than the available labour force.

**Agrarian neglect**: public investment in agriculture lagged.
**Crony capitalism**: gains concentrated among large, politically connected firms.

10.s: India's GDP growth in 1994–95 was about:
10.x: Growth was below 1% in 1991–92, about 5% in 1992–94 and 6.3% in 1994–95.
xa: Average growth: **5.18%** in the 1980s vs **6.8%** from **1993-94**.
GDP growth had been **1.1%** in **1990-91**.

10.s: Foreign-exchange reserves increased from approximately $975 million in 1991 to about
10.x: Foreign-exchange reserves rose from about $975 million in 1991 to approximately $701.4 billion, providing around 11 months of import cover as stated.
10.tq: Handle changes in units carefully when comparing a million figure with a billion figure.
xs: Reserves rose from **$975 million** (1991) to about **$701.4 billion** — option **(3)**.
That gives about **11 months** of import cover.
xa: ⚠ Forex cover: **2 weeks (1991)** vs **over 11 months** now.

10.s: Which one of the following sectors remained largely a state monopoly after the reforms?

10.tq: Find the sector that was comparatively untouched among reform-exposed industries.
xs: **Railways** remained a **state monopoly** — option **(2)**.

**Civil aviation**, **consumer electronics** and **telecom** saw private entry.
xa: Other slow sectors: **power distribution** (DISCOM privatisation debated), **agriculture**, **ports**.
**Civil aviation** saw **private airlines** enter.

10.s: Which of the following best illustrates the criticism of crony capitalism?
o: Agricultural investment increases uniformly across regions
Small firms exclusively control public-sector disinvestment
All firms receive equal access to public resources
Gains are concentrated among large, politically connected firms

xs: Crony capitalism = **gains concentrated among large, politically connected firms** — option **(4)**.

xa: **Jobless growth**: output rose faster than jobs.
**Agrarian neglect**: public investment in agriculture lagged.
**Washington Consensus** is now seen as obsolete (14 Mar 2026).

10.s: The criticism of 'jobless growth' made against India's post-1991 growth refers to a situation in which:
o: Unemployment was eliminated but output stagnated

xs: Jobless growth = **output rose faster than employment** — option **(1)**.
Many **graduates** end up in **gig work**.
Option (2) is the reverse of the criticism.
xa: Growth was concentrated in **capital-intensive** sectors.
Other criticisms: **agrarian neglect** and **crony capitalism**.
Some formalisation, but the **informal sector** stays dominant.

10.s: Which of the following statements about post-1991 trends is incorrect?
o: The share of agriculture in GDP increased enormously.
India's share in global exports grew.

n: Foreign Direct Investment inflows increased after 1991. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
India's foreign-exchange reserves expanded after 1991. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
India's share in global exports grew after 1991. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Agriculture's share in GDP did not increase enormously after the 1991 reforms. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
Agriculture's share in GDP declined after the 1991 reforms. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **the share of agriculture in GDP increased enormously** — so option **(2)** is the answer.

Options 1, 3, 4 are correct: **forex reserves expanded**, **India's share in global exports grew** and **FDI inflows increased**.

⚠ After 1991, **imports grew faster than exports** (APPSC 2025).

10.s: India's 1991 balance of payments crisis was marked by:
o: Stable prices, rising gold reserves and a balanced budget
High inflation, low foreign exchange reserves and a large fiscal deficit
Low inflation, high reserves and a fiscal surplus
High exports, falling public debt and a current account surplus

10.s: The strategy of export-led growth was introduced in India as part of:
o: The Second Five Year Plan's Mahalanobis model
The Green Revolution strategy of the 1960s

34.s: The theory of absolute advantage in international trade is associated with:

**Dumping** is exporting below home-market price or cost.
xa: **Comparative advantage** (**Ricardo**): specialise in the good with lower opportunity cost.
**Composition** = items traded; **direction** = country-wise/region-wise pattern.
**Volume** = money value of exports and imports.

34.s: According to the Marshall–Lerner condition, devaluation improves the trade balance when:
o: Only export demand is perfectly inelastic
The sum of export and import demand price elasticities is greater than one

xs: **Marshall-Lerner condition**: devaluation improves the trade balance only if export + import demand price elasticities sum to **greater than 1** — option **(2)**.

xa: **J-curve**: the trade balance first worsens after depreciation.
Depreciation makes **exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home**.

imports become costly and exports become cheaper

34.x: Imports and Exports both are included in foreign trade. So that, Balance of Payment can't be related alone with 'the merits of imports' or 'the merits of exports'. While the multiplier of foreign trade defines the amount by which the national income of a country will be raised by a unit increase in exports. Balance of payment is a account of international transactions (in which foreign trade is included) of any country for a specific time period (normally one year). o: Worsens only when exports become cheaper abroad
Remains unchanged because prices do not change

xs: **J-curve**: after depreciation the trade balance **first worsens** (import bills rise at once) and **improves only as volumes adjust** — option **(4)**.

xa: **Marshall-Lerner condition**: devaluation improves the balance only if export + import demand elasticities sum to **greater than 1**.
Depreciation makes **exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home**.

Capital Account includes international purchases and sales of assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
xa: **Full current account convertibility** came in **August 1994** (IMF **Article VIII**).
**LERMS** (**1992-93 Budget**): **40%** official / **60%** market rate; unified **1 March 1993**.
⚠ **FEMA** enacted **1999**, in force **1 June 2000**.

33.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Current Account includes visible trade involving exports and imports of goods.
Foreign Direct Investment is included in the Current Account.
The Capital Account includes foreign loans, FDI and portfolio investment.
The Current Account includes services, transfer payments and net income as invisible transactions.
33.x: Option B is incorrect: FDI is a capital flow, so it goes in the capital account with foreign loans and portfolio investment. The current account has goods, services, transfers and income.
33.tq: Sort each flow into current or capital account.
n: Current Account contains visible trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Visible trade consists of exports and imports of goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account contains invisible transactions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Invisible transactions consist of services, transfer payments, and net income. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Capital Account includes foreign loans. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Capital Account includes Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Capital Account includes portfolio investment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Foreign loans are included in the Capital Account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is included in the Capital Account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Portfolio investment is included in the Capital Account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Capital Account consists of cross-border capital movements. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **FDI is included in the Current Account** — so option **(2)** is the answer.
**FDI** is a capital movement and belongs to the **Capital Account**, with **foreign loans** and **portfolio investment**.
The **Current Account** has **visible trade** (goods) and **invisibles** — **services**, **transfer payments**, **net income**; options 1, 3, 4 are correct.
xa: **Private remittances** are in the Current Account (Invisibles → Private Transfers).
**ECB** and **NRI deposits** (FCNR(B)) are capital account items.
Purchase of foreign assets = **debit**; sale of Indian assets to foreigners = **credit**.

33.s: A Current Account Deficit occurs when payments exceed receipts from:
o: Goods, services, transfers and net income
33.x: The current account has visible trade plus invisibles (services, transfers, net income); a CAD means payments on these exceed receipts.
n: Current Account contains visible trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Visible trade consists of exports and imports of goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account contains invisible transactions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Invisible transactions consist of services, transfer payments, and net income. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account Deficit occurs when payments exceed receipts. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account Deficit concerns payments and receipts from goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account Deficit concerns payments and receipts from services. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account Deficit concerns payments and receipts from transfers. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account Deficit concerns payments and receipts from net income. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]

33.s: Which of the following is wrongly matched?
o: Balance of Trade – Exports of goods minus imports of goods
Balance of Payments – Complete record of transactions with the rest of the world
Capital Account – Includes the Balance of Trade
Current Account – Includes the Balance of Trade
33.x: The capital account covers cross-border capital movements; it is the current account that includes the Balance of Trade.
n: Balance of Trade equals exports of goods minus imports of goods. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Trade is part of the Current Account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
xa: Identity: Current + Capital + Financial Account + Net Errors & Omissions = **0**.
⚠ BoT = goods only; current account balance = goods **and services** + transfers.
**Overall BoP** positive → adds to reserves; negative → draws them down.

33.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Balance of Trade covers only goods or visible trade.
A Balance of Trade deficit occurs when goods imports exceed goods exports.
Balance of Trade is the complete record of economic transactions with the rest of the world.
A Balance of Trade surplus occurs when goods exports exceed goods imports.
33.x: Option C is incorrect: the full record of transactions with the world is the balance of payments. The balance of trade covers only goods.
n: Balance of Trade records only goods or visible trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #52-2 · pp 78-79]
A Balance of Trade surplus occurs when goods exports are greater than goods imports. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #52-2 · pp 78-79]
A Balance of Trade deficit occurs when goods imports are greater than goods exports. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #52-2 · pp 78-79]
Balance of Payments is the complete record of economic transactions with the rest of the world. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #52-2 · pp 78-79]
xs: The incorrect statement is that **Balance of Trade is the complete record** of transactions with the rest of the world — so option **(3)** is the answer.
That complete record is the **Balance of Payments**; the BoT covers **goods only** (**visible trade**).
Options 1, 2, 4 are correct: **BoT deficit** = goods imports > goods exports; **BoT surplus** = goods exports > goods imports.
xa: BoT is **part of the Current Account**.
**Balance of current account** = exports minus imports of goods **and services** + net unilateral transfers (APPSC-GS 2019 key).
Merchandise deficit FY 2025-26: **$337.3 bn**.

33.s: The balance of the current account is represented by which of the following expressions?
o: Exports minus imports of goods and services plus net primary and net secondary income
Capital inflows minus capital outflows plus errors and omissions
Exports and imports of goods only plus changes in foreign exchange reserves
Foreign direct investment plus portfolio investment minus external debt
33.x: The current-account balance equals exports minus imports of goods and services, plus net primary income and net secondary income.
33.tq: Reconstruct the identity by adding goods, services, primary income and secondary income.
xs: **Current account balance** = (exports − imports of **goods and services**) + **net primary income** + **net secondary income** — option **(1)**.
Capital flows and reserve changes (options 2, 3) belong to the capital account.
xa: APPSC-GS 2019 key: exports minus imports of goods **and services** + net unilateral transfers.
⚠ **BoT** = goods only; current account balance = goods **and services** + transfers.
A **CAD** must be financed by a capital account surplus or by drawing down reserves.

33.s: Why are FCNR(B) deposits and external commercial borrowings viewed cautiously in discussions on India's external-sector sustainability?
o: They are domestic tax receipts and do not affect the balance of payments.
They are temporary inflows, whereas FDI is expected to support a self-sustaining capital surplus.
They are permanent grants and therefore cannot reverse suddenly.
They are components of merchandise exports and reduce the trade deficit directly.
33.x: FCNR(B) and ECB inflows are considered temporary sources of financing. The preferred long-term basis for a self-sustaining capital surplus is stronger FDI.
33.tq: Distinguish temporary financing flows from durable investment flows.
xs: **FCNR(B)** and **ECB** inflows are **temporary**; **FDI** must drive a **self-sustaining capital surplus** — option **(2)**.
They are capital account items (**NRI deposits**, **external commercial borrowings**), not tax receipts, grants or merchandise exports.
xa: RBI's special **FCNR(B)** scheme drew **$127 bn** in NRI deposits — a possible **one-time comfort**.
FY26 **net FDI** was only **$6.9 bn**, down from **$44.0 bn** in **2020-21**.
Unlike **ECB/FPI** debt, **remittances** create **no repayment obligation**.

33.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the components of India’s foreign exchange reserves?
33.x: India’s foreign exchange reserves include Foreign Currency Assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve position in the IMF. Fiscal deficit deposits are not a reserve component.
33.tq: Find the non-member of a standard reserve-components list.
xs: **Fiscal deficit deposits** are not a reserve component — option **(2)**.
Reserves = **FCA**, **gold**, **SDRs** and the **Reserve Tranche Position** with the IMF.
xa: Reserves of **$701.4 bn** (**Jan 2026**) covered about **94%** of external debt.
A positive **overall BoP** adds to reserves.
**Reserve changes** are recorded in the capital account.

33.s: In India's Balance of Payments, software services exports are recorded under:
33.x: Software exports are invisible services in the current account; foreign loans go to the capital account and crude oil imports to merchandise trade.

Capital Account includes Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Capital Account includes portfolio investment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Foreign loans are included in the Capital Account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is included in the Capital Account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Portfolio investment is included in the Capital Account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Private remittances are included in the Current Account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]

33.s: The combined share of exports and imports of goods was 14.2 percent of GDP in 1990-91. In 2011-12 this share became :
33.x: As per the question period, option (b) was the correct answer. According to the World Bank data, the combined share of exports and imports of goods (total merchandise trade) is at 30.4 percent of GDP in 2023 and 29.7 percent in 2024.

33.s: In the balance of payments, shipping, banking, tourism and software are classified as:
33.x: These are non-factor services, part of invisibles along with primary (factor) income and transfers.
xa: Primary income = **interest, dividends, profits, wages**.
Secondary income = **remittances**, gifts, grants.
**Software services** are the largest part of the services surplus.

33.s: In the balance of payments, reserve changes and official borrowing are examples of:
33.x: Accommodating transactions such as reserve changes and official borrowing fill the gap left by autonomous transactions.
xa: The **monetary authority** is the ultimate financier of any BoP deficit.
**Overall BoP** negative → draws down reserves.
The **IMF** is the **last resort** when reserves cannot cover the deficit.

33.s: India recorded a current account surplus for three consecutive years during:
33.x: India had current account surpluses for three consecutive years from 2001-02 to 2003-04.
xa: **Q4 2023-24** also saw a **surplus**, due to a **surge in services exports**.
CAD peaked at **4.8% of GDP** in **FY13** (taper tantrum).

33.s: India's current account surplus in the fourth quarter of 2023-24 was driven by:
o: A sharp rise in gold imports
A rise in crude oil imports
33.x: The Q4 2023-24 surplus came from a surge in services exports, not from gold imports.
xa: **FY24 recovery**: moderation in merchandise exports + **sharp fall in imports**.

33.s: Which of the following is a cyclical, not structural, cause of India's current account deficit?
o: Dependence on imported oil and gold
33.x: A temporary global slowdown is cyclical; oil and gold imports, weak export competitiveness and the savings-investment gap are structural.
xa: Cyclical causes: **commodity shocks**, global slowdown, **rupee volatility**.
**May 2026**: PM appealed to cut **gold** and **fuel** consumption as the Iran conflict raised prices.
**FY26** merchandise deficit: **$337.3 bn**.

33.s: India's current account deficit reached its peak of about 4.8% of GDP in:
o: 1990-91, during the balance of payments crisis
FY24, after the fall in imports
H1 FY26, after the US tariffs
33.x: The CAD peaked at about 4.8% of GDP in FY13, the taper tantrum period. In the 1990-91 crisis it was about 3.1-3.2% of GDP. FY24 saw a recovery, with a surplus in Q4, and H1 FY26 had a CAD of only 0.8% of GDP.
xs: India's CAD peaked at **4.8% of GDP** in **FY13**, around the **taper tantrum** — option **(2)**.
The **1990-91** crisis CAD was **3.1-3.2%**; **FY24** saw a recovery; **H1 FY26** CAD was only **0.8%**.
xa: In the **2013** taper tantrum **Morgan Stanley** named India one of the **"Fragile Five"**.
**Rangarajan Committee**: sustainable CAD about **1.6% of GDP**.

33.s: Which of the following increases a country's external vulnerability?
o: Adequate forex reserves for import cover
Reduced reliance on volatile FPI and debt flows
33.x: Greater dependence on hot money increases vulnerability; adequate reserves, low short-term debt and less volatile flows are safeguards.
xa: Forex reserves **$701.4 bn** (**Jan 2026**) covered about **94%** of external debt.
US Fed hikes push **"hot money"** out of emerging markets.
**2013**: India among the **"Fragile Five"**.

33.s: During the 2013 taper tantrum, Morgan Stanley included India among the:
33.x: Morgan Stanley described India as one of the ‘Fragile Five’ during the 2013 taper tantrum because of external-sector vulnerability.
33.tq: Recall the distinctive group label associated with the external shock.
xs: During the **2013 taper tantrum**, **Morgan Stanley** named India one of the **"Fragile Five"** — option **(3)**.
The CAD then peaked at **4.8% of GDP** (**FY13**).
xa: In **May 2026** India's BoP was described as weak as the 2013 "Fragile Five" phase.
US Fed hikes → **hot money** exits → weaker rupee.
Safeguards: adequate reserves, low **short-term debt**.

33.s: Which of the following is an IMF lending window for balance of payments support?
33.x: The Extended Fund Facility (like the Stand-By Arrangement) is an IMF window; RBI's swap facilities and SRVAs are not IMF instruments.
xa: The IMF is the **last resort** for a BoP crisis.
India drew on the IMF in the **1991** crisis.
Reserves include **SDRs** and the **Reserve Tranche Position** with the IMF.

33.s: The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed approximately what proportion of the merchandise deficit?
33.x: The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed about two-thirds of the merchandise deficit. Remittances also acted as a cushion.
33.tq: Identify the comparative proportion rather than treating the services surplus as full financing of the merchandise deficit.
xs: The record **services surplus** of **$188.8 bn** in **FY25** financed about **two-thirds** of the merchandise deficit — option **(4)**.
**Remittances** were the other **cushion**.
xa: **Software services** = largest part of the services surplus.
Net services in **Q1 FY27**: **$51.6 bn**.
Net **primary income** is an outflow — **$10.5 bn** in Q1 FY27.

33.s: India was estimated to be the world's largest recipient of remittances in FY25. What was the approximate amount of remittances and their share in India's GDP, respectively?
33.x: India received approximately $135.4 billion in remittances in FY25, equivalent to about 3.5% of its GDP.
33.tq: Use the paired numerical figures and distinguish the annual estimate from other remittance measures.
xs: India, the **world's largest recipient**, got **$135.4 billion** (**3.5%** of GDP) in **FY25** — option **(1)**.
**$188.8 bn** is the **services surplus**; **$110.47 bn** and **$87.55 bn** are **workers' remittances** for FY26 and the year before.
xa: ⚠ **$135.4 bn** (FY25 total) vs **$110.47 bn** (FY26, workers' remittances — narrower measure).
Remittances exceed gross **FDI** inflows.

33.s: Which one of the following best explains the significance of remittances in India's external sector?
o: They are counter-cyclical and do not create a debt burden or repayment obligation.
They are classified entirely as foreign direct investment inflows.
They can be received only through external commercial borrowings.
They are pro-cyclical and create a direct repayment obligation for the recipient country.
33.x: Remittances are counter-cyclical and do not create a repayment obligation, unlike debt-related flows such as ECBs or certain portfolio liabilities.
33.tq: Apply the contrast between stable transfer inflows and debt-creating capital flows.
xs: Remittances are **counter-cyclical** and create **no debt burden / no repayment obligation** — option **(1)**.
Unlike **ECB/FPI** debt, they need no repayment; they are not FDI (they in fact **exceed gross FDI** inflows).
xa: Remittances = **$135.4 bn (3.5% of GDP)** in **FY25**.
Workers' remittances: **$110.47 bn** in **FY26**.
Critics warn of dependence on remittances + one-time deposit schemes instead of stable **FDI**.

33.s: A capital-account transaction involving the purchase of foreign assets by residents is recorded as:
o: A current-account credit because assets are goods
A debit because foreign exchange flows out for acquiring the assets
A credit because foreign exchange enters the country
33.x: Purchase of foreign assets by residents is a capital-account debit. Conversely, sale of Indian assets to foreigners is recorded as a credit.
33.tq: Follow the direction of the financial flow to distinguish a debit from a credit.
xs: **Purchase of foreign assets** by residents is a capital-account **debit** — foreign exchange flows out — option **(3)**.
**Sale of Indian assets to foreigners** is a **credit**.
xa: BoP is kept on **double-entry** bookkeeping, so it always balances in accounting terms.
Capital account items: **FDI**, **FPI/FII**, ADRs/GDRs, **ECB**, NRI deposits.
Surplus in one account = **deficit** in another.

33.s: How do increases in US Federal Reserve interest rates and a strong US dollar generally affect emerging markets such as India?
o: They automatically increase India’s net FDI
They raise US yields, attract hot money away from emerging markets and weaken the rupee
They reduce US yields and cause capital to flow into emerging markets
They eliminate exchange-rate volatility in emerging markets
33.x: US rate hikes and a strong dollar raise US yields, encouraging hot-money outflows from emerging markets and putting downward pressure on the rupee.
33.tq: Follow the capital-flow chain from interest-rate differential to exchange-rate pressure.
xs: **US Fed** rate hikes + a **strong dollar** → **higher US yields** → **"hot money" leaves emerging markets** → **weaker rupee** — option **(2)**.
So they do not lower US yields or raise India's FDI.
xa: **2013 taper tantrum**: India named one of the **"Fragile Five"**.
Safeguard: less reliance on volatile **FPI** and debt flows.
The rupee fell **~6.5%** against the dollar.

33.s: Which of the following is an expenditure-switching measure for correcting a BoP deficit?
33.x: Devaluation, like import tariffs and export incentives, switches demand from foreign to domestic goods; the others reduce expenditure.
xa: Other switching tools: **import quotas**, **import substitution**, **tourist incentives**.
Devaluation makes **home goods cheaper relative to foreign goods**.
⚠ Raising government spending is **NOT** a correction tool (PYQ 2025).

33.s: Which of the following is an expenditure-reducing measure for correcting a BoP deficit?
o: Tight monetary policy through higher interest rates
33.x: Tight monetary policy reduces aggregate expenditure and imports; devaluation, import substitution and export promotion are expenditure-switching.
xa: Other reducing tool: **tight fiscal policy** — cut government spending, raise taxes.
Financing tools: **foreign loans**, **IMF assistance**, encouraging FDI.
**Devaluation** = classic expenditure-switching policy.

33.s: A country whose reserves cannot cover its Balance of Payments deficit may approach which institution as lender of last resort?
33.x: The IMF assists a country that cannot cover its external deficit from its reserves and other sources.
xa: IMF lending windows: **Stand-By Arrangement** + **Extended Fund Facility**.
India drew on the IMF in the **1991** crisis.
**SDRs** and **Reserve Tranche Position** with the IMF are part of India's reserves.

33.s: The increase in import duty on gold, when used to reduce external pressure, is best classified as:
33.x: A higher import duty makes imported gold less attractive and helps switch demand towards domestic alternatives or away from imports. It is therefore an expenditure-switching measure.
33.tq: Trace how an import duty changes the relative attractiveness of foreign goods.
xs: A **gold import duty hike** is an **expenditure-switching** step — option **(1)**.
Import tariffs/duties switch demand away from imports; it is not a monetary or transfer item.
xa: **May 2026**: the PM appealed to cut **gold** and **fuel** consumption as the **Iran** conflict raised prices.
Oil (**>80%** imported) and gold are **structural** causes of the CAD.
Other switching tools: **devaluation**, **export incentives**.

33.s: Which of the following pairs relating to the IMF is wrongly matched?
o: Reserve Tranche – Unconditional drawing right from quota subscription
Rapid Financing Instrument – Rapid assistance for urgent BoP needs
Rapid Credit Facility – Concessional assistance to Low-Income Countries
IMF core function – Concessional lending to Low-Income Countries
