35.s: At present, in India, Foreign Direct Investment is completely prohibited in which sector?
Most recently, FDI has now opened in which of the following sectors in India?
35.x: In 2006, the Government eased policy for FDI in retail sector for the first time, allowing up to 51 percent FDI through the single-brand retail route. In 2012, the Government allowed up to 51 percent FDI in multi-brand retail. The Government also approved 100 percent FDI in single-brand retail, with the requirement of 30 percent local sourcing, preferably from MSMEs and cottage industries etc.

35.s: Which country among the following has the highest share in cumulative FDI inflows into India ?
In terms of the share in Foreign Direct Investment Equity inflows in India during 2016-17, which of the following countries is on the top?
35.x: In terms of the share in FDI equity inflows in India during 2016-17, top 3 countries were in following order : Mauritius > Singapore > Japan. As per the latest data, descending order of top investing countries' FDI equity inflows (in 2024-25) is : Singapore > Mauritius > USA > Netherlands > UAE.

35.s: India receives largest inflow of foreign capital in equity investment from :
35.x: As per the question period, Mauritius was the correct answer. But in recent years, India received largest inflow of foreign capital in equity investment from Singapore. Top 5 investing countries' FDI equity inflows in India in 2024-25 are as follows : 1. Singapore (US $ 14942 million), 2. Mauritius (US $ 8344 million), 3. USA (US $ 5457 million), 4. Netherlands (US $ 4620 million), 5. UAE (US $ 4345 million). In 2023-24, Top 5 investing countries in descending order in terms of FDI equity inflows in India were : Singapore > Mauritius > USA > Netherlands > Japan. However, in terms of cumulative FDI equity inflows from April, 2000 to December, 2025, share of top 5 investing countries in terms of FDI equity inflows in India are as follows (In descending order) : Singapore (24.79%), Mauritius (23.82%), USA (10.10%), Netherlands (7.16%) and Japan (6.13%).

35.s:
Given below are two statements, one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other as Reason (R).
Assertion (A) : During 2023-24, Singapore emerged as the largest source of FDI to India.
Reason (R) : The India-Mauritius Tax Treaty amendment has brought a major shift in countries as major sources of FDI to India.
Select the correct answer from the codes given below:
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct
35.x: Singapore became India's top Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) source, surpassing Mauritius, largely due to the India-Mauritius tax treaty amendment that reduced the attractiveness of routing investments through Mauritius. The amended treaty introduced clauses to curb tax avoidance and increased tax rates on certain income, shifting investors to more favourable jurisdictions like Singapore. Singapore is a preferred alternative due to its status as a financial hub and favourable tax environment. Consequently, Singapore has been India's leading FDI source for several years, including the fiscal year 2023-24 and 2024-25, when it contributed significantly to India's record inflows. Hence, both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

35.s: In the last one decade, which one among the following sectors has attracted the highest Foreign Direct Investment inflows into India ?
35.x: As per the question period, option (d) was the correct answer. While in the present context, services sector has attracted the highest Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) inflows into India in the last two decades. During April 2000 to December, 2025, Foreign Direct Investment attracting top five sectors (in terms of US$) are as follows : Services Sector (16.38%), Computer Software and Hardware (15.63%), Trading (6.56%), Telecommunications (5.17%) and Automobile Industry (5.11%). Total FDI inflow into India 2024-25 (April-March) is estimated at US $ 50018 million. Sectors attracting highest FDI equity inflows during 2024-25 (April-March) are as follows : 1. Services Sector (US $ 6640 million), 2. Computer Software and Hardware (US $ 7814 million), 3. Trading (US$ 4176 million), 4. Non-Conventional Energy (US $ 4012 million), 5. Construction (Infrastructure) Activities (US $ 2245 million).

35.s: Limit of investment for outstanding corporate bond for Foreign Portfolio Investment in Union Budget 2020-21 has been extended upto :
35.x: Limit of investment in outstanding corporate bonds for Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) in Union Budget 2020-21 had been extended upto 15% from the previous upto 9%. The limits for FPI investment in corporate bonds shall remain unchanged at 15% of outstanding stock of securities for FY 2023-24, 2024-25 and 2025-26. The limits for FPI investment in Government securities (G-secs) and State Government Securities (SGSs) are at 6% and 2% respectively.

35.s: Foreign investment by a person resident outside India in an unlisted Indian company is treated as:
o: FPI, if the stake is below 10%
FPI, whatever the size of the stake
FDI, whatever the size of the stake
35.x: Any stake in an unlisted company counts as FDI; the 10% line applies only to listed companies.

35.s: Vodafone's acquisition of Hutchison Essar is an example of:
35.x: Brownfield FDI is investment through acquisition of an existing firm, as in Vodafone-Hutchison Essar; greenfield means a new facility.

35.s: The 10% threshold separating FDI from FPI is based on the recommendation of the:
35.x: The Arvind Mayaram Committee set the 10% line: 10% or more in a listed company is FDI, below it FPI.

35.s: Along with FPI, which flow into India is regarded as among the most unstable, being interest-rate driven?
35.x: FPI and NRI deposits are the most unstable flows because they respond to interest rates; FDI in any form is long-term and stable.

35.s: FCNR(B) deposits replaced FCNR(A) deposits on:
35.x: FCNR(B), a fixed deposit held in foreign currency, replaced FCNR(A) on 15 May 1993.

35.s: A rupee-denominated bond issued abroad by an Indian entity is called a:
35.x: A masala bond is a rupee bond issued abroad; FCCBs are debt and GDRs are equity raised abroad.

35.s: The Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) was abolished in:
35.x: FIPB ended in June 2017; applications now go to ministries through the FIF Portal under DPIIT.

35.s: After the FIPB's abolition, Government-route FDI proposals are filed for ministry approval through the:
o: Securities and Exchange Board of India
35.x: Government-route proposals need prior approval of the concerned ministry via the FIF Portal, part of the National Single Window System since August 2022.

35.s: The Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999 replaced the:
35.x: FEMA 1999 replaced FERA 1973; the RBI regulates ECBs under FEMA.

35.s: Foreign investment in public sector banks in India is capped at:
35.x: Public sector banks allow 20% through the Government route; private banks allow 74% (49% automatic).

35.s: For foreign investors other than NRIs, FDI in scheduled civil aviation is allowed under the automatic route up to:
35.x: Scheduled civil aviation allows 100% FDI, of which 49% is automatic; NRIs may invest 100% under the automatic route.

35.s: FDI in single-brand retail was first eased, up to 51%, in:
35.x: Single-brand retail was first opened up to 51% in 2006; in 2012 it went to 100% and multi-brand retail to 51%.

35.s:
Consider the following statements about FDI in insurance:
1. The cap was raised from 26% to 49% in 2015.
2. It was raised to 74% with effect from 19 May 2021.
3. Insurance is listed in Entry 47 of the State List.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
35.x: Statements 1 and 2 are true. Statement 3 is false: insurance is Entry 47 of the Union List.

35.s: FDI in trading, including e-commerce, of food products made in India is permitted up to:
35.x: Trading of food products made in India, including through e-commerce, allows 100% FDI under the Government route.

35.s:
Consider the following statements about FDI in India:
1. Railway infrastructure allows 100% FDI under the automatic route.
2. Railway operations are prohibited for FDI, except permitted activities.
3. Chit funds and Nidhi companies allow 100% FDI under the automatic route.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
35.x: Statements 1 and 2 are true: only railway operations are barred. Statement 3 is false: chit funds and Nidhi companies are prohibited sectors.

35.s: FDI is prohibited in India in the manufacture of:
35.x: Manufacture of cigars and cigarettes of tobacco is a prohibited sector; medical devices and pharma allow 100% automatic, defence 74% automatic.

35.s: Under Press Note 3 (April 2020), all FDI from a country sharing a land border with India must come through the:
35.x: Press Note 3 requires Government approval for all FDI from land-border countries; China is not named in it.

35.s: Under the March 2026 amendment to Press Note 3, 'beneficial owner' is defined as per the:
35.x: The amendment uses the beneficial-owner definition of the Prevention of Money Laundering (PML) Rules, 2005.

35.s: India's net FDI reached its peak of $44.0 billion in:
35.x: Net FDI peaked at $44.0 bn in 2020-21; in 2024-25 it was only $353 mn.

35.s: FDI into Andhra Pradesh in FY 2025-26 was about:
35.x: AP drew $608.59 mn in FY 2025-26, up from $233.14 mn in 2024-25 and $92.13 mn in 2023-24; $250.67 mn was the metallurgical share.

35.s:
Consider the following statements about FDI in Andhra Pradesh:
1. Metallurgical industries led FDI inflows in FY 2025-26.
2. Industrial Development Policy 4.0 targets FDI of at least $10 billion.
3. FDI in FY 2025-26 was lower than in 2024-25.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
35.x: Statements 1 and 2 are true. Statement 3 is false: AP's FDI rose from $233.14 mn in 2024-25 to $608.59 mn in FY 2025-26.

35.s: According to the World Investment Report 2026, the country that was both the largest recipient and the largest investor of FDI in 2025 was:
35.x: WIR 2026 reports global FDI up 6% to $1.6 trillion, with the US the largest recipient and source; India is the largest recipient in South Asia.

35.s: Under the General Route, FPIs may hold up to what share of outstanding State Government securities?
35.x: The General Route limits are 6% of Central G-secs and 2% of State securities; 15% is the corporate bond limit.

35.s: FPI outflows in FY 2025-26 were about:
35.x: FPI outflows in FY26 were about ₹2.2 lakh crore; ₹24,829 crore was the equity outflow in May 2026 alone.

35.s: The India-UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) came into force on:
35.x: The India-UAE CEPA came into force on 1 May 2022; the Australia ECTA followed on 29 December 2022.

35.s: Which of the following agreement–partner pairs is correctly matched?
35.x: India's ECTA is with Australia; TEPA is with EFTA, CETA with the UK and CEPA with the UAE.

35.s:
Consider the following statements about India's trade agreements:
1. The India-EFTA TEPA came into force on 1 October 2025.
2. The India-UK CETA came into force on 15 July 2026.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
35.x: Both are true: TEPA (signed 10 March 2024) came into force on 1 October 2025, and CETA (signed 24 July 2025) on 15 July 2026.

35.s: The South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) among the eight SAARC members came into force in:
35.x: SAFTA came into force in 2006; SAPTA was signed in 1993 and came into force in 1995.

35.s: How many countries signed the RCEP on 15 November 2020?
35.x: RCEP was signed by 15 members: ASEAN 10 plus China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand.

35.s: Which of the following is NOT a member of the RCEP?
35.x: India opted out of RCEP in 2019; Australia, New Zealand and South Korea are among its 15 members.

35.s: India's trade deficit with China, a key reason for leaving RCEP, was $53.5 billion in:
35.x: The deficit with China was $53.5 bn in 2018-19, when India opted out, and rose to $99.2 bn by 2024-25.

24.s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of instruments or markets associated with the organised financial system?
o: Artisans, farmers, small traders and nidhis
Call money, Treasury bills, commercial bills and certificates of deposit
Indigenous bankers, chit funds, nidhis and moneylenders
Unregulated loan companies, repo, nidhis and moneylenders
24.x: Call money, Treasury bills, commercial bills and certificates of deposit are components of the organised financial system. The other sets include unorganised institutions or users.
24.tq: Classify each item before selecting the all-organised set.
xs: **Call money, T-bills, commercial bills and CDs** are all instruments of the **organised** (RBI-regulated) money market — option **(2)**.
**Indigenous bankers**, **moneylenders**, **chit funds**, **nidhis** and unregulated loan companies are **unorganised**; farmers, artisans and small traders are users, not instruments.
xa: Other organised instruments: **CPs**, **repo**, **MMMFs**.
Organised institutions: commercial banks, cooperative banks, foreign banks, **DFHI**, provident funds, **STCI**, mutual funds.
⚠ APPSC-G2 **2017** key: **finance companies** are **not** part of the organised money market.

24.s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of indigenous bankers?
o: Chit funds, loan companies, moneylenders and RRBs
24.x: Shroffs, Seths, Multanis and Chettiars are identified as indigenous bankers who accept deposits and deal in hundis.
24.tq: Identify the complete membership of a traditional financial-intermediary group.
xs: **Shroffs, Seths, Multanis and Chettiars** are indigenous bankers — option **(3)**.
**RRBs**, **DCCBs**, **StCBs**, **NABARD**, banks and **NBFCs** are all organised/regulated institutions.
xa: **Mahajans** are also indigenous bankers.
Indigenous bankers deal in **hundis** and combine banking with trade/commission business.
⚠ "Lends only in kind" does **not** describe an indigenous banker.

24.s: Professional and agricultural moneylenders in India are governed by:
o: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
24.x: Moneylenders fall under state money-lending laws; the Chit Funds Act, 1982 relates to chit funds.
xa: Unregulated non-bank intermediaries: **indigenous bankers**, **moneylenders**, **loan companies**, **chit funds**.
**Nidhis** are also part of the unorganised market.

24.s: Shadow banking refers to:
o: only illegal lending by unlicensed moneylenders
credit intermediation outside full bank regulation, including activity by NBFCs and money-market or liquid funds
the issue of currency by the central bank
24.x: Shadow banking is bank-like credit intermediation outside full banking regulation; NBFCs and money-market or liquid funds are examples.
24.tq: Apply the definition to distinguish broad shadow banking from illegal lending alone.
xs: **Shadow banking** is **bank-like credit intermediation** (**NBFCs**, **money-market/liquid funds**) **outside full bank regulation** — option **(2)**.
It is not just illegal moneylending, nor cooperative deposit-taking.
xa: **Liquid debt mutual funds** are NBFCs' main **short-term funding** source.
Criticism: **regulatory arbitrage** (shadow banking).
RBI's response to NBFC stress: the **SBR framework** + closer supervision.
**IL&FS (Sep 2018)** defaults triggered a liquidity crisis.

24.s: Which of the following belongs to the unorganised money market?
o: Certificates of Deposit and Commercial Paper
24.x: Indigenous bankers and moneylenders form part of the unorganised money market. T-Bills, commercial bills, CDs, CPs and repos belong to the organised segment.
24.tq: Classify the lender or instrument by the organised–unorganised divide.
xs: **Indigenous bankers and moneylenders** belong to the **unorganised** money market — option **(3)**.
**CDs, CPs, repos, call money, T-bills, commercial bills** are **organised** market instruments.
xa: Unorganised: also **chit funds**, **nidhis** and unregulated finance/loan companies.
The unorganised market serves **farmers, artisans, small traders**.
⚠ APPSC-G2 **2017** key placed **finance companies** outside the organised market.

24.s: Urban Cooperative Banks traditionally operated under which form of dual control?
o: State Registrar of Cooperative Societies and RBI
24.x: UCBs traditionally faced dual control by the State Registrar of Cooperative Societies and the RBI.
24.tq: Identify the two authorities sharing cooperative and banking oversight.
xs: **UCBs** were under **dual control** of the **State RCS** and **RBI** — option **(3)**.
NABARD, IRDAI, SEBI have no such role over UCBs.
xa: **BR (Amendment) Act 2020** (after the **PMC Bank** crisis) put UCBs under RBI supervision like commercial banks.
**NUCFDC** is the UCB umbrella body.

24.s: Which institution was set up as an umbrella body for Urban Cooperative Banks?
24.x: NUCFDC was set up as an umbrella body for Urban Cooperative Banks.
24.tq: Match the institutional acronym with its sector rather than with rural cooperative banking.
xs: **NUCFDC** is the **umbrella body** for **UCBs** — option **(1)**.
**NHB** is a housing DFI; **APCOB** is AP's apex cooperative bank.
xa: **Sahakar Sarathi** (NABARD) is a shared-services entity for **rural** cooperative banks.
RBI is resuming UCB licensing **on tap**.

24.s: In which year was NABARD established?
24.x: NABARD was set up in 1982, on the Shivaraman Committee's advice. SIDBI followed in 1990.
24.tq: Arrange the institutions in time order.
n: NABARD was established in 1982. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
xs: **NABARD** was established in **1982** (**12 July 1982**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
It was set up under the **NABARD Act 1981** on the **B. Sivaraman Committee / CRAFICARD** recommendation.
**1964** = IDBI and UTI; **1990** = SIDBI.
xa: NABARD refinances **StCBs, RRBs, LDBs** and runs **RIDF**.
It launched the **SHG-Bank Linkage Programme** as a pilot in **1992**.
HQ: **Mumbai**.

24.s: The National Housing Bank, wholly owned by the RBI until then, was taken over by the Central Government in:
24.x: NHB was set up in 1988 and stayed wholly RBI-owned until the Central Government took over its ownership in 2019.
xa: NHB Act **1987**; apex housing finance body; **C. Rangarajan** high-level group.
HFC **regulation** also moved to **RBI** in **2019**.
NHB launched **RESIDEX** in **2007**.

24.s: NABARD came into existence in the year :
Which of the following institutions performs a quasi-regulatory role in relation to Housing Finance Companies?
24.x: NHB plays a quasi-regulatory role in relation to Housing Finance Companies; NABARD and SIDBI have comparable roles in other sectors.
24.tq: Match the quasi-regulator with the financial institution category it relates to.
xs: **NHB** is the **quasi-regulator** for **HFCs** — option **(1)**.
**NABARD** plays this role for **RRBs/cooperatives** and **SIDBI** for **SFCs**; **SEBI** is a full regulator.
xa: HFC **regulation** moved from NHB to the **RBI** (**Finance Act 2019**); NHB keeps **supervision and refinance**.
**90 HFCs** were registered (**June 2025**).
NHB: statutory, **1988** (**NHB Act 1987**).

24.s: Which one of the following institutions was established on a World Bank initiative and later became a universal bank?
o: Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India
24.x: ICICI was established in 1955 on a World Bank initiative and subsequently became a universal bank.
24.tq: Identify the institution through its founding association and later transformation.
xs: **ICICI** (**1955**) was set up on a **World Bank initiative** and later became a **universal bank** — option **(4)**.
**IFCI** (**1948**) was the first DFI; **IDBI** (**1964**) the apex industrial DFI; **EXIM Bank** (**1982**) finances foreign trade.
xa: ICICI provided **industrial credit**.
Older AIFI class: **IFCI, ICICI, IDBI, SIDBI, IIBI**.
⚠ **IDBI** later became a **commercial bank**, reclassified **private** after **LIC** control (**2019**).

24.s: After LIC acquired majority control in 2019, IDBI Bank was reclassified as a:
24.x: Following LIC's majority acquisition in 2019, IDBI Bank was reclassified as a private sector bank.
xa: IDBI: **1964** under RBI; autonomous **1976**; reverse-merged **2004-05**.
Govt + LIC are offloading a combined **60.72%** stake (bidding under way).
**LIC** was set up in **1956**.

24.s: For regulatory purposes, which of the following are classified by the Reserve Bank of India as refinance institutions?
24.x: RBI classifies NABARD, NHB and SIDBI as refinance institutions. EXIM Bank is classified as a term-lending institution.
24.tq: Separate refinance institutions from term-lending institutions.
xs: RBI classes **NABARD, NHB and SIDBI** as **refinance institutions** — option **(4)**.
**EXIM Bank** is a **term-lending institution**; IFCI, IDBI, LIC and NaBFID are not refinance institutions.
xa: APPSC GS **2024** picked **NHB** against **IFCI, TFCI and EXIM**.
The **5** RBI-regulated AIFIs: **EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI, NaBFID**.
NABARD refinances **StCBs, RRBs, LDBs**; NHB refinances **HFCs and banks**.

24.s: Which of the following institutions are regulated and supervised by the Reserve Bank of India as All-India Financial Institutions?
o: IFCI, ICICI, IDBI, IIBI and LIC
EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID
NABARD, LIC, GIC, UTI and SIDCs
NHB, SIDBI, IFCI, TFCI and SFCs
24.x: The five RBI-regulated and supervised AIFIs are EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID.
24.tq: Start with the sure institutional names and eliminate older classifications.
xs: The **5** RBI-regulated and supervised **AIFIs** are **EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI** and (since **2022**) **NaBFID** — option **(2)**.
**LIC, GIC, UTI** are investment institutions; **SFCs, SIDCs** are state-level FIs; **IFCI** is now an NBFC.
xa: Older notes list only the first **four**.
⚠ APPSC GS **2024** ("out of **17** AIFIs") keyed **9** — the notes do not explain that count.
**NaBFID** (**2021**) is the newest DFI.

24.s: Which development finance institution was the first DFI in India and was established for long-term industrial finance?
24.x: IFCI, established in 1948, was the first development finance institution and provided long-term industrial finance.
24.tq: Link the institutional first and its distinctive purpose.
xs: **IFCI** (**July 1948**, special Act) was **India's first DFI**, for long-term industrial credit — option **(1)**.
**IDBI** came in **1964**, **EXIM Bank** in **1982**, **SIDBI** in **1990**.
xa: Exam angle: IFCI's setting up **began the era of development financing** (APPSC GS **2018**).
It gave long-term project loans (**25 years+**).
Today IFCI is a **public sector NBFC-ND-SI** that manages **PLI** projects.
FIRST/LAST: IFCI first (**1948**); **NaBFID** newest (**2021**).

24.s: Which of the following institutions was set up mainly to finance MSMEs?
24.x: SIDBI focuses on MSME finance. IDBI was the apex industrial development bank, Exim Bank finances export-import activity and ICICI gave private-sector industrial credit.
xa: Years: **ICICI 1955**, **IDBI 1964**, **EXIM Bank January 1982**, **SIDBI 1990**.
ICICI was set up on a **World Bank** initiative.
SIDBI began as an **IDBI subsidiary**.

24.s: In which year was the Unit Trust of India (UTI) established?
24.x: UTI was set up in 1964. LIC dates to 1956, GIC to 1972 and CRISIL to 1987.
xa: **ICRA 1991**; **CARE Ratings 1993**.
LIC, UTI, GIC = public sector **investment institutions**.

24.s: LIC, UTI and GIC were collectively regarded as the:
24.x: LIC, UTI and GIC were the public-sector investment institutions.
24.tq: Identify the common classification shared by three institutions.
xs: **LIC, UTI and GIC** were the **public sector investment institutions** — option **(2)**.
Refinance institutions are **NABARD, NHB, SIDBI**; regulators include **SEBI, IRDAI**; credit-rating bodies are **CRISIL, ICRA, CARE**.
xa: Older classes: **specialised FIs** (**RCTC**, **TFCI**), **state-level FIs** (**SFCs**, **SIDCs**).

24.s: The NBFC Ombudsman Scheme, 2018 was subsequently merged into:
24.x: The NBFC Ombudsman Scheme, 2018 was merged into the RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021.
24.tq: Arrange the institutional schemes by identifying the later integrated framework.
xs: The **NBFC Ombudsman Scheme 2018** merged into the **RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021** — option **(4)**.
**RB-IOS** is an RBI scheme, not a SEBI or other scheme.
xa: RB-IOS now also covers **state and central cooperative banks**.
**RBI** regulates **NBFCs** and **HFCs**.

24.s: In September 2018, the default of which entity set off a liquidity crisis in India?
o: National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development
24.x: Defaults by Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Limited (IL&FS), an infrastructure NBFC, set off a liquidity crisis in September 2018.
24.tq: Use the date-event association to distinguish the two major NBFC stress episodes.
xs: **IL&FS** (**Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services**) defaults in **Sep 2018** set off a **liquidity crisis** — option **(3)**.
**DHFL** was a **2019** episode; **Tata Sons** and **NaBFID** had no such default.
xa: IL&FS was an **infrastructure NBFC**.
Govt **superseded the board** (**NCLT** order); the new board handled asset sales.
Response: the **SBR framework** + closer supervision.

24.s: The Andhra Pradesh Mutually Aided Cooperative Societies (MACS) Act was enacted in:
24.x: The AP MACS Act dates from 1995; the AP Cooperative Societies Act dates from 1964.
xa: The **AP Cooperative Tribunal** (**Sec. 75**, 1964 Act) is **appellate** under the 1964 Act.
It has **original jurisdiction** under the **MACS Act**.
Cooperative societies are registered under **State Cooperative Societies Acts** + the **BR Act 1949**.

24.s: Which statement correctly describes the jurisdiction of the AP Cooperative Tribunal?
o: It has only advisory jurisdiction under both Acts.
It has original jurisdiction under the 1964 Act and appellate jurisdiction under the MACS Act.
It has appellate jurisdiction under the 1964 Act and original jurisdiction under the MACS Act.
It exercises jurisdiction only over Urban Cooperative Banks.
24.x: Under Section 75 of the AP Cooperative Societies Act, 1964, the Tribunal is appellate under that Act and has original jurisdiction under the MACS Act.
24.tq: Compare the two Acts carefully because the Tribunal’s jurisdiction is reversed between them.
xs: The **AP Cooperative Tribunal** is **appellate** under the **1964 Act** and has **original jurisdiction** under the **MACS Act** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) reverses the two roles.
xa: It is set up under **Sec. 75** of the **AP Cooperative Societies Act, 1964**.
MACS Act year: **1995**.
**UCBs** are under **RBI** supervision after the **BR (Amendment) Act 2020**.

24.s: Which of the following institution–year of establishment pairs is correctly matched?
24.x: IDBI was set up in 1964. IFCI dates from 1948, ICICI from 1955 and SIDBI from 1990.
n: IFCI was established in 1948. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
ICICI was established in 1955. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
IDBI was established in 1964. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
SIDBI was established in 1990. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
xa: **IFCI** (July **1948**) was **India's first DFI** — it began the era of development financing.
**NaBFID** (**2021**) is the newest DFI, for infrastructure.

24.s: Which one of the following regulator–entity pairs is correctly matched?
24.x: Chit fund companies are regulated by the State Government. Merchant bankers are regulated by SEBI, insurance companies by IRDAI and NBFCs by RBI.
24.tq: Start with the sure regulator–entity pair and eliminate swapped authorities.
xs: **Chit fund companies** are regulated by the **State Government** — option **(3)**.
**Merchant bankers** come under **SEBI**, **insurance companies** under **IRDAI**, and **NBFCs** under the **RBI**.
xa: Chit funds: **Chit Funds Act 1982**.
**PFRDA** regulates pension/**NPS** under the **PFRDA Act, 2013**.
**IFSCA** (**April 2020**) is the unified regulator of **IFSCs** (GIFT City).

24.s: The International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) Act was enacted in:
24.x: The IFSCA Act dates to 2019. The PFRDA Act is of 2013, the IRDA Act of 1999, and SEBI became statutory in 1992.

Financial transactions and other activities of
Foreign bank operating in another country for bank-
24.x: ‘Shadow banking’ in fact, symboizes one of the many failings of the financial system leading up to the global financial crisis. The term ‘Shadow Bank’ was coined by the American economist Paul McCulley in 2007. ‘Shadow banking’ refers to the practice of banking-like activities (mainly lending) performed by non-banking financial intermediaries, which are not subject to strict regulation. These institutions function as intermediaries between the investors and borrowers, providing credit and generating liquidity in the system. Although these entities do not accept traditional demand deposits offered by banks, they do provides services similar to what commercial banks offer.

24.x: IFCI Ltd. (IFCI) was set up as a Statutory Corporation (‘The Industrial Finance Corporation of India’) in 1 July, 1948 for providing medium and long term finance to industry. IFCI was the first development financial institution of India set up to propel economic growth through development of infrastructure and industry. Since then IFCI has contributed significantly to the economy through its continuous support to projects in all the three spheres of growth and development – manufacturing, infrastructure & services and agriculture allied sectors. In 1993, after repeal of the IFC Act, IFCI became a Public Limited Company (effected from October 1999), registered under the Companies Act, 1956. Currently, IFCI is a Government Company with Government of India holding 72.57% (as on 31 March, 2026) of paid-up capital of IFCI. Consider the following statements about Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) in India:
1. NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits.

3. NBFCs form part of the payment and settlement system and can issue cheques.
4. Deposit insurance of DICGC is not available for NBFC deposits.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
24.x: Statement 1 is correct: NBFCs are explicitly prohibited from accepting demand deposits (like savings or current accounts deposits that can be withdrawn at any time). Only banks are authorised to accept demand deposits. Some NBFCs can accept deposits, but only term deposits (fixed deposits) for a specified period. Statement 2 is incorrect: Not all NBFCs have to register with the RBI. To avoid dual regulation, certain categories of NBFCs regulated by other financial regulators are exempted from RBI registration. For example, Venture Capital Funds, Merchant Banking companies, and Stock Broking companies are registered with SEBI; Insurance Companies are regulated by IRDAI; Nidhi companies are regulated by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs; and Chit Fund companies are regulated by the respective State Governments. Statement 3 is incorrect: Unlike banks, NBFCs do not form part of the payment and settlement system. Consequently, they cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves. Statement 4 is correct: The deposit insurance facility provided by the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC), which currently insures bank deposits up to ₹5 lakh per depositor, is available only to commercial and cooperative banks. It is not available for depositors of NBFCs.

Pension fund management, as described in Statement III, is not included among RBI’s authorized core functions and income heads. Since the regulation of the National Pension System lies with a separate Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA), pension fund management cannot be treated as a source of RBI’s income; therefore, Statement III is incorrect. Under Section 17 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, RBI can provide loans/advances only to governments, scheduled banks, cooperative banks, etc., and not to private or nonbanking companies; hence, Statement IV is also incorrect. Expenditure on note printing is a cost for the RBI, and it does not earn income from the printing and distribution of currency notes; therefore, Statement V is also incorrect. Thus, only Statements I and II align with RBI’s sources of income, while Statements III, IV, and V are incorrect.

4. It is freely convertible against commercial bank money and cash.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct: Digital Rupee or e₹ is India's Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC). It is the digital form of India's physical currency, the Rupee (₹). e₹ is issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in digital form and offers features similar to physical cash, like convenience of use, guarantee of RBI, finality of settlement, etc. e₹ is stored in the user's digital wallet and can be used to receive/send money, and/or make payment for transactions, just like any physical ₹ note. In terms of Section 26 of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Act, 1934, every ₹ bank note shall be legal tender at any place in India in payment or on account for the amount expressed therein and is guaranteed by the Central Government. e₹, being a digital form of the ₹ bank note, is legal tender and is the liability of the Reserve Bank of India. Indian Economy: Financial System PMF IAS IE – 91 Statement 3 is incorrect: The digital rupee is not inherently insured against inflation. Its value can still erode due to inflation, just like physical currency.

17.s:
Consider the following statements in respect of the digital rupee:
1. It is a sovereign currency issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in alignment with its monetary policy.
2. It appears as a liability on the RBI’s balance sheet.
3. It is insured against inflation by its very design.
4. It is freely convertible against commercial bank money and cash.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
17.x: Issued by The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), the Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) or Digital Rupee (or e`) is a digital variant of physical currency. Reserve Bank broadly defines CBDC as the legal tender issued by a central bank in a digital form. It is akin to sovereign paper currency but takes a different form, exchangeable at par with the existing currency and shall be accepted as a medium of payment, legal tender and a safe store of value. As per the RBI’s concept Note on Central Bank Digital Currency, the features of CBDC include : z CBDC is sovereign currency issued by central banks in alignment with their monetary policy. z It appears as a liability on the central bank’s balance sheet. z Must be accepted as a medium of payment, legal tender, and a safe store of value by all citizens, enterprises, and government agencies. z Freely convertible against commercial bank money and cash. z Fungible legal tender for which holders need not have a bank account. z Expected to lower the cost of issuance of money and transactions. Hence, statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct, while statement 3 is incorrect because digital rupee is same as physical rupee and exchangeable at a 1:1 ratio. Thus, like physical rupee it is also not inherently insured against inflation and its value can be decreased by the inflation.

16.s: If you withdraw Rs. 1,00,000 in cash from your Demand Deposit Account at your bank, the immediate effect on aggregate money supply in the economy will be
o: to increase it by more than ₹ 1,00,000
16.x: M1 is the money supply that is composed of currency, demand deposits, and other liquid deposits, which include savings deposits. M1 includes the most liquid portion of the money supply because it contains currency and assets that are either cash or can be quickly converted to cash. However, "near money" and "near, near money," which fall under M2 and M3, cannot be converted to currency as quickly. When you withdraw Rs. 1,00,000 in cash from Indian Economy: Financial System PMF IAS IE – 98 your Demand Deposit Account, it alters the composition of the money supply but does not impact the overall money supply. Demand Deposit Accounts are part of M1, a broader measure of the money supply that includes currency (cash) and demand deposits (such as checking accounts). Withdrawing Rs. 1,00,000 in cash simply converts demand deposits into cash. As a result, the immediate effect on the composition of the money supply is a reduction in demand deposits by Rs. 1,00,000 and a corresponding increase in cash by the same amount. However, the aggregate money supply (M1) remains unchanged because the total value of money (demand deposits + cash) is constant.

16.s: If you withdraw Rs. 1,00,000 in cash from your Demand Deposit Account at your bank, the immediate effect on aggregate money supply in the economy will be:
o: to increase it by more than Rs. 1,00,000
16.x: M3 = M1 (Currency with the public + Demand deposits with banks + Other deposits with RBI) + Time deposits with banks. M3 is the most commonly used measure of money supply. It is also known as aggregate money supply (Broad money). Now, if we withdraw Rs.1,00,000, Demand deposits component will fall by Rs. 1,00,000 and CU (Currency held by public) will increase by Rs.1,00,000. It means, it leaves the money supply unchanged. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

Hence, it is the money which a creditor is under compulsion to accept in settlements of his claims. The metallic money (coins) in circulation in a country is part of legal tender which includes banknotes also. But, there may be some limitations (as in India) for coins to be legal tender in payment. The coins issued by Government of India under Section 6 of The Coinage Act, 2011, shall be legal tender in payment or on account provided that a coin has not been defaced and has not lost weight so as to be less than such weight as may be prescribed in its case. Coin of any denomination not lower than one rupee shall be legal tender for any sum not exceeding one thousand rupees. Fifty paise (half rupee) coin shall be legal tender for any sum not exceeding ten rupees. While anyone cannot be forced to accept coins beyond the limits mentioned above, voluntarily acccepting coins for amounts exceeding the limits mentioned above is not prohibited. 16.x: All options are correct: An increase in the money supply: When there is more money in the economy, people have more money to spend. 16.x: Liquidity refers to how easily and quickly an asset can be converted into cash without significant loss in value. Currency is the most liquid asset, as it is already in cash form and can be used immediately for transactions. Demand deposits with the banks are also highly liquid as they can be withdrawn on demand, typically without any limitations or penalties. Savings deposits with the banks are slightly less liquid than demand deposits. While Indian Economy: Financial System PMF IAS IE – 83 they can generally be withdrawn without penalties, there may be restrictions on the number or amount of transactions. Time deposits with the banks are the least liquid among the options. These deposits, like fixed deposits, have a set maturity date, and withdrawing funds before this date often results in penalties or loss of accrued interest.

If more people deposit money in banks, it increases the funds available for banks to lend, thus increasing the money multiplier. Option (a) is incorrect: Increase in the cash reserve ratio: This would decrease the money multiplier since a higher CRR means banks have to keep more reserves and can lend less. This increase in deposits allows banks to create more loans, thereby increasing the money supply and boosting the money multiplier. This reduces the amount available for lending, thus decreasing the money multiplier. o: Increase in the Cash Reserve Ratio in the banks

16.x: The money multiplier describes how an initial deposit leads to a greater final increase in the total money supply. It identifies the ratio of decrease and/or increase in the money supply in relation to the commensurate decrease and/or increase in deposits. Increase in banking habit of the population will lead to more deposits in the banking system and hence, banks have more money to lend out, which leads to the increase in money multiplier. On the other hand, increase in reserve ratios like Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) decreases the money multiplier, while the increase in the population does not necessarily leads to the increase in banking deposits/money multiplier.

16.x: 'Pure Monetary Theory of Trade Cycle' was propagated by the British economist R.G. Hawtrey. According to Hawtrey, "the trade cycle is a purely monetary phenomenon, because general demand is itself a monetary phenomenon." He took a monetary approach towards the economic ups and downs of industry and commerce, advocating changes in the money supply through adjustment in the bank rate of interest, foreshadowing the later work of Keynes.

16.s: Supply of money remaining the same when there is an increase in demand for money, there will be
o: a fall in the level of prices
an increase in the rate of interest
a decrease in the rate of interest
an increase in the level of income and employment
16.x: When the demand for money increases while the supply of money remains constant, there is a shortage of liquidity in the economy. People prefer to hold more cash (for transactions, precaution, or speculation), which reduces the availability of money for lending. As a result, to balance this higher demand with the unchanged supply, the rate of interest rises. Higher interest rates discourage borrowing and encourage saving, thereby restoring equilibrium in the money market. Thus, the immediate effect is an increase in the rate of interest, making option (b) correct.

Marginal Standing Facility – absorbs surplus liquidity from banks without collateral
Bank Rate – rate at which the RBI rediscounts bills of exchange
Standing Deposit Facility – absorbs surplus liquidity without collateral
19.x: MSF is overnight emergency borrowing above the repo rate that lets banks dip into SLR; absorbing surplus liquidity without collateral is the SDF.
n: The MSF rate traditionally carries a higher cost than the repo rate. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Repo is used for regular liquidity management. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) can involve dipping into the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) portfolio. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Repo is the principal policy lending rate in the source framework. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
xa: **SDF** began **April 2022**, enabled by **Budget 2018-19**; first proposed in **2015**.
Rates: **SDF 5.00%**, **repo 5.25%**, **MSF = bank rate 5.50%**.
Corridor order: **SDF** (floor) < **repo** < **MSF = bank rate** (ceiling).

19.s: Open Market Operations (OMO) are associated with which of the following?
19.x: Open market operations, the RBI buying and selling government securities, are a monetary-policy tool. Public revenue belongs to fiscal policy.
19.tq: Discriminate monetary from fiscal tools.
n: OMO is a monetary policy instrument. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 75-77]
xs: **Open Market Operations** are associated with **monetary policy** — option **(1)**.
OMO means the **RBI buying or selling government securities**; a **sale absorbs** and a **purchase injects** liquidity.
⚠ **Public revenue** is associated with **fiscal policy**, which uses **spending, taxes, subsidies and borrowing**.
xa: **OMOs** are the main tool for **durable** liquidity — e.g. **₹1 lakh crore** of purchases in **Dec 2025**.
FY26 OMO purchases: **₹2.39 lakh crore** (**Apr-May 2025**).
A **decrease** in the **Bank Rate** **increases liquidity**; an increase is **contractionary**.
To control inflation (**dear money**), the RBI **sells G-secs**; to boost growth, it **buys G-secs**.

19.s: A bank is allowed to lend ₹70 against a security valued at ₹100. If the margin requirement is raised, the immediate effect will generally be to
o: increase the value of the security automatically
convert the loan into an equity investment
reduce the loan available against the same security
increase the loan available against the same security
19.x: The margin is the gap between the value of the security and the loan. Raising the margin reduces the amount that can be borrowed against the same security.
19.tq: Apply the inverse relationship between margin requirements and credit availability.
xs: Raising the margin will **reduce the loan available against the same security** — option **(3)**.
**Margin** = gap between the **value of the security** and the **loan**.
Higher margin = **smaller loan** → cuts credit against that security.
xa: Margin requirement is a **qualitative (selective)** tool.
⚠ **Moral suasion**, **margin requirements**, **direct action** = qualitative; **CRR, SLR, OMO** = quantitative.

19.s: Why do interest rates on outstanding MCLR-linked loans generally respond more slowly than rates on EBLR-linked loans?
o: MCLR-linked loans reset only periodically, whereas EBLR-linked loans reprice quickly
MCLR-linked loans are unrelated to bank funding costs
Outstanding loans are excluded from monetary transmission
EBLR-linked loans are reset only once a year by law
19.x: MCLR-linked loans reset at periodic intervals, creating a lag. EBLR-linked loans are directly linked to an external benchmark and reprice more quickly.
19.tq: Discriminate between periodic reset behaviour and rapid external-benchmark repricing.
xs: **MCLR-linked loans reset only periodically**, whereas **EBLR-linked loans reprice quickly** — option **(1)**.
That is why outstanding-loan WALR (**9.26%**) lagged fresh-loan WALR (**8.5%**) in Sep **2025**.
xa: **Deposit rates** and **MCLR** adjust slowly.
WALR on fresh loans fell **64 bps** in **FY26** (ES **2025-26**).

19.s: ‘Repurchase Option’ is used :
o: to reduce the heavy sell off pressure of rupee in
to increase the sell off pressure of rupee in Exchange
to reduce the value of rupee in Exchange market
19.x: ‘Repurchase Option’ (or Repo Rate) is used by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to regulate the money supply and inflation in the economy. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.

19.s: The gradual reduction in the SLR from its 1991-92 level was undertaken on the advice of the
19.x: The SLR was gradually reduced after the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee on financial-sector reforms.
19.tq: Use the committee-recommendation trap by matching the reform with the correct committee.
xs: SLR was cut gradually on the **Narasimham Committee**'s advice — option **(2)**.
It fell from **38.5%** of NDTL (**1991-92**) to **18%** now.
xa: SLR statutory range: **0-40%**; the **25%** floor went in **2007**.
SLR is governed by **Sec 24** of the **BR Act, 1949**.

19.s: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is governed by which section of the RBI Act, 1934?
19.x: CRR is governed by Section 42 of the RBI Act; SLR by Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
xa: CRR now **3%** of NDTL; SLR **18%**.
"Required reserve ratio" = **CRR** (APPSC **2023**).

19.s: The SLR, which was 38.5 per cent in 1991–92, stood at what level in September 2023?
19.x: The SLR was 18 per cent in September 2023, down from 38.5 per cent in 1991–92.
xa: SLR was cut gradually on the **Narasimham** Committee's advice.
SLR statutory range **0-40%**; **25%** floor removed in **2007**.
CRR was **4%** before the **2025** cuts → **3%** now.

19.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Quantitative tools — Margin requirements and moral suasion
Quantitative tools — Change the volume and cost of total credit
Qualitative tools — Direct the flow of credit among sectors or borrowers
19.x: Margin requirements and moral suasion are qualitative or selective tools. Quantitative tools include repo, reverse repo, OMO, CRR and SLR.
19.tq: Separate tools by whether they alter total credit or direct credit to selected borrowers.
xs: **Quantitative tools — margin requirements and moral suasion** is wrong — option **(1)**.
**Margin requirements** and **moral suasion** are **qualitative (selective)** tools.
Quantitative tools: **bank rate, repo, reverse repo, OMO, CRR, SLR**; they act on the **volume and cost** of total credit.
xa: Qualitative tools **direct credit to sectors or borrowers**; also called **selective credit control**.
Quantitative tools are also called **traditional methods of control**.
Other qualitative tools: **credit rationing**, **direct action**, consumer credit regulation.

19.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the monetary policy framework followed in India during 1985–1998?
19.x: During 1985–1998, India followed monetary targeting with feedback, with M3 as the principal monetary aggregate.
19.tq: Directly identify the framework associated with the given period.
xs: During **1985-1998** India followed **monetary targeting with feedback** (using **M3**) — option **(3)**.
The **multiple indicator approach** came in **1998-2016**; **flexible inflation targeting** from **2016**.
xa: Landmarks of that phase: **Chakravarty Committee 1985**, **Vaghul Committee 1987** (money market).
Multiple-indicator landmarks: **LAF 2000**, **MSS 2004**, **Base Rate 2010**, **MSF 2011**, **MCLR 2016**.
**Shaktikanta Das** traced these phases in "**Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy**" (**24 Jan 2020**).

19.s: The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) was introduced in:
19.x: MSF came in 2011, after LAF (2000) and MSS (2004), and before MCLR (2016).
xa: **Base Rate** came in **2010**, between MSS and MSF.
**SDF** began in **April 2022**, under the FIT phase.
All four belong to the **1998-2016** multiple indicator era (MCLR at its end).

19.s: India's flexible inflation-targeting framework is based on the recommendations of which committee?
19.x: The Urjit Patel Committee reported in 2014, the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement followed in 2015 and the RBI Act was amended in 2016.
xa: **SDF** (**2022**) is a later landmark of the FIT phase.
Under FIT, the **repo rate** is the **single operating policy rate**.
**Price stability** is the paramount objective.

19.s: India adopted the flexible inflation-targeting framework in:
19.x: Flexible inflation targeting began in 2016, after the multiple indicator approach of 1998–2016.
xa: **Money supply (M3)** targeting was the **1985-1998** framework.
The approach was dropped for being **opaque**.
Landmarks of the era: **LAF 2000**, **MSS 2004**, **MSF 2011**.

19.s: Which of the following rates is correctly classified as a rate fixed by the RBI or the Monetary Policy Committee rather than by an individual bank or the market?
o: Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate
19.x: The MSF rate is fixed by the RBI/MPC. MCLR is computed by each bank, EBLR is linked to an external benchmark, and the call money rate is market-determined.
19.tq: Separate official policy rates from bank-specific benchmarks and market-determined rates.
xs: The **Marginal Standing Facility rate** is fixed by **RBI/MPC** — option **(3)**.
**MCLR** is set by **each bank**; **EBLR** is a bank's spread over an external benchmark.
The **call money rate** (WACR) is **market-determined**.
xa: RBI/MPC also fix **repo, SDF, bank rate, reverse repo, CRR, SLR**.
⚠ **SLR** and **CRR** are set by RBI, not by banks.

19.s: The Base Rate system of bank lending was introduced on:
19.x: The Base Rate came on 1 July 2010 and was based on the average cost of funds; MCLR (2016) uses the marginal cost of funds.
xa: Base Rate gave **slow transmission**.
**EBLR** from **1 October 2019**.

19.s: MCLR was introduced on
19.x: The Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate system was introduced on 1 April 2016.
19.tq: Test the close dates of successive lending-rate benchmark reforms.
xs: **MCLR** was introduced on **1 April 2016** — option **(2)**.
**1 July 2010** is the **Base Rate**; **1 October 2019** is **EBLR**.
xa: MCLR is based on the **marginal cost of funds** + CRR/SLR carry + operating cost + **tenor premium**.
**Janak Raj** group (**2017**) found MCLR transmission weak.
MCLR came at the end of the **1998-2016** multiple-indicator phase.

19.s: From 1 October 2019, new floating-rate personal, retail and micro, small and medium enterprise loans were required to be linked to
o: an external benchmark such as the repo rate or specified Treasury-bill yield
the BPLR fixed by the RBI
the average call money rate of the preceding financial year
an internal benchmark selected by the borrowing customer
19.x: From 1 October 2019, such loans had to be linked to an external benchmark, including the repo rate, the three- or six-month Treasury-bill yield, or an FBIL-published rate.
19.tq: Apply the external-benchmark rule to the specified category of floating-rate loans.
xs: From **1 October 2019**, such loans must link to **an external benchmark such as the repo rate or T-bill yield** — option **(1)**.
Benchmarks: **repo rate**, **3-month** or **6-month** T-bill yield, or an **FBIL**-published rate.
**BPLR** was an old bank-set benchmark; the choice is not the borrower's internal pick.
xa: Loans linked directly to repo are the **fastest route** of transmission.
The mandate followed the **Janak Raj** Internal Study Group (**2017**).

19.s: Which of the following best distinguishes the Base Rate system from the MCLR system?
o: Base Rate used average cost of funds, whereas MCLR uses marginal cost of funds
Base Rate used marginal cost of funds, whereas MCLR used average cost of funds
Base Rate is applicable only to government securities, whereas MCLR applies only to deposits
Both Base Rate and MCLR are directly linked to the repo rate
19.x: The Base Rate was based on the average cost of funds and therefore transmitted policy changes slowly. MCLR uses marginal cost components, including marginal deposit costs, CRR/SLR carry, operating cost and tenor premium.
19.tq: Discriminate between two closely related benchmark-rate systems by their cost-of-funds basis.
xs: **Base Rate used average cost of funds**, whereas **MCLR uses marginal cost of funds** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses them.
Neither is directly linked to repo; that is **EBLR** — option (4) is wrong.
xa: Base Rate: **1 July 2010**; MCLR: **1 April 2016**.
MCLR adds **CRR/SLR carry**, **operating cost** and **tenor premium**.

19.s: Which one of the following represents the fastest route of monetary-policy transmission to lending rates?
o: Loans linked to fixed small-savings rates
Loans linked to the Base Rate
19.x: EBLR links lending rates directly to an external benchmark such as the repo rate, allowing loans to reprice more quickly than Base Rate or MCLR loans.
19.tq: Identify the institutional mechanism that transmits a policy-rate change most directly.
xs: **Loans linked to EBLR** are the fastest transmission route — option **(1)**.
EBLR loans linked directly to **repo** **reprice quickly**.
**MCLR** and deposit rates adjust **slowly**; **Base Rate** was slow too.
xa: **Administered small-savings rates** hold deposit rates up — an obstacle to transmission.
Outstanding-loan WALR (**9.26%**) lags fresh loans (**8.5%**) because MCLR loans reset periodically.

19.s: The Internal Study Group on the working of the MCLR system, constituted by the RBI in 2017, was chaired by whom?
19.x: The RBI’s Internal Study Group on the working of the MCLR system was chaired by Janak Raj in 2017.
19.tq: Use the committee-chairperson association to identify the correct answer.
xs: The **2017** Internal Study Group on MCLR was chaired by **Janak Raj** — option **(2)**.
It found **MCLR transmission weak** and recommended an **external benchmark**.
xa: Outcome: **EBLR mandate from 1 Oct 2019**.
⚠ **Urjit Patel Committee** (**2014**) led to **flexible inflation targeting**, not EBLR.

19.s: Following the RBI's Internal Study Group on MCLR, the external benchmark-based lending rate (EBLR) became mandatory from:
19.x: The study group found weak MCLR transmission and recommended an external benchmark, leading to the EBLR mandate from 1 October 2019.
xa: EBLR benchmarks: **repo**, **3-month**/**6-month** T-bill yield, or an **FBIL** rate.
EBLR covers new floating **personal/retail and MSME** loans.

19.s: Which of the following about the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is NOT correct?
o: It is an overnight borrowing facility
Banks borrow from the RBI under it
Its rate is usually repo plus 0.25%
Its rate is lower than the repo rate
19.x: MSF costs more than repo, usually repo plus 0.25%; it is an overnight emergency window, while repo is for regular liquidity.
n: Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is an overnight borrowing facility. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Banks borrow from the RBI through the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF). [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
The MSF rate traditionally carries a higher cost than the repo rate. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Repo is used for regular liquidity management. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
xa: Under MSF banks can **dip into** their **SLR portfolio** up to **2%** of NDTL.
MSF began **May 2011** at repo + **100 bps**, up to **1%** of NDTL.
Corridor: **SDF (5.00%)** floor, **MSF (5.50%)** ceiling — **50 bps** wide.

19.s: The Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS), introduced in April 2004, was meant to:
o: Sterilise excess liquidity created by foreign-exchange purchases
Replace the repo for daily liquidity adjustment
19.x: Under the MSS the RBI issues Treasury Bills and securities to absorb rupees created by forex purchases; the proceeds sit in a separate account the Government cannot spend.
xa: **MSS** securities count towards banks' **SLR**.
Sterilisation tools: **OMO/MSS** sales and **VRRRs**.

19.s: Sterilisation by the Reserve Bank of India refers to:
o: Increasing currency circulation after a fall in exports
Absorbing or offsetting excess rupee liquidity created by foreign-exchange inflows
Replacing open market operations with fiscal expenditure
Converting all foreign-exchange reserves into gold
19.x: When foreign-exchange inflows increase rupee liquidity, the RBI may sell government securities or conduct liquidity-absorption operations to offset the impact. This process is called sterilisation.
19.tq: Identify the policy operation by linking foreign-exchange inflows with offsetting domestic liquidity action.
xs: **Sterilisation** = **absorbing or offsetting excess rupee liquidity created by forex inflows** — option **(2)**.
RBI sells G-secs (**OMO/MSS**) or runs **VRRRs** to offset it.
xa: Sep **2026** case: **FCNR(B)** inflows of **$127.23 bn**.
**MSS** began in **April 2004**.
Under an **open capital account**, flows move liquidity and the rupee.

19.s: The policy repo rate is regarded as the main monetary-policy instrument because the Monetary Policy Committee sets it primarily to
o: achieve the inflation target and guide money-market rates
determine the annual SLR ceiling of 40 per cent
fix the exchange rate of the Indian rupee permanently
19.x: The MPC sets the policy repo rate to achieve the inflation target, while liquidity operations help keep money-market rates close to that rate.
19.tq: Connect the policy instrument with the objective it is designed to achieve.
xs: The MPC sets the repo rate to **achieve the inflation target and guide money-market rates** — option **(1)**.
Liquidity is managed so **money-market rates stay near** the repo rate.
The **SLR ceiling of 40%** is statutory, not set via the repo rate.
xa: The repo is the **single operating policy rate** under **FIT** and the **most-watched signal**.
**OMOs** are the main tool for **durable** liquidity.

19.s: When the RBI raises the repo rate, the first effect in the transmission sequence is:
19.x: The sequence is higher money-market rates, then costlier credit, then lower consumption and investment, and finally lower aggregate demand.
xa: A rate cut **increases investment expenditure** (UPSC **2014**).
⚠ A rate cut does not raise savings or tax collection.
Transmission channels: **interest rate, credit, exchange rate, asset price, expectations**.

19.s: Surplus liquidity in the banking system generally pulls market rates:
o: Below the repo rate, speeding up transmission
Above the repo rate, speeding up transmission
Above the repo rate, weakening transmission
Below the repo rate, weakening transmission
19.x: Surplus liquidity can lower market rates below the repo rate and aid transmission; deficit liquidity tends to weaken it.
xa: By **3 Sep 2026** surplus of about **₹10.32 lakh crore** had pushed the **call rate below repo**.
RBI drained it via **VRRR**.
Governor (Feb **2026**): RBI to keep "**sufficient liquidity**" for transmission.

19.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: Exchange-rate channel — lower rates can weaken the rupee and support exports
Asset-price channel — higher bond and equity prices can create a wealth effect
Expectations channel — a credible target necessarily removes all uncertainty about inflation
Credit channel — greater bank funds and increased lending
19.x: A credible target anchors inflation expectations; it does not necessarily remove all uncertainty. The other three channel descriptions are correct.
19.tq: Find the overstatement in an otherwise accurate list of transmission-channel effects.
xs: **Expectations channel — a credible target removes all uncertainty** is NOT correct — option **(3)**.
A credible target only **anchors inflation expectations**.
The **exchange-rate**, **asset-price** and **credit** channel descriptions are correct.
xa: **Interest rate** channel: cheaper loans raise consumption and **investment**.
Under **FIT**, the MPC sets the repo to hit the inflation target.

19.s: The RBI may sterilise the liquidity effects of capital flows through MSS, OMO and:
19.x: Under an open capital account, flows alter liquidity and the rupee, and the RBI can sterilise them through MSS, OMO and VRRR.
xa: Example: **FCNR(B)** inflows of **$127.23 bn** (Sep **2026**).
**MSS** (April **2004**) proceeds sit in a separate account the Government cannot spend.
By **4 Sep 2026** RBI absorbed about **₹6.02 lakh crore** through two **3-day** VRRRs.

19.s: Which of the following monetary-policy stances is INCORRECTLY described?
o: Neutral – rates can move either way, depending on the data
Accommodative – supports growth with ample liquidity; rate cuts likely
Calibrated tightening – no cuts; hikes measured, not at every meeting
Hawkish – worried about growth, with a bias towards easing
19.x: A hawkish stance worries about inflation and tightens; concern for growth with an easing bias is dovish.
xa: Stance path: neutral → **accommodative** (Apr **2025**) → **neutral** (**June 2025**) → retained through Aug **2026**.
**Hawkish** stance tightens: **raises rates** and **drains liquidity**.

19.s: A rise in the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) generally:
o: Raises demand for goods and services
19.x: A higher CRR withdraws lendable funds, reducing money in circulation and demand.
xa: CRR = share of **NDTL** kept as **cash with RBI**, earning **no interest**.
CRR is now **3%** of NDTL after a **100 bps** cut.
To control inflation (dear money): **raise** CRR, SLR, repo; **sell** G-secs.

19.s: The RBI's primary window for managing day-to-day liquidity through repo, reverse repo and SDF operations is the:
19.x: LAF is the framework through which the RBI injects liquidity via repo and absorbs it via reverse repo and SDF on a day-to-day basis.
xa: LAF was introduced in **2000**.
The LAF corridor: **SDF (5.00%)** floor, **MSF (5.50%)** ceiling — **50 bps** wide.
**VRR/VRRR** are auction-based LAF tools.

19.s: Which LAF instrument absorbs surplus liquidity for maturities longer than the overnight SDF?
19.x: VRRR is an auction-based tool that absorbs liquidity for maturities longer than the overnight SDF, while VRR injects liquidity.
xa: They keep **short rates near repo**.
By **4 Sep 2026** RBI absorbed about **₹6.02 lakh crore** through two **3-day** VRRRs.

19.s: Fine-tuning operations of the Reserve Bank of India are primarily conducted to
o: keep system liquidity in line with the monetary policy stance
determine the annual financial statements of banks
fix the statutory floor for the SLR
replace all permanent open market operations
19.x: Fine-tuning operations, generally involving short-term VRR or VRRR auctions, are conducted to align liquidity conditions with the prevailing monetary policy stance.
19.tq: Match a specialised operational tool with its precise policy objective.
xs: Fine-tuning operations aim to **keep liquidity in line with the monetary policy stance** — option **(1)**.
They are **short VRR/VRRR auctions**.
xa: RBI ran **49** fine-tuning operations in **FY2024** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
**OMOs** remain the main tool for **durable** liquidity — fine-tuning does not replace them.
Stance was **neutral** through Aug **2026**.

19.s: The temporary incremental CRR (I-CRR) announced by the RBI on 10 August 2023 was:
19.x: The temporary I-CRR was 10%, announced on 10 August 2023; it impounded about ₹1.1 lakh crore.
xa: In APPSC-G2 **2025**, both I-CRR statements asked were correct.
Regular **CRR** is now **3%** of NDTL.
**Fine-tuning operations**: **49** in **FY2024**.

19.s: Open Market Operations (OMO) of the RBI involve outright purchase or sale of:
19.x: OMO is the outright purchase or sale of government securities to manage durable liquidity, conducted through banks.
xa: FY26 injections: **₹2.39 lakh crore** OMO purchases (Apr-May **2025**).
OMO **sale absorbs**; **purchase injects**.
**₹1 lakh crore** of purchases in Dec **2025** to **stabilise bond yields**.

19.s: A USD/INR buy-sell swap conducted by the RBI, such as a 3-year swap of $5 billion in December 2025, primarily:
o: Directly fixes the yield on all government securities
Injects rupee liquidity without changing the size of the RBI's balance sheet
Raises the CRR without affecting market liquidity
Absorbs rupee liquidity and permanently reduces foreign-exchange reserves
19.x: The specified buy-sell swap injects rupee liquidity while not changing the size of the RBI's balance sheet.
19.tq: Identify the liquidity and balance-sheet effect of a central-bank foreign-exchange swap.
xs: The buy-sell swap **injects rupee liquidity without changing the size of RBI's balance sheet** — option **(2)**.
Example: **$5 bn**, **3-year**, **Dec 2025**.
xa: In Dec **2025** RBI paired it with **₹1 lakh crore** of OMO purchases.
Dec **2025** tightness came from **currency leakage, tax outflows, reserve needs**.
**LTRO (2020)**: **1-3 year** funds at the repo rate.

19.s: Which of the following measures is most appropriate for a supply-driven food or fuel inflation shock rather than a purely demand-driven inflationary situation?
o: Buffer stocks, duty cuts and farm reforms
Reducing the money multiplier through higher CRR
19.x: Supply-driven food and fuel inflation may require buffer stocks, duty cuts and farm reforms, whereas CRR, SLR and policy rates primarily influence aggregate demand.
19.tq: Apply the demand-side versus supply-side distinction to select the suitable response.
xs: For supply-driven shocks, **buffer stocks, duty cuts and farm reforms** are needed — option **(2)**.
**Monetary tools are demand-side tools only** — rate hikes cannot add onions or tomatoes to the market.
So raising the **repo**, **CRR** or **SLR** alone (options 1, 3, 4) does not fix a supply shock.
xa: **Food inflation** is mostly **supply-driven**; RBI has little reach over it.
**Fiscal policy** acts on demand **directly**; monetary policy **indirectly** through interest rates.

19.s: Automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills was discontinued in 1997 and replaced by
19.x: The system of automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills ended in 1997 and was replaced by Ways and Means Advances.
19.tq: Test the reform by distinguishing the replacement mechanism from other liquidity instruments.
xs: Automatic monetisation through **ad hoc T-bills** ended in **1997** and was replaced by **Ways and Means Advances** — option **(1)**.
This was a response to **fiscal dominance** (large Government borrowing).
**MSS** (**2004**) is for **sterilisation**; **EBLR** (**2019**) is a lending benchmark; **MSF** (**2011**) is a penal window.
xa: **Heavy Government borrowing** keeps yields high (**crowding out**) and weakens transmission.
Other post-1991 challenges: **exchange-rate volatility** (main one), **external shocks**, weak transmission.

19.s: Which one of the following was the main post-1991 challenge to monetary policy identified in India?
o: Exchange-rate volatility arising from capital flows
19.x: Exchange-rate volatility caused by capital inflows and outflows was a major post-1991 challenge. The other conditions were not identified as the principal challenge.
19.tq: Use elimination of reversed or exaggerated macroeconomic conditions to identify the principal challenge.
xs: The main post-1991 challenge was **exchange-rate volatility arising from capital flows** — option **(2)**.
This was asked in APPSC-GS **2023**.
⚠ Forex reserves were NOT a problem, inflation was not low, revenue was not in surplus — so options (1), (3), (4) are traps.
xa: Under an **open capital account**, RBI sterilises flows via **MSS, OMO, VRRR**.
Other challenges: **external shocks** (oil, global rate cycles, wars), **fiscal dominance**, weak transmission.

19.s: Fiscal dominance in the monetary-policy context is most closely associated with
o: exclusive reliance on foreign capital for infrastructure
large government borrowing exerting pressure on money supply and inflation
the RBI losing authority over the call money market
banks independently fixing the CRR and SLR
19.x: Large government borrowing, and earlier automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills, could increase money supply and inflation, producing fiscal dominance.
19.tq: Translate the institutional term into its cause-and-effect relationship with borrowing, money supply and inflation.
xs: **Fiscal dominance** = **large government borrowing** pressuring money supply and inflation — option **(2)**.
Earlier it worked through **automatic monetisation via ad hoc T-bills**, ended in **1997**.
**CRR and SLR** are set by **RBI**, not banks — option (4) is wrong.
xa: Ad hoc T-bills were replaced by **Ways and Means Advances**.
**Heavy Government borrowing** keeps yields high (**crowding out**), an obstacle to transmission.

19.s: A narrowing spread between Indian sovereign yields and US bond yields:
o: Ends the need for domestic bond issuance
19.x: A narrower spread reduces the relative cost of borrowing for India.
xa: **S&P** upgraded India from **BBB- to BBB** (**2025-26**).
G-sec yields are driven by the **US Fed**, **RBI** and **inflation/short-term rates**.

19.s: Which of the following is used by the RBI to absorb surplus liquidity?
19.x: Absorbing surplus liquidity is the role of reverse repo; the Bank Rate is the RBI's long-term rediscount rate on bills of exchange and commercial paper.
n: The Reverse Repo Rate is used to absorb surplus liquidity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
The Bank Rate is a traditional rate associated with RBI lending or rediscounting. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
Bank Rate transactions involve bills of exchange or commercial paper. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]

18.s: Which committee recommended monetary targeting with feedback and was associated with the organised money market in India?
18.x: The Sukhamoy Chakravarty Committee, constituted in 1985, recommended monetary targeting with feedback and dealt with the organised money market.
18.tq: Use the committee–recommendation association to distinguish closely related monetary-policy committees.
xs: The **Sukhamoy Chakravarty Committee** (**1985**) recommended **monetary targeting with feedback** — option **(1)**.
It dealt with the **organised money market** (UPSC), with money supply growth as the anchor.
**Vaghul** (**1987**) gave the money-market blueprint; **Tarapore** dealt with capital account convertibility; **Urjit Patel** (**2014**) with FIT.
xa: ⚠ Order: **1985** Chakravarty – **1987** Vaghul – **1997** Tarapore – **2014** Urjit Patel.
Monetary targeting was the framework of **1985-1998**.

18.s: The blueprint for the money market that subsequently led to the introduction of Commercial Paper in 1990 was associated with which committee?

xs: The **N. Vaghul** Committee (**1987**) gave the **money-market blueprint** that led to **Commercial Paper** (**1990**) — option **(2)**.
**Chakravarty** (**1985**) gave monetary targeting; **Tarapore** (**1997**) the convertibility roadmap.
xa: **Urjit Patel** Committee (**2014**): **CPI** as nominal anchor, **4% ±2%** target, an MPC.
⚠ **1985** Chakravarty – **1987** Vaghul – **1997** Tarapore – **2014** Urjit Patel.

18.s: Which one of the following was NOT a feature of the Urjit Patel Committee’s recommendations?
o: Creation of a committee to decide policy rates
Adoption of CPI as the nominal anchor
A 4 per cent inflation target with a tolerance band of 2 percentage points
Continuation of the multiple-indicator approach as the sole framework

18.tq: Find the option that reverses the committee’s recommendation rather than merely changing a date or name.
xs: **Continuation of the multiple-indicator approach** was NOT recommended — option **(4)**; the Committee said **drop** it for **FIT**.
It did recommend **CPI as nominal anchor** (CPI-C), a **4% ±2%** target and a committee (**MPC**) to decide rates.
xa: Full name: **Expert Committee to Revise and Strengthen the Monetary Policy Framework**, set up by **RBI** in **2014**.
APPSC-G2 **2017** key: committee headed by **Urjit Patel**.
It was followed by the **Monetary Policy Framework Agreement** (**2015**).

xs: The **RBI (Amendment) Act, 2016** inserted **Sections 45Z to 45ZO** — option **(4)**.
These sections gave **statutory backing** to **flexible inflation targeting** and the **MPC**.
xa: **45ZA**: Centre (with RBI) sets the **inflation target** every five years.
**45ZB**: **MPC** constituted as a statutory body.
**45ZN**: failure = CPI **above 6% or below 2%** for **three consecutive quarters**.
APPSC-GS **2022** key: Act amended in **2016**.

18.s: In which year was the RBI Act, 1934 amended to give statutory backing to flexible inflation targeting and the Monetary Policy Committee?

xs: The RBI Act was amended for FIT in **2016** — option **(3)** (APPSC-GS **2022** key).

**2014** = **Urjit Patel** Committee; **2015** = **Monetary Policy Framework Agreement** (not a statute).

18.s: The inflation target is set by the Central Government, in consultation with the RBI, under which section of the RBI Act, 1934?
18.x: Section 45ZA covers the inflation target (set every five years and notified in the Gazette); Section 45ZB constitutes the MPC.
xa: ⚠ Many books wrongly print **45ZB** for the target.
**45ZN** = failure clause.

18.s: Under Section 45ZN of the RBI Act, failure to meet the inflation target is deemed to occur when the average CPI inflation remains
o: above 4 per cent or below 2 per cent for four consecutive quarters
above 6 per cent or below 2 per cent for three consecutive quarters
above 6 per cent or below 2 per cent for three consecutive months
above 5 per cent or below 3 per cent for two consecutive quarters
18.x: Failure is defined as average CPI inflation remaining above 6 per cent or below 2 per cent for three consecutive quarters. The statutory wording refers to quarters, not months.
18.tq: Trap the month-versus-quarter confusion while retaining the correct inflation bands.
xs: Failure = average CPI **above 6 per cent or below 2 per cent** for **three consecutive quarters** — option **(2)**.
The Act says **quarters**, not months — option (3) is the common error.
xa: RBI must report the **reasons**, **remedial action** and **time to return** to target.
First invoked in **2022**, after CPI stayed above **6%** from **January 2022**.

18.s: When the inflation target is missed in the statutory manner, the Reserve Bank of India is required to report to the Government the
o: exchange-rate level it will maintain for the next financial year
reasons for failure, remedial actions and estimated time to return to the target
names of all MPC members and their individual salaries
future Union Budget allocations and tax rates
18.x: The RBI must report the reasons for the failure, the remedial actions proposed and the period within which inflation is expected to return to the target.
18.tq: Ask what the responsible institution must do after a statutory failure.
xs: RBI must report the **reasons for failure, remedial actions and estimated time to return to the target** — option **(2)**.
This is under **Section 45ZN** of the RBI Act.
xa: Failure: CPI **above 6% or below 2%** for **three consecutive quarters**.
First invoked in **2022**.
Under the **2015** Agreement, RBI is **answerable to the Government** when it misses.

18.s: The Monetary Policy Committee is constituted under which provision of the RBI Act, 1934?

xs: The MPC is constituted under **Section 45ZB** — option **(4)**.
**45ZA** = inflation target; **45ZN** = failure clause.

They are appointed by the **Central Government**, not the RBI Board — option (3) is wrong.

18.s: Which one of the following is the primary objective of monetary policy under the flexible inflation-targeting framework?

18.x: In May 2016, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Act, 1934 was amended to provide a statutory basis for the implementation of the flexible inflation targeting framework. The amended RBI Act also provides for the inflation target to be set by the Government of India, in consultation with the Reserve Bank, once in every five years. Accordingly, the Central Government has notified in the Official Gazette 4 percent Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation target with tolerance level of + / – 2 percent for the period from 5 August, 2016 to 31 March, 2021. Prior to the amendment in the RBI Act in May, 2016 the flexible inflation targeting framework was governed by an Agreement on Monetary Policy Framework between the Government and the RBI of 20 February, 2015. Note : The Government of India retained the CPI inflation target at 4 percent (with the upper tolerance level of 6 percent and the lower tolerance level of 2 percent) for the five year period 1 April, 2021 to 31 March, 2026. In March, 2026, the Government of India again retained the same CPI inflation target at 4 percent (with a tolerance band of +/– 2 percent) for the five year period from 1 April, 2026 to 31 March, 2031.
