20.s: Which one of the following is not a nationalized bank ?
20.x: ICICI (Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India) was formed in 1955 at the initiative of the World Bank, the Government of India and representatives of Indian Industry. The principal objective was to create a development financial institution for providing medium and long-term project financing to Indian business. ICICI bank was incorporated in 1994 as a part of the ICICI group. ICICI bank is a leading private sector bank in India. In 1999, ICICI become the first Indian company and the first bank or financial institution from non-Japan Asia to be listed on the New York Stock Exchange. Rest are nationalized Banks.

20.s: The ‘Lead Bank’ Scheme was launched in :
20.x: The genesis of the Lead Bank Scheme (LBS) can be traced to the Study Group headed by Prof. D.R. Gadgil (Gadgil Study Group) on the Organizational Framework for the Implementation of the Social Objectives, which submitted its report in October, 1969. A Committee of Bankers on Branch Expansion Programme of Public Sector Banks appointed by the Reserve Bank of India under the Chairmanship of F.K.F. Nariman (Nariman Committee) endorsed the idea of an ‘Area Approach’ in its report (November, 1969), recommending that in order to enable the Public Sector Banks to discharge their social responsibilities, each bank should concentrate on certain districts where it should act as a ‘Lead Bank’. Pursuant to the above recommendations, the Lead Bank Scheme was introduced by the Reserve Bank of India in December, 1969. The Scheme aims at coordinating the activities of banks and other developmental agencies through various fora in order to achieve the objective of enhancing the flow of bank finance to the priority sector and other sectors and to promote banks’ role in the overall development of the rural sector. For coordinating the activities in the district, a particular bank is assigned ‘Lead Bank’ responsibility of the district. The Lead Bank is expected to assume a leadership role for coordinating the efforts of the credit institutions and the Government. The Lead Bank Scheme was last reviewed by the High Level Committee headed by Smt. Usha Thorat, the then Deputy Governor of the Reserve

20.s: Which one of the following is different from others?
20.x: According to Companies Act 2013, a company that is limited by shares refers to a company that has the liability of the members (shareholders) limited by such an amount that is unpaid on their respectively held shares. The company can enact this liability while the company is in existence or as it is ending. When incorporating a company limited by shares, the total share capital consists of all of the shares held by each member at incorporation. Those shares can either be : fully paid; partly paid; or unpaid. Partly paid or unpaid shares are shares where a member is due to pay the company. In contrast, fully paid shares are where the full value of the shares have been paid to the company. In companies limited by shares, the liability of members is limited to any unpaid amount of shares that they hold. If a member has fully paid for their shares, they should have no further liabilities as a member.

20.s: The Service Area Approach was implemented under the purview of :
20.x: The Service Area Approach (SAA) was implemented under the purview of Lead Bank Scheme (LBS).The Service Area Approach (SAA) introduced in April, 1989 for planned and orderly development of rural and semi-urban areas was applicable to all scheduled commercial banks including Regional Rural Banks. Under SAA, each bank branch in rural and semi-urban area was designated to serve an area of 15 to 25 villages and the branch was responsible for meeting the needs of bank credit of its service area. The primary objective of SAA was to increase productive lending and forge effective linkages between bank credit, production, productivity and increase in income levels. The SAA scheme was reviewed from time to time and appropriate changes were made in the scheme to make it more effective. The Service Area Approach scheme was last reviewed in December, 2004 and it was decided to dispense with the restrictive provisions of the scheme while retaining the positive features of the SAA such as credit planning and monitoring of the credit purveyance. Accordingly, under SAA the allocation of villages among the rural and semi-urban branches of banks were made not applicable for lending except under Government Sponsored schemes. Thus, while the commercial banks and RRBs are free to lend in any rural and semi-urban area, the borrowers have the choice of approaching any branch for their credit requirements. The Narasimham Committee for Financial Sector Reforms has suggested reduction in :
o: SLR, CRR and Priority Sector Financing

CRR, Priority Sector Financing and Financing to
21.x: Two expert Committees were set up in 1990s under the Chairmanship of M. Narasimham (an ex-RBI Governor) which are widely credited for spearheading the financial sector reforms in India. The first Narasimham Committee (Committee on the Financial System – CFS) was constituted in 1991 and the second one (Committee on Banking Sector Reforms) was appointed in 1997. These two committees submitted their reports in 1991 and 1998 respectively. The Narasimham Committee I for Financial Sector Reforms had suggested reduction in Statutory Liquidity Ratio and Cash Reserve Ratio. The Committee was of the view that the reduction of the prempted portion of banks’ resources through the SLR and CRR would, in any case, enlarge the abilities of banks to dispense credit to priority sectors.

**SEBI** became statutory in **1992**.

21.s: The Banks Board Bureau started working from:

2. Under it, the Centre gave up its 50% share in RRBs.

21.x: The cover was raised from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh in Budget 2020-21 after the PMC Bank crisis.

21.s: The Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025 raised the tenure of co-operative bank directors from 8 years to:
21.x: The Act raised co-operative bank directors' tenure from 8 to 10 years.

21.s: What stake in IDBI Bank is on sale in its disinvestment?
21.x: A 60.72% stake in IDBI Bank is on sale.

22.s: Debt Recovery Tribunals were set up under:
o: Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993
22.x: DRTs were established under the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993; they are also used under SARFAESI.
xa: **39 DRTs** and **5 DRATs**; debts **above ₹20 lakh**.
**e-DRT** launched **1 Oct 2018**; e-filing mandatory from **1 Feb 2023**.
⚠ **1987** = Lok Adalats; **1993** = DRTs; **2002** = SARFAESI.

22.s: Debt Recovery Tribunals deal with debts due to banks and financial institutions above:
22.x: The DRTs and DRATs handle debts above ₹20 lakh under the stated framework.
22.tq: Use ascending monetary thresholds to distinguish DRT jurisdiction from the CIRP default threshold.
xs: DRTs handle debts **above ₹20 lakh** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**₹1 crore** is the minimum default for triggering **CIRP** under the IBC.
xa: DRTs were set up under the **RDDBFI Act, 1993**.
**Lok Adalats** handle **small NPAs** only.
**e-DRT**: launched **1 Oct 2018**.

22.s: Which mechanism accounted for the largest share of bank recoveries in FY 2024?
22.x: In FY 2024, IBC accounted for 48% of recoveries, SARFAESI 32%, DRTs 17% and Lok Adalats 3%.
xa: **Lok Adalats** handle small NPAs only.
Comparison: **SARFAESI** (secured lenders, no court) vs **IBC** (collective, NCLT-led) vs **DRT** (tribunal recovery).
FM: IBC realises **94.95%** of fair value.

22.s: The Lok Adalats that facilitate settlement of small non-performing assets derive their statutory status from which enactment?
o: The Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993
22.x: Lok Adalats are statutory forums under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
22.tq: Identify the statute specifically associated with the forum.
xs: Lok Adalats are statutory forums under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**1993** is the **RDDBFI Act** (DRTs); **2002** is **SARFAESI**; **2016** is the **IBC**.
xa: They offer **quick, fee-free settlement** of small loans by compromise.
**National Lok Adalat (13 Sep 2026)**: **DRT Visakhapatnam bench** settled **13** cases worth **₹46.11 crore**.
Lok Adalats delivered **3%** of FY24 bank recoveries.

22.s: The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) replaced the Company Law Board, the BIFR and the:
22.x: NCLT replaced the Company Law Board, BIFR and AAIFR; it did not replace the Securities Appellate Tribunal.
xa: **BIFR** was dissolved on **1 Dec 2016**; cases went to NCLT/NCLAT.
The IBC replaced **SICA 1985/BIFR** and scattered Companies Act provisions.
NCLT/NCLAT constituted **1 June 2016**.

22.s: Which authority is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016?
22.x: The NCLT is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency under the IBC, 2016. The DRT is the authority for individuals and partnership firms.
22.tq: Ask which body would handle the dispute by distinguishing corporate from individual insolvency.
xs: The **National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)** is the adjudicating authority for corporate insolvency (**companies and LLPs**) — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC GS 2019 key).
The **DRT** handles **individuals and partnership firms**; the **NCLAT** hears appeals.
xa: NCLT also handles **personal guarantors of corporate debtors**.
CIRP is triggered by a default of at least **₹1 crore**.
⚠ NCLT = **companies and LLPs**; DRT = **individuals and partnership firms**.

22.s: Recovery by secured lenders without court intervention is the principal feature of:
22.x: SARFAESI allows secured lenders to recover without courts; IBC is collective, NCLT-led resolution and DRTs are tribunal-based recovery.
xa: FY24 recovery shares: **IBC 48%**, **SARFAESI 32%**, **DRTs 17%**.

22.s: Under the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework, capital infusion, a change of management or a merger may be ordered by the:
22.x: Under PCA, the RBI may restrict lending, branch expansion, dividends and pay, and may order capital infusion, a management change or a merger.
xa: Curbs last until capital and asset quality improve.
PCA was introduced in **2002**; full form **Prompt Corrective Action**.

22.s: In Andhra Pradesh, the NCLT bench is located at:
22.x: The NCLT bench sits at Amaravati, while the DRT bench is at Visakhapatnam.
xa: **13 Sep 2026** National Lok Adalat: DRT Visakhapatnam settled **13** cases worth **₹46.11 crore**.

22.s: An Interest Coverage Ratio (ICR) below 1 means the firm:
o: Cannot service its interest from earnings
22.x: ICR = EBIT ÷ interest payable; below 1, earnings do not cover interest.
xa: Lenders use ICR to judge a borrower's **present and emerging risk**.
**PCR** = provisions / gross NPA; higher PCR → more resilient bank.
**Twin Balance Sheet problem**: over-leveraged corporates + capital-starved banks.

22.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the SARFAESI Act, 2002?
o: Lenders holding 60% of the dues can issue a 60-day notice under Section 13(2)
The threshold was 75% of dues before the 2016 amendment
Under Section 13(4), lenders can take possession of the secured asset, take over management or sell it
Under Section 13(8), the borrower can redeem the asset after the auction notice by paying 25% of the dues
22.x: Under Section 13(8) the borrower can redeem only by paying the full dues, not 25%.
xa: **Sec 17**: appeal to the **DRT** within **45 days**; **Sec 18** bars civil courts.

22.s: The SARFAESI Act, 2002 was based on the recommendations of the:
22.x: The SARFAESI Act, 2002 was based on the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee.
xa: Core feature: banks enforce security on NPAs **without court intervention**.
⚠ The **IBC** was based on the **T.K. Viswanathan Committee (2015)**, not Narasimham.
**ARCs** under SARFAESI are registered with and regulated by **RBI**.

22.s: Under Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act, an appeal lies to the DRT within:
22.x: Section 17 allows an appeal to the DRT within 45 days; the Section 13(2) demand notice is of 60 days.
xa: ⚠ **60%** of lenders + **60-day** notice; appeal within **45 days**.

22.s: The NCLAT hears appeals against orders of the NCLT, IBBI, CCI and:
22.x: NCLAT hears appeals from NCLT, IBBI, CCI (from 26 May 2017) and NFRA (from 7 May 2018).
xa: Further appeal from NCLAT lies to the **Supreme Court**.
NCLAT sits at **New Delhi** (Principal Bench) and **Chennai**.

22.s: Under the IBC waterfall mechanism, which of the following ranks above government dues?
22.x: Resolution costs, workmen's dues and secured creditors' claims are placed above government dues in the IBC waterfall.
xa: The **2026** amendment cut liquidation to **180 + 90 days**.
FM: IBC realises **94.95%** of fair value; "not a debt-recovery tool".
Criticism: **deep haircuts** and guarantor liability.

22.s:
Consider the following about Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs):
1. They acquire NPAs, generally at a discount.
2. They are regulated by SEBI.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
22.x: ARCs acquire NPAs, generally at a discount, and are regulated by the RBI, not SEBI.
xa: **NARCL**, India's "bad bank", pays **15% cash** + **85% in Security Receipts**.
SARFAESI is based on the **Narasimham Committee**.

22.s: Which of the following earlier debt-resolution mechanisms was introduced first?
22.x: Corporate Debt Restructuring came in 2001, followed by the 5/25 scheme (2014), Strategic Debt Restructuring (2015) and S4A (2016).

22.s: The Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets (S4A) was introduced by the RBI in:
22.x: S4A came in 2016 and split a stressed firm's debt into sustainable and unsustainable parts; 2018 is Project Sashakt.
xa: S4A was an **RBI** scheme to rework the financial structure of stressed firms.
**SDR (2015)** preceded it.

22.s: Project Sashakt (2018) for resolving stressed assets was based on the recommendations of the:
22.x: Project Sashakt came from the Sunil Mehta Committee; its plan binds all lenders once 66% approve, with the lead bank driving it.
xa: Its **Inter-Creditor Agreement** aimed at **faster resolution of stressed assets** (UPSC 2019 key).
The **Prudential Framework (2019)** made the ICA mandatory.

22.s: The deterrent effect of the IBC is shown mainly by:
o: Completion of all cases by NCLT within 330 days
Settlement of a large number of cases before admission
Transfer of all recovery cases to Lok Adalats
22.x: The settlement of 30,310 cases worth ₹13.78 lakh crore before admission was cited as evidence of the IBC's deterrent effect.
xa: FM: IBC realises **94.95%** of fair value; "not a debt-recovery tool".
IBC delivered **48%** of bank recoveries in FY24.

22.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the RBI's Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets?
o: Lenders must review the borrower account within 30 days of default
Signing an Inter-Creditor Agreement is voluntary
22.x: The framework makes the Inter-Creditor Agreement mandatory, not voluntary; it also requires a 30-day review and resolution within 180 days.

22.s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
o: ARCs — registered with RBI under SARFAESI
CDR — restructuring outside court for large multi-bank borrowers
Lok Adalats — conversion of lender debt into a 51 per cent equity stake
ARCs — purchase bad loans against security receipts
22.x: Conversion of lender debt into a 51 per cent or more equity stake is associated with Strategic Debt Restructuring, not Lok Adalats. ARCs, CDR and Lok Adalats have the other stated functions.
22.tq: Find the wrong mechanism-feature pairing by checking who performs the action.
xs: **Lok Adalats — 51% equity conversion** is wrongly matched — so option **(3)** is correct.
Converting debt into a **51%+** equity stake is **SDR (2015)**; Lok Adalats settle small loans by compromise.
The rest are right: **ARCs** are registered with RBI and buy bad loans against **security receipts**; **CDR** restructures large multi-bank loans out of court.
xa: Lok Adalats are statutory under the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**.
ARCs buy NPAs **at a discount**.

22.s: A higher Provision Coverage Ratio (PCR) indicates a bank that is:
22.x: PCR = provisions ÷ gross NPA; a higher PCR means more bad loans are provided for, so the bank is more resilient.
xa: SCB PCR: **76.3%** (Mar 2025, FSR basis).
Govt data gives **93.14%** for SCBs — a different basis.

22.s: The March 2026 SCB Gross NPA ratio of 1.93 per cent was characterised as a:
22.x: The March 2026 Gross NPA ratio of 1.93 per cent was described as a decadal low.
22.tq: Match the latest numerical value with its stated trend description.
xs: SCB GNPA of **1.93%** in **Mar 2026** was a **decadal low** — so option **(3)** is correct.
NNPA was **0.39%**.
xa: Up next: **ECL** provisioning and higher risk weights on unsecured consumer credit + NBFC exposures.

22.s: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 was based on the recommendations of the:
22.x: The IBC came from the T.K. Viswanathan (Bankruptcy Law Reforms) Committee, 2015; Narasimham is linked to SARFAESI.
xa: ⚠ PYQ: "September assent" and "13-member IBBI" were both wrong (IBBI has **10** members).
IBC completed **10 years** in May 2026.

22.s: Which change in the control structure of insolvency proceedings was introduced by the IBC?
22.x: The IBC shifted the framework from debtor-in-possession to creditor-in-control.
22.tq: Test a paired conceptual comparison by identifying the direction of institutional change.
xs: The IBC shifted control **from debtor-in-possession to creditor-in-control** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses the change.
xa: It created a single, **time-bound** process — a structural reform.
The **2026** amendment's **CIIRP** is a hybrid of debtor-in-possession + creditor-in-control.
The **Committee of Creditors** (financial creditors) votes on resolution plans.

22.s: A promoter classified as a wilful defaulter, or a promoter associated with an NPA, is generally barred from bidding under which provision of the IBC?
22.x: Section 29A prevents wilful defaulters and promoters of NPAs from submitting resolution bids, subject to the statutory framework.
22.tq: Direct recall of the relevant statutory provision.
xs: **Section 29A** bars **wilful defaulters**/NPA promoters from bidding for their own firms — so option **(2)** is correct.
They are **barred from bidding under IBC** (May 2026), so they cannot regain the firm cheaply.
xa: The **Committee of Creditors** votes on resolution plans.
**Lalit Kumar Jain v. UoI (2021)**: **personal guarantors** stay liable after plan approval.
The **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018** covers cases of **₹100 crore** and above.

22.s: The minimum default required to trigger the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) is:
22.x: CIRP needs a default of at least Rs 1 crore; it can be triggered by financial or operational creditors.
xa: CIRP timeline: **180 days** + **90 days**; outer limit **330 days** incl. litigation.
**Sec 29A**: wilful defaulters/NPA promoters cannot bid for their own firms.
NCLT is the adjudicating authority for **companies and LLPs**.

22.s: The outer time limit for completing CIRP, including litigation, is:
22.x: CIRP ordinarily runs 180 days with extension, with an outer limit of 330 days including litigation; actual cases have often taken longer.
xa: **67%** of cases exceed the timeline (ES 2025-26).
Causes: protracted litigation, NCLT capacity/staff shortages.

22.s: The Pre-Packaged Insolvency Resolution Process for MSMEs was introduced in:
22.x: The PPIRP for MSMEs was introduced in 2021 and has a 120-day limit.
22.tq: Combine the launch year and time limit to distinguish the pre-pack process from ordinary CIRP.
xs: **PPIRP** for **MSMEs** came in **2021** with a **120-day** limit — so option **(4)** is correct.
**180 days** is the CIRP period; **330 days** is the CIRP outer limit.
xa: Only **14 admissions in 4 years** under PPIRP (ES 2025-26).
⚠ Timelines: CIRP **180 + 90** (outer **330**); PPIRP **120**; CIIRP **150**.

22.s: Under the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026, the liquidation timeline has been cut to:
22.x: Liquidation is cut to 180 + 90 days; the Act also adds the hybrid Creditor-Initiated Insolvency Resolution Process (Secs 54C–54P).
xa: CIIRP: **150 days**, needs **51%** by value of notified financial creditors.
Criticism: **limits on who can start CIIRP**.

22.s: Under which provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 are the NCLT and NCLAT respectively set up?
22.x: NCLT is established under Section 408 and NCLAT under Section 410 of the Companies Act, 2013.
22.tq: Check the order of the statutory provisions instead of treating the two tribunals as interchangeable.
xs: NCLT is set up under **Sections 408** and NCLAT under **410** of the **Companies Act 2013** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses them; **Sec 61** (IBC) is the NCLAT appeal provision; **Secs 202 and 211** relate to IBBI.
xa: Both were constituted on **1 June 2016**.
NCLT has **16 benches**, incl. **Amaravati** and **Hyderabad**.
NCLAT: Principal Bench **New Delhi** + a bench at **Chennai**.

22.s: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT) sits at:
22.x: NCLAT sits in New Delhi and Chennai and hears appeals from NCLT under Section 61 of the IBC.
xa: NCLT has **16 benches**, incl. **Amaravati** and **Hyderabad**.
Further appeal lies to the **Supreme Court**.

22.s: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) regulates:
22.x: IBBI regulates insolvency professionals, insolvency professional agencies, information utilities and registered valuers.
xa: IBBI (**2016**) is the apex statutory regulator; it has **10** members.
IBBI proposed stronger safeguards for **guarantor insolvency** (**16 Sep 2026**).

22.s: Which of the following is NOT cited as a reason for the decline in banks' NPAs?
22.x: The fall in NPAs is credited to the 4R strategy, higher (not lower) provisioning, the IBC and NARCL. A match could not be built honestly from these facts, so a NOT question is used.

22.s: Under the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026, the NCLT must admit or reject a CIRP plea within:
22.x: The 2026 amendment requires admission or rejection within 14 days; resolution plans must be ruled on within 30 days.

22.s: The IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026 changed 'may' to 'shall' in Section 7(5)(a) of the Code. This change overturned the ruling in:
o: Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India
Swiss Ribbons v. Union of India
22.x: The change from 'may' to 'shall' in Sec 7(5)(a) makes admission of a financial creditor's CIRP plea mandatory once default is proved, overturning the Vidarbha Industries ruling, which had read 'may' as giving the NCLT discretion. Lalit Kumar Jain (2021) concerns personal guarantors' liability; Swiss Ribbons and Essar Steel are other IBC judgments not affected by this change.
xs: Changing "may" to "**shall**" in **Sec 7(5)(a)** overturned the **Vidarbha Industries** ruling — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Lalit Kumar Jain v. UoI (2021)** is about **personal guarantors** staying liable after plan approval.
xa: Other 2026 changes: NCLT admission within **14 days**, plan ruling within **30 days**.
New **CIIRP**: **150 days**, **51%** of notified financial creditors.
Clean-slate protection + cross-border insolvency framework.

22.s: NARCL, described as India’s ‘bad bank’, was announced in which Budget?
22.x: The National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL) was announced in Budget 2021–22.
22.tq: Use the announcement-year distinction among closely placed Budgets.
xs: **NARCL**, India's "bad bank", was announced in **Budget 2021-22** — so option **(2)** is correct.
NARCL was one of the cited reasons for the fall in NPAs, alongside the **4R strategy** and **IBC**.
xa: It aggregates large stressed loans **above ₹500 crore**, targeting about **₹2 lakh crore**.
**IDRCL** resolves the assets, incl. by sale to **AIFs**.
Funding: **15% cash** + **85% in Security Receipts**.

22.s: NARCL pays for stressed assets ____ in cash and the rest in Security Receipts.
22.x: NARCL pays 15% in cash and 85% in Security Receipts; the Government guarantee of Rs 30,600 crore runs for 5 years.
xa: NARCL targets about **₹2 lakh crore** of fully or partly provided assets, in phases.
**₹2,410 crore** recovered by **30 Jun 2025**.

22.s: NARCL primarily targets stressed loans above which threshold and an aggregate asset value of approximately what amount?
22.x: NARCL takes over large stressed loans above ₹500 crore, targeting about ₹2 lakh crore of fully or partly provided assets.
22.tq: Combine the eligibility threshold with the aggregate target.
xs: NARCL targets stressed loans **above ₹500 crore**, about **₹2 lakh crore** in all — so option **(3)** is correct.
These are **fully or partly provided** assets, taken in phases.
xa: By **30 Jun 2025**: **27 accounts**, **₹1,57,215 crore** exposure.
**IDRCL** resolves them; IDRCL is majority private.

22.s: The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 applies to offenders in cases involving amounts of:
22.x: The Fugitive Economic Offenders Act, 2018 covers offenders in cases involving ₹100 crore or more.
22.tq: Recall the statutory monetary threshold without confusing it with NARCL’s loan threshold.
xs: The **Fugitive Economic Offenders Act 2018** covers cases of **₹100 crore** and above — so option **(1)** is correct.
The ₹500, ₹50 and ₹10 crore figures are not the Act's threshold.
xa: **FIU-IND**: suspicious transaction reports up **45%**.
**Sec 29A** of the IBC bars wilful defaulters from bidding.
**Lalit Kumar Jain v. UoI (2021)**: personal guarantors remain liable.

22.s: What is meant by ‘evergreening’ of loans?
o: Writing off an old loan after full recovery
Giving a fresh loan to repay an old loan so that the NPA remains hidden
Increasing the maturity of a standard loan without any new borrowing
Converting every NPA into a government-guaranteed bond
22.x: Evergreening occurs when fresh loans are used to repay old loans, thereby concealing the underlying NPA.
22.tq: Discriminate between concealment through fresh lending and genuine recovery.
xs: **Evergreening** = a **fresh loan to repay an old loan**, so the **NPA stays hidden** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **AQR** exposed this practice.
xa: Other causes of NPAs: **loan frauds and diversion of funds**, weak credit appraisal, slow recovery machinery, corporate over-leverage.
The **twin balance sheet problem** stalls private capex and squeezes **MSME** credit.
**ICR** below **1** → the firm cannot service its interest.

22.s: In the context of banking supervision, PCA stands for:
22.x: PCA stands for Prompt Corrective Action, a framework used by the Reserve Bank of India to intervene in banks with weakening financial health.
22.tq: Test the exact expansion of a frequently confused institutional acronym.
xs: **PCA = Prompt Corrective Action** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2019 key).
RBI uses it to intervene in banks whose financial health is failing.
xa: Introduced by RBI in **2002**.
Current triggers: **capital, asset quality, leverage**.
Curbs: **lending, branch expansion**, risky exposures, **dividends**, management pay.

22.s: The Prompt Corrective Action framework was introduced by the Reserve Bank of India in:
22.x: The RBI introduced the Prompt Corrective Action framework in 2002 to monitor and restrict banks whose financial metrics deteriorate.
22.tq: Use the year-based direct-recall method for a regulatory framework.
xs: RBI introduced the **PCA** framework in **2002** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Weak banks are placed under watch and restricted until capital and asset quality recover.
xa: Revised **Nov 2021**, effective **1 Jan 2022**.
The older **profitability (RoA)** trigger was dropped.
⚠ **2002** is also the year of **SARFAESI**.

22.s: Which of the following pairs of PCA trigger parameter and indicator is INCORRECTLY matched?
22.x: Asset quality is assessed through the net NPA ratio; the Tier-1 leverage ratio measures leverage.
xa: Revised framework effective **1 Jan 2022**.
2017 framework: Net NPA **6-9%** = threshold 1; **12%** or more = threshold 3.

22.s: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code came into force from
22.x: The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), a landmark reform consolidating and streamlining India's insolvency resolution framework, was enacted and came into force in 2016, significantly speeding up the resolution of corporate insolvency and bankruptcy cases.

22.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes insolvency from bankruptcy?
o: Bankruptcy is the inability to pay debts as they fall due, whereas insolvency is a court-approved resolution plan
Insolvency is a legal declaration, whereas bankruptcy is a financial state
Insolvency is the inability to pay debts as they fall due, whereas bankruptcy is the legal declaration or process that follows
Both insolvency and bankruptcy refer exclusively to liquidation of companies
22.x: Insolvency is the financial state of being unable to pay debts when due. Bankruptcy is the legal declaration or process that follows insolvency.
22.tq: Discriminate between two closely related legal terms by identifying the state and the subsequent legal process.
xs: **Insolvency** = inability to pay debts as they fall due; **bankruptcy** = the legal declaration/process that follows — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option (2) swaps the two — the **BPSC 2023** trap.
xa: Insolvency is a **financial state**; bankruptcy is a **legal** process.
The IBC moved from **debtor-in-possession to creditor-in-control**.

22.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about personal guarantors in insolvency?
o: Personal guarantors remain liable after approval of a resolution plan
The Supreme Court affirmed it in 2021
The principle was affirmed in Lalit Kumar Jain v. Union of India
Approval of a resolution plan automatically releases every personal guarantor
22.x: Approval of a resolution plan does not automatically release guarantors; they remain liable, as affirmed in Lalit Kumar Jain (2021).
xa: **IBBI** proposed stronger safeguards for guarantor insolvency (**16 Sep 2026**).
Draft rules for personal-guarantor repayment plans: valuation + bar on related-party voting.
NCLT also handles **personal guarantors of corporate debtors**.

22.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a criticism or debate concerning the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code?
22.x: Protracted litigation, limited NCLT capacity, deep haircuts and guarantor liability are identified concerns. The Code has not eliminated guarantor liability.
22.tq: Find the option that contradicts the listed criticisms through an absolute claim.
xs: **Complete elimination of guarantor liability** is NOT a criticism — so option **(3)** is correct.
The debate is about **guarantor liability** continuing, not ending.
Real criticisms: **deep haircuts**, **protracted litigation**, **NCLT capacity** shortages.
xa: **67%** of cases exceed the timeline.
Limits on who can start **CIIRP** are another debate.

22.s: Which of the following statements best describes the term 'Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets (S4A)', recently seen in the news?
o: It is a procedure for considering the ecological costs of developmental schemes formulated by the Gov-
It is a scheme of RBI for reworking the financial structure of big corporate entities facing genuine difficul-
It is a disinvestment plan of the Government regarding Central Public Sector Undertakings.
It is an important provision in 'The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code recently implemented by the Gov-
22.x: ernment. The RBI had introduced the S4A scheme in 2016 and ended it in February 2018. It aims to provide a framework for banks to segregate sustainable and unsustainable portions of debt, thereby facilitating a more effective resolution process.

22.s: What was the purpose of the Inter-creditor Agreement signed by Indian banks and financial institutions recently?
o: To lessen the Government of India's perennial burden of fiscal deficit and current account deficit
To support the infrastructure projects of Central and State Governments
To act as an independent regulator in case of applications for loans of Rs 50 crore or more
To aim at faster resolution of stressed assets of Rs 50 crore or more, which are under consortium lending
22.x: The Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA) for resolution of stressed Assets was signed in July, 2018 by 33 banks / financial institutions. The inter-creditor agreement is aimed at resolving loan accounts of ₹50 crore or more that are under the control of a group of lenders. It is part of the "Sashakt" plan approved by the government to address the problem of resolving bad loans. According to the agreement, a two-thirds majority of the loans within a consortium of lenders should now be sufficient to override any objection to the resolution process from dissenting lenders.

22.s:
Consider the following statements regarding insolvency and bankruptcy :
1. Bankruptcy refers to a financial state in which an individual or entity is unable to pay off their debts as they become due.
2. Insolvency refers to a legal process, where the assets of the debtor are liquidated or reorganized for the benefit of creditors.
3. Bankruptcy is a state whereas insolvency is the conclusion.
4. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) is the regulatory body responsible for overseeing insolvency and bankruptcy proceedings.
Which of the above statements is/are correct?
22.x: Insolvency refers to a financial state in which an individual or entity is unable to pay off their debts as they become due. While bankruptcy refers to a legal process, where the assets of the debtor are liquidated or reorganized for the benefit of creditors.Though both terms deal with excessive debts, insolvency is a state that can lead to declaring bankruptcy. Thus, insolvency is a state whereas bankruptcy is the conclusion. Hence, statements 1, 2 and 3 are incorrect. Statement 4 is correct as the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI) is the regulatory body responsible for overseeing insolvency and bankruptcy proceedings. It was established on 1 October, 2016 and given statutory powers through the ‘Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016.’ 4. Consider the following statements: Statement-I: Syndicated lending spreads the risk of borrower default across multiple lenders. Statement-II: The syndicated loan can be a fixed amount/lump sum of funds, but cannot be a credit line. Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements? (a) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I (b) Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I (c) Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect (d) Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct I.A.S. (Pre) 2024 Ans. (c) A syndicated loan is financing offered by a syndicate made up of a group of lenders that work together

22.s: Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) is a regulatory action by Central Bank to check
22.x: Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) is an RBI regulatory framework that restricts the operations of commercial banks showing weak financial health, primarily to contain rising Non-Performing Assets (NPAs).

22.s: A loan becomes a Non-Performing Asset when interest or principal remains overdue for more than:
22.x: An NPA is a loan whose interest or principal is overdue for more than 90 days; SMA-0/1/2 (up to 90 days) are still standard.

22.s: An NPA that has remained sub-standard for more than 12 months is classified as a:
22.x: A sub-standard asset is an NPA for up to 12 months; beyond 12 months it becomes doubtful. A loss asset is one identified but not written off.

22.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about asset classification of bank loans?
o: SMA-2 accounts are still standard assets
A sub-standard asset is an NPA for up to 12 months
A loss asset is identified but not yet written off
SMA-0 accounts are classified as NPAs
22.x: SMA-0, SMA-1 and SMA-2 accounts (overdue up to 90 days) are still standard assets, not NPAs.

22.s: The Asset Quality Review (AQR) that exposed the evergreening of bank loans was conducted in:
22.x: The RBI's Asset Quality Review of 2015 exposed evergreening that had hidden NPAs.

22.s: The 'twin balance sheet' problem refers to:
o: Rising fiscal and current account deficits
Stressed NBFCs and stressed microfinance institutions
22.x: The twin balance sheet problem is the combination of over-leveraged corporates and capital-starved banks.

22.s: In March 2026, the Net NPA ratio of scheduled commercial banks stood at:
22.x: In March 2026 SCB Gross NPA was 1.93% and Net NPA 0.39%, a decadal low.

22.s: The Interest Coverage Ratio (ICR) of a firm is calculated as:
22.x: ICR = EBIT ÷ interest payable; provisions ÷ gross NPA is the Provision Coverage Ratio.

22.s: Appeals against orders of Debt Recovery Tribunals lie with the:
22.x: DRTs set up under the RDDBFI Act 1993 are backed by 5 Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunals (DRATs) for appeals.

22.s: India has 39 Debt Recovery Tribunals and how many Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunals?
22.x: There are 39 DRTs, with appeals going to 5 DRATs.

22.s: Lok Adalats help settle small NPAs mainly through:
22.x: Lok Adalats, under the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987, settle small NPAs by compromise.

22.s: In FY 2024, Lok Adalats accounted for about what share of bank recoveries?
22.x: Lok Adalats had a 3% share in FY24, against 17% for DRTs, 32% for SARFAESI and 48% for the IBC.

22.s: Under Section 13(8) of the SARFAESI Act, a borrower can redeem the secured asset only by paying:
22.x: Section 13(8) allows redemption only on payment of the full dues, not 25%.

22.s: Under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act, lenders holding at least what share of the dues may issue a 60-day notice?
22.x: Section 13(2) lets lenders with 60% of the dues issue a 60-day notice to the borrower.

22.s: Under the Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR) scheme of 2015, lenders could convert debt into equity of at least:
22.x: SDR (2015) let lenders convert debt into 51% or more equity and take control of the firm.

22.s: The 5/25 scheme of 2014 provided for:
o: Splitting of debt into sustainable and unsustainable parts
Infrastructure loans amortised over 25 years and refinanced every 5 years
22.x: The 5/25 scheme let infrastructure loans run over 25 years with refinancing every 5 years; 51% equity was SDR and the debt split was S4A.

22.s: Under the Inter-Creditor Agreement of July 2018, a resolution plan binds all lenders once approved by lenders holding:
22.x: The ICA under Project Sashakt (33 banks, loans of ₹50 crore+) binds all lenders once 66% approve.

22.s: Under the IBC, which body votes on the resolution plan of a corporate debtor?
22.x: During CIRP, the Committee of Creditors votes on the resolution plan; the NCLT adjudicates.

22.s: The Creditor-Initiated Insolvency Resolution Process (CIIRP) under the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2026 must be completed within:
22.x: CIIRP has a 150-day timeline and needs 51% creditors; CIRP has 330 days and PPIRP 120 days.

22.s: The IBC 2016 replaced which earlier law under which the BIFR functioned?
22.x: The IBC replaced the Sick Industrial Companies Act (SICA) 1985 and the BIFR.

22.s: Under the IBC, the adjudicating authority for insolvency of individuals and partnership firms is the:
22.x: The DRT handles individuals and partnership firms, while the NCLT handles companies and LLPs.

22.s: Which of the following was NOT replaced by the National Company Law Tribunal?
22.x: The NCLT replaced the CLB, BIFR and AAIFR; it did not replace SAT.

22.s: Appeals against orders of the NCLAT lie to the:
22.x: NCLAT (Delhi and Chennai) hears appeals from the NCLT, and its orders go on appeal to the Supreme Court.

22.s: The Government guarantee on security receipts issued by NARCL is:
22.x: The Government guarantees NARCL's security receipts up to ₹30,600 crore for 5 years.

22.s: In India's bad bank structure, which entity resolves the stressed assets aggregated by NARCL?
22.x: NARCL aggregates the stressed loans; IDRCL (majority private) resolves them.

22.s:
Consider the following statements about NARCL and IDRCL:
1. Public sector banks hold a majority in NARCL.
2. IDRCL is majority privately owned.
3. NARCL resolves the assets, while IDRCL aggregates them.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
22.x: PSBs hold a majority in NARCL and IDRCL is majority private; statement 3 reverses the roles: NARCL aggregates, IDRCL resolves.

22.s: Which of the following is NOT a trigger parameter under the RBI's Prompt Corrective Action framework?
22.x: The PCA triggers are capital (CRAR/CET1), asset quality (net NPA) and leverage (Tier 1 leverage ratio).

22.s: Which of the following is a restriction that may be imposed on a bank under PCA?
o: Mandatory listing on a stock exchange
22.x: Under PCA the RBI may curb lending, branch expansion, dividends and management pay.

22.s: The RBI's Prompt Corrective Action framework of 2002 was last revised in:
22.x: PCA was introduced by the RBI in 2002 and revised in November 2021.

22.s: Under the RBI Master Direction of July 2024, wilful default must be examined in NPA accounts of:
22.x: The Master Direction of 30 July 2024 requires examination of wilful default in NPAs of ₹25 lakh and above.

22.s: Under the RBI Master Direction of July 2024, the classification of a wilful defaulter must be completed within:
22.x: The 2024 Master Direction requires classification within six months, and wilful defaulters get no restructuring.

23.s: The National Mission for Financial Inclusion was announced on which date and formally launched on which date?

23.s: Which one of the following statements is not true about Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojna?
o: It is a personal accident cover
It is open to anyone between the age of 18 and 50 years
It is open to anyone between the age of 18 and 70 years
Premium payable is Rs. 12 per annum
23.x: & (d) ‘Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana’ (PMSBY) was announced by Finance Minister in Budget Speech of the financial year 2015-16. Through the Budget Speech 2015, three ambitious social security schemes pertaining to insurance and pension sector, Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY), Pradhan Mantri Jeevan Jyoti Bima Yojana (PMJJBY) and the Atal Pension Yojana (APY) were announced to move towards creating universal security system. In particular, PMSBY is aimed at covering the poor and the under-privileged at an highly affordable premium of just Rs. 20 (earlier Rs. 12) per year. The scheme provides benefit to the age group of the people between 18 to 70 years. Risk coverage under the scheme is Rs. 2 lakh for accidental death and permanent total disability and Rs. 1 lakh for partial disability for one year period stretching from 1st June to 31st May on annual renewal basis. Hence, as per the question period, only statement of option (b) was not true while at present, statements of option (b) and (d) both are incorrect.

23.s: PMJDY accounts may be linked with PMJJBY, PMSBY and:
23.x: PMJDY accounts are linked with PMJJBY, PMSBY and the Atal Pension Yojana.

**PMSBY**: **₹2 lakh** accidental death/full disability, **₹20/yr**, age **18-70**.

23.s: The annual premium under the Pradhan Mantri Suraksha Bima Yojana (PMSBY) is:
23.x: PMSBY costs Rs 20 a year for ages 18-70, paying Rs 2 lakh for accidental death or full disability and Rs 1 lakh for partial disability.
xa: **PMJJBY**: **₹436/yr**, age **18-50** (premium revised **2022**).
Enrolment: PMSBY **57.92 crore**, PMJJBY **27.33 crore**.
⚠ PMJJBY = **life**; PMSBY = **accident**.

23.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Atal Pension Yojana?
o: It provides a pension of ₹1,000 to ₹5,000 per month after age 60
Taxpayers cannot newly enrol from 1 October 2022

23.s: The wholesale pilot of India's e-rupee (e-rupee-W) began on:

23.x: PMMY was launched on 8 April 2015. MUDRA Ltd was established earlier, on 18 March 2015.

o: Loans restricted exclusively to large corporate enterprises
23.x: PMMY targets non-corporate, non-farm micro and small enterprises, not large corporate enterprises. Loans are collateral-free up to ₹20 lakh, supported by CGFMU guarantees, and linked with the MUDRA Card.
23.tq: Find the option that reverses the target group of the scheme.

23.s: DAY-NRLM, launched in 2011 to promote rural livelihoods through SHGs, is run by which Union Ministry?
o: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs

23.s: Andhra Pradesh, which ranks first in SHG-bank linkage, accounts for about what share of the national total?
23.x: AP ranks 1st with about 36% of the national share; its SHG model is run by SERP, not directly by NABARD.

23.s: Which committee is related to financial inclusion?
23.x: The C. Rangarajan Committee on Financial Inclusion (2008) made key recommendations for expanding banking access to underserved populations in India.

23.s: Which one of the following is a hindrance in the process of financial inclusion?
23.x: According to the C. Rangarajan Committee on Financial Inclusion, financial inclusion is the process of ensuring access to financial services and timely and adequate credit where needed by vulnerable groups such as weaker sections and low income groups at an affordable cost. Low income, illiteracy and lack of banks’ branches – all of these are hindrances in the process of financial inclusion.

23.s: ‘Financial Inclusion’ can be encouraged :
o: by issuing a ‘specific letter of credit’ to the deserving
by providing banking services to people of lower
by providing financial services to low income
23.x: ‘Financial Inclusion’ is a method of offering banking and financial services to individuals. It aims to include everybody in society by giving them basic financial services regardless of their income or savings. It focuses on providing financial solutions to the economically underprivileged. Hence, all of the given statements are correct and option (d) is the correct answer.

23.s: Who chaired the Committee on Comprehensive Financial Services for Small Businesses and Low-Income Households, which provided the basis for PMJDY and payments and small finance banks?

**Deepak Mohanty (2015)** drew the medium-term path on financial inclusion; **Ratan Watal (2016)** dealt with **digital payments**.
**C. Rangarajan** chaired the committee on **financial inclusion** (**2008**; **2006** in other notes).
xa: Mor also suggested a **universal account**, **basic savings account** and **Aadhaar + mobile banking**.
**Y.H. Malegam (2010)** examined the **microfinance sector** after the AP crisis.
⚠ **Malegam** = microfinance; **Watal** = digital payments; **Naidu** = CMs' committee on digital payments.

It worked on **cashless transactions after demonetisation**.
xa: Naidu later hailed **10 years of UPI** (**Aug 2026**).
**Ratan Watal Committee (2016)** of the **Ministry of Finance** also examined **digital payments**.
⚠ **Naidu** = CMs' committee; **Watal** = MoF committee on digital payments.

23.s: The three tenets of PMJDY are banking the unbanked, securing the unsecured and:
23.x: PMJDY's tenets are banking the unbanked, securing the unsecured and funding the unfunded.

"Funding" via the **overdraft up to ₹10,000**.
**JAM** = **Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile**.

23.s: Which of the following committees is wrongly matched with its subject?
o: Ratan Watal Committee – microfinance sector after the AP crisis
Deepak Mohanty Committee – medium-term path on financial inclusion
Y.H. Malegam Committee – microfinance sector after the AP crisis
23.x: The Ratan Watal Committee dealt with digital payments; the microfinance sector after the AP crisis was the Malegam Committee's subject.
xa: **Nachiket Mor (2013)** → comprehensive financial services; basis of **PMJDY**.
**N. Chandrababu Naidu (2016-17)** → **Committee of Chief Ministers on digital payments**.
AP's **2010 microfinance crisis** reshaped national MFI regulation.

23.s: Which Union Ministry administers the Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana?
o: Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises
Ministry of Finance through the Department of Financial Services
23.x: PMMY is run by the Ministry of Finance, specifically through the Department of Financial Services.

xs: PMMY is run by the **Ministry of Finance** through the **Department of Financial Services** — option **(2)**.

o: Compulsory transfer of all bank deposits to the RBI
Consent-based sharing of financial data among financial institutions
Direct lending by the Government to first-time borrowers
Issue of physical credit cards by payments banks

23.s: Which of the following is an objective of financial inclusion?
o: Restricting access to formal financial services
Limiting banking infrastructure to urban areas

Financial inclusion promotes financial literacy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 86-88]
xs: **Promoting financial literacy** is an objective of financial inclusion — option **(1)**.
Inclusion **promotes financial literacy** through **awareness** and **informed use**.

Payments and remittances through the formal system
23.x: Financial inclusion increases, not reduces, financial security; it eases formal payments and widens access to insurance and credit.
n: Financial inclusion facilitates payments and remittances through the formal financial system. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #58 · pp 86-88]

o: bringing the small entrepreneurs into formal financial
providing loans to poor farmers for cultivating

23.x: Pradhan Mantri MUDRA Yojana (PMMY) is a scheme launched by the Prime Minister Narendra Modi on April 8, 2015 for providing loans upto Rs.10 lakh to the non-corporate, non-farm small/micro enterprises. To strengthen support for aspiring entrepreneurs, the finance minister announced an increase in loan limit to Rs. 20 lakh during the Union Budget 2024-25 in July, 2024. This new limit took effect from 24 October, 2024. These loans are classified as MUDRA(Micro Units Development & Refinance Agency Ltd.) loans under PMMY. These loans are given by Commercial Banks, RRBs, Small Finance Banks, MFIs and NBFCs, while MUDRA will refinance these institutions. The borrower can approach any of the lending institutions mentioned above or can apply online through the portal www.udyamimitra.in . Under the aegis of PMMY, MUDRA has earlier created three products namely ‘Shishu’ (for loans upto Rs. 50,000), ‘Kishore’ (for loans of Rs. 50,001 upto Rs. 5 lakh) and ‘Tarun’ (for loans above Rs. 5 lakh and up to Rs. 10 lakh) to signify the stage of growth/development and funding needs of the beneficiary micro unit/entrepreneur and also provide a reference point for the next phase of graduation/growth. As per the announcement of Union Budget 2024-25, a new loan category 'Tarun Plus' (for loans above Rs. 10 lakh and upto Rs. 20 lakh) is also added, which is designed specifically for those who have previously availed and successfully repaid loans under the Tarun category.

Consider the following statements in respect of RTGS and NEFT :
I. In RTGS, the settlement time is instantaneous while in case of NEFT, it takes some time to settle payments.
II. In RTGS, the customer is charged for inward transactions while that is not the case for NEFT.
III. Operating hours for RTGS are restricted on certain days while this is not true for NEFT.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
23.x: Practically, settlement in RTGS is considered almost realtime, whereas in NEFT, due to batch-based settlement, it may take some time (around two hours). Therefore, Statement I is correct. No charges can be levied on the beneficiary for an inward (incoming) RTGS credit. No charges are levied on the beneficiary for inward (incoming) NEFT transactions either. Hence, Statement II is incorrect. Even under the earlier system, both RTGS and NEFT had restrictions on operating hours, and under the new 24×7 system, there is no separate restriction applicable to one and not the other. Therefore, Statement III–stating that RTGS hours are restricted on certain days but NEFT hours are not– is incorrect as per the current rules.

Money transferred via UPI is "commercial bank money" (your bank deposits), meaning it is a liability of your respective commercial bank. The Digital Rupee (CBDC), however, is a direct liability of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). It is a sovereign fiat currency, just like physical cash. 25.x: Deflation is defined in standard economics texts as a sustained decrease in the general price level of goods and services over a period of time. Thus, inflation brings about a redistribution of real wealth in favour of debtors at the cost of creditors. Investors in bonds and securities with fixed interest rates, consumers, fixed income groups pensioners etc. also lose in real terms during inflation.

25.s:
With reference to the Indian economy, demand-pull inflation can be caused/ increased by which of the following? Indian Economy PMF IAS IE – 13
1. Expansionary policies
2. Fiscal stimulus
3. Inflation-indexing wages
4. Higher purchasing power
5. Rising interest rates
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
25.x: Expansionary policies are correct: Demand-pull inflation is the upward pressure on prices that follows a shortage of supply, where too much money chases too few goods. Expansionary monetary or fiscal policies aim to increase aggregate demand by lowering interest rates or increasing government spending. This can boost consumer and business spending, leading to higher demand for goods and services. As demand outstrips supply, it results in demand-pull inflation. Fiscal stimulus is correct: Fiscal stimulus involves increasing government spending or reducing taxes to boost economic activity. This increases disposable income and encourages spending, which can lead to higher aggregate demand and, consequently, demand-pull inflation. Inflation-indexing wages is incorrect: Inflation-indexing wages means adjusting wages based on the rate of inflation. This can lead to cost-push inflation rather than demand-pull inflation. 28.s: A redistribution of income in a country can be best brought about through :
28.x: Redistribution of income and wealth are respectively the transfer of income and wealth (including physical property) from some individuals to others by means of taxation, monetary policies, welfare policies, public services, land reforms etc. This can be achieved with a combination of progressive taxation and progressive expenditure. A progressive tax is one where the average tax burden increases with income. It applies higher tax rates to higher levels of income. High-income families pay a disproportionate high share of the tax burden, while low-and middle-income taxpayers shoulder a relatively small tax burden. Regarding the distributive impact of public expenditure, the principle of maximum social welfare should be the underlying criteria of public spending. Therefore, progressive public expenditure (like free medical aid, free education, subsidized houses etc. to poors) is the best antidote to reduce income inequality existing in the society.

28.s: Which of the following is a direct tax?
28.x: Direct Taxes : A direct tax is a kind of charge, which is imposed directly on the taxpayer and paid directly to the government by the persons/entities on whom it imposed. A direct tax is one that cannot be shifted by the taxpayer to someone else. Examples : Income Tax, Corporation Tax, Property Tax, Wealth Tax, Gift Tax etc. Indirect Taxes : An indirect tax is a tax collected by an intermediary (such as a retail store) from the person who bears the ultimate economic burden of the tax (such as the customer). An indirect tax is one that can be shifted by the taxpayer to someone else. An indirect tax may increase the price of a good so that consumers are actually paying the tax by paying more for the products. Examples : Customs Duty, Central Excise Duty, Service Tax, Sales Tax, GST, Value Added Tax (VAT) etc.

28.s: MODVAT is related to :
28.x: MODVAT (Modified Value Added Tax) is basically related to the excise duties. In the mid 1980s, the excise duty reforms focused on relieving tax cascading, rationalization of duty rates, and simplification of rules and procedures. As a first step towards mitigating tax cascading, MODVAT was incorporated in the Indian tax system in the year 1986, covering a few limited commodities initially. This permitted the manufacturers to avail of tax credit for the excise duty paid on their purchase of specified raw materials (and not capital goods) used in the manufacturing of specified goods. After being in froce for around 15 years, MODVAT was replaced by CENVAT (Central Value Added Tax) from 1 April, 2000. MODVAT/CENVAT is different from the VAT as under MODVAT/CENVAT, excise is levied on final value and then rebate is given on inputs while under VAT, tax is levied on value addition at each stage of transaction in the production-distribution chain.

Tax imposed by the State Government but collected

28.x: During the question period, Sales tax was a form of indirect tax imposed on the sale and purchase of goods within India. The tax imposed on the sale and purchase of goods within the State was called Sales Tax while the Central Sales Tax was charged by the Central Government for the inter-state transfers. Hence, the sales tax we had to pay while purchasing a toothpaste during the question period, was a tax imposed and collected by the State Government. Sales tax (or VAT) has been replaced by the Goods and Services Tax (GST) since 1 July, 2017. Under the GST regime, when the supply of goods or services happens within a State called intra-state transactions, then both the CGST (Central GST) and SGST (State GST) will be collected. Whereas if the supply of goods or services happens between the States called as inter-state transactions, then only IGST (Integrated GST) will be collected. Under the GST law, the Central Government would levy and collect CGST and IGST, while the State Governments would levy and collect SGST.

28.s: Direct Tax Code in India is related to which of the following?
28.x: Among the given options, Direct Tax Code (DTC) in India is related to Income Tax (and other direct taxes). Through DTC, the government's aim was simplify the structure of direct tax laws into a single legislation. The DTC was planned to replace the Income Tax Act, 1961 and other direct tax legislations like the Wealth Tax Act, 1957. The first Direct Tax Code Bill was introduced in the Parliament in 2010, but it was lapsed. In 2017, the government set up a task force (headed by Akhilesh Ranjan) to draft a new DTC. The report of the task force on DTC was submitted to Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman in August, 2019. It is to be noted that the new Income Tax Bill, 2025, received the President's assent on 21 August, 2025 and officially notified as the Income Tax Act, 2025 to replace the decades-old Income Tax Act, 1961. It came into force from 1 April, 2026.

28.x: Income tax is a direct tax. Income tax in India is a tax paid by the individuals or entities depending on the level of their earning or gains during a financial year. The Government of India decides the rate of income tax as well as income tax slabs on which individuals or entities are taxed. It is levied and collected by the Union Government. It is a progressive tax. A progressive tax is a tax in which the tax rate increases as the taxable amount increases. However, Income tax in India is also overall degressive as after a certain limit, its rate becomes fl at or constant. Hence, only statement I and II are correct while statement III and IV are incorrect.

28.s: What kind of Tax System is found in India?
28.x: The tax system in India is progressive in nature but overall degressive. In the degressive tax system, the tax rate is increased firstly with the increase in income and then, the rate remains fl at or constant with further increase in income.

28.s: According to the Union Budget 2016-17, a surcharge of 15% is payable if the income is :
28.x: Income tax surcharge is an additional charge payable on income tax. It is an added tax on the taxpayers having a higher income inflow during a particular financial year. According to the Union Budget 2016-17, surcharge shall be levied at the rate of fifteen percent, if the individual's income is above Rs. one crore. At present (for Assessment Year 2026-27/FY 2025-26), surcharge rates (for individuals) on different income slabs under old tax regime are as follows : Income Tax Slab Surcharge rate Upto Rs. 50 lakh Nil Above Rs. 50 lakh to Rs. 1 crore 10% Above Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 2 crore 15% Above Rs. 2 crore to Rs. 5 crore 25% Above Rs. 5 crore 37% In, Union Budget 2023-24, the highest surcharge of 37% was reduced to 25% under the new tax regime, which is applicable from 1 April, 2023. Under the new tax regime the surcharge rates are same as old tax regime upto income of Rs. 5 crore, while surcharge rate of 25% is also applicable to income above Rs. 5 crore instead of 37% of old tax regime. Note : The dual-year system of 'Financial Year' (FY) and 'Assessment Year' (AY) is now eliminated. The Income Tax Act, 2025 unifies these into a single concept called the 'Tax Year', effective from April 1, 2026. Income is now taxed in the same 12-month period it is earned, removing dual-year confusion.

29.s: Under the new tax regime from Budget 2025-26, income in the slab of ₹20–24 lakh and income above ₹24 lakh are taxed respectively at:
29.x: The ₹20–24 lakh slab carries a 25% rate, while income above ₹24 lakh is taxed at 30%.

xs: Under the new regime, **₹20-24 lakh is taxed at 25%** and **above ₹24 lakh at 30%** — option **(2)**.
**30%** is the top rate; no slab carries **35%**, ruling out options (1) and (3).
**20%** belongs to the **₹16-20 lakh** slab, so option (4) is one slab too low.
xa: In the **2020-21** first new regime, the **30%** rate started **above 15 lakh**.
**Budget 2026-27** made **no change** in slabs.

29.s: Under the first new optional income-tax regime of Budget 2020-21, income in the slab of Rs 5 lakh to Rs 7.5 lakh was taxed at:
29.x: In the 2020-21 new regime, 0-2.5 lakh was nil, 2.5-5 lakh 5%, 5-7.5 lakh 10% (APPSC 2019 key), 7.5-10 lakh 15% and 10-12.5 lakh 20%. So 5%, 15% and 20% belong to other slabs.

xa: The rest of that ladder: **0-2.5 lakh nil**; **12.5-15 lakh 25%**; **above 15 lakh 30%**.
**Budget 2023-24** raised the nil slab to **3 lakh** and cut the top surcharge **37% → 25%**.
From **Budget 2025-26**, **₹8-12 lakh** is the **10%** slab.

xa: Other changes: **simpler language**; **obsolete provisions removed**.

29.s: Income tax was first introduced in India in 1860 by:
29.x: James Wilson, the first Finance Member, introduced income tax in India in 1860. Dalhousie and Ripon were Governors-General/Viceroys known for other reforms, and Kaldor advised on tax reform in 1956.
xs: Income tax was first introduced in India in **1860** by **James Wilson** — option **(2)**.
**Nicholas Kaldor** came much later: his **1956** advice led to **wealth tax (1957)**, **expenditure tax (1958)** and **gift tax (1958)**.
xa: The **Income Tax Department** was created under the **1922 Act**.
**Expenditure tax (1958)** was the first introduced in independent India, by FM **T.T. Krishnamachari** (APPSC 2019).
The **Income-tax Act, 1961** (effective **1 April 1962**) was replaced by the **Income-tax Act, 2025** from **1 April 2026**.

29.s: Minimum Alternate Tax is primarily imposed on companies which:
o: Have no book profits but earn only agricultural income
Are registered as unlisted start-ups receiving share premium
Show book profits but otherwise pay little or no regular income tax

29.tq: Apply the purpose of the tax to a company’s accounting and regular-tax situation.
xs: MAT targets companies that **show book profits but pay little or no regular income tax** — option **(4)**.
It taxes so-called **"zero-tax companies"** on **book profits** at **15%**.
Share premium of unlisted start-ups was **angel tax**; dividends were hit by **DDT**; rural agricultural income is **exempt**.
xa: MAT was introduced in the **1986-87 Budget** at **15.75%**.
Companies opting into the **2019 concessional rates** (115BAA/115BAB) are **outside MAT**.
**Budget 2026-27**: MAT **14%**, a **final tax**; old credit set off up to **1/4** of liability.

29.s: Income tax is generally classified as which of the following?

29.s: Income tax in India was introduced by :
29.x: The first Income Tax Act was introduced in India in 1860 by James Wilson. The act received the assent of the governor-general on 24 July, 1860, and came into effect immediately. Under this act, income was classified in four schedules : 1. Income from landed property; 2. Income from professions and trade; 3. Income from securities, annuities and dividends; and 4. 29.s: The Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) was introduced in the Budget of the Government of India for the year:
29.x: The Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) is a tax first introduced in India by the Union Budget 1987-88 (Finance Act, 1987) with effect from assessment year 1988-89. Later on, it was withdrawn by the Finance Act, 1990 and then reintroduced by the Union Budget 1996-97 (Finance Act, 1996) with effect from 1 April, 1997. The objective of introduction of MAT is to bring into the tax net 'zero tax companies' which in spite of having earned substantial book profits and having paid handsome dividends, do not pay any tax due to various tax concessions and incentives provided under the Income Tax Law. At present, MAT is computed by 15% (plus surcharge and cess as applicable) on book profit. It is levied at the rate of 9% (plus surcharge and cess as applicable) in case of a company being a unit of an International Financial Services Centre and deriving its income solely in convertible foreign exchange.

29.s: Tax on sale of inherited property is :
29.x: Tax on sale of inherited property is called 'Capital Gain Tax'. Any profit or gain that arises from the sale of a 'capital asset' is a capital gain. Capital gains are not applicable to an inherited property as there is no sale, only a transfer of ownership. Under Section 56 (ii) of the Income Tax Act, there is no inheritance tax applicable in India irrespective of the cost of the inherited property. However, if the person who inherited the asset decides to sell it, capital gains tax will be applicable.

Whereas Capital Gains Tax is not related to income of corporate. It is a levy on the profit that an investor gains from the sale of an investment in capital assets like stocks, bonds, real estate etc.

29.s: The term 'Base Erosion and Profit Shifting' is sometimes seen in the news in the context of
o: mining operation by multinational companies in resource-rich but backward areas
curbing of the tax evasion by multinational companies
exploitation of genetic resources of a country by multinational companies
lack of consideration of environmental costs in the planning and implementation of developmental projects
29.x: Base Erosion and Profit Shifting occurs when multinational companies exploit gaps or mismatches in tax rules to artificially shift profits to lowor no-tax jurisdictions, even if their business activities are not substantively present there. This reduces their tax liability in the countries where they operate and generate revenue, ultimately eroding those countries' tax bases. India has ratified the Multilateral Convention to Implement Tax Treaty Related Measures to Prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (MLI). The Multilateral Convention/MLI is an outcome of the OECD / G20 Project to tackle Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (the "BEPS Project").

29.x: Statement I is incorrect: Agricultural income is exempted from tax under the Income-tax Act, 1961. It is important to note that income from allied agricultural activities like poultry farming, wool rearing, etc., is not considered agricultural income. Hence, tax may be levied on incomes from such activities. However, many states levy a tax on agricultural income under their respective state policies. It is highly unlikely that allied activities such as poultry farming or wool rearing would be completely outside any taxation system. Once Statement I is eliminated, only option (d) is left.

29.s: A PAN has initially a five-alphabet series like AFZPK 7190K. Here P stands for :
29.x: Permanent Account Number (PAN) is a 10-character alphanumeric identifier, which is used as an identity proof. It is used mainly for the tax related purposes. The first five characters of PAN are letters from the English alphabet, the next four characters are numbers and last character is also a letter. The fourth character for a majority of PAN holders is the letter "P", which stands for 'Person (Individual)'. The other nine letters that can represent the fourth character are C, H, F, A, T, B, L, J and G : C – Company H – Hindu Undivided Family (HUF) F – Firm A – Association of Persons (AoP) T – Trust B – Body of Individuals (BoI) L – Local Authority J – Artificial Juridical Person G – Government Agency

29.x: Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) refers to tax planning strategies used by multinational enterprises that exploit gaps and mismatches in tax rules to make profit 'disappear' for tax purpose or to shift profits to locations where there is little or no real activity but taxes are low, resulting in little or no overall corporate tax being paid. Developing countries’ higher reliance on corporate tax means they suffer from BEPS disproportionately. BEPS practices cost countries about USD 100-240 billion in lost revenue annually. Working together within OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework on BEPS, over 145 countries and jurisdictions are collaborating on the implementation of 15 measures to tackle tax avoidance, improve the coherence of international tax rules and ensure a more transparent tax environment.

As per the terms of reference, the Task Force on Direct Taxes was mandated to make recommendations on rationalisation and simplification of direct taxes, improvement in tax payer services and redesigning procedures for strengthening enforcement. 30.x: One of the most important aspects of Goods and Services Tax (GST) is the Input Tax Credit (ITC) Mechanism, which ensures a seamless flow of credit, reduces the tax burden on businesses, and avoids the cascading of taxes and double taxation. Cascading of taxes, in simple language, is 'tax on tax'. Under the earlier system of taxation, credit of taxes being levied by Central Government was not available as set-off for payment of taxes levied by State Governments, and vice versa. One of the most important features of the GST system is that the entire supply chain would be subject to GST to be levied by Central and State Government concurrently. As the tax charged by the Central or the State Governments would be part of the same tax regime, credit of tax paid at every stage would be available as set-off for payment of tax at every subsequent stage. Input Tax Credit (ITC) refers to the credit that businesses receive for the GST paid on the purchase of goods or services intended for business use. ITC plays a crucial role in the GST framework by reducing the overall tax burden for businesses and ensuring that tax is levied only on the value addition. The ITC mechanism allows registered taxpayers to reduce their overall GST liability by claiming the credit for taxes paid on their inputs (purchases). 30.x: Uninterrupted and seamless chain of input tax credit (ITC) is one of the key features of Goods and Services Tax. ITC is a mechanism to avoid cascading of taxes. Any registered person can avail credit of tax paid on the inward supply of goods or services or both, which is used or intended to be used in the course or furtherance of business subject to certain conditions. Thus, ITC means the credit of input tax on the supplies of goods and services or both received by a registered person. Eligibility of ITC includes taxable supply and zerorated supply, but non-taxable, exempt and nil-rated supplies are not eligible for ITC. Zero-rated supply is different from nil-rated supply (goods and services on which 0% GST is applicable). Any supplies made by a registered dealer as an export (both goods or services) or supply to an SEZ qualifies for zero-rated supplies in GST and ITC is available for them. Hence, statement 1 is correct while statement 2 is incorrect.
