30.x: Article 246A gives GST law-making power; 269A covers IGST and 279A the GST Council, while 268A (service tax) was omitted.

30.s: By the 101st Constitutional Amendment, Article 268A relating to service tax was:
30.x: The 101st Amendment omitted Article 268A on service tax, since service tax was subsumed in GST.

30.s: In the GST Council, the Union Minister of State in charge of Revenue or Finance is:
30.x: The Union Finance Minister chairs the Council; the MoS in charge of Revenue or Finance is only a member.

30.s: The Vice-Chairperson of the GST Council is chosen by:
o: The State members from among themselves
30.x: The State members of the GST Council choose the Vice-Chairperson from among themselves.

30.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the GST Council?
o: It recommends tax rates, exemptions and threshold limits
It sets up a mechanism to settle Centre-State disputes
Its recommendations bind Parliament and the States
Its proceedings are not invalid because of a vacancy
30.x: In Mohit Minerals (2022) the Council's recommendations were held persuasive, not binding; legislative power stays with Parliament and the States.

30.s: Which of the following was subsumed in GST?
30.x: Entry tax was subsumed in GST; stamp duty, Basic Customs Duty and electricity duty were not.

30.s:
Consider the following statements about taxes and GST:
1. Service tax and CVD on imports were subsumed in GST.
2. State excise on alcoholic liquor was subsumed in GST.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
30.x: Service tax and CVD were subsumed; State excise on alcoholic liquor was retained outside GST.

30.s: UTGST is levied on intra-UT supplies in:
30.x: UTGST is levied by the Centre for Union Territories without a legislature.

30.s: IGST is levied by the Centre on:
30.x: IGST under Article 269A applies to inter-State supplies and imports, and settles to the consuming State.

30.s: Under the GST Acts, the ceiling rate for IGST is:
30.x: The GST Acts set ceilings of 20% for CGST and 40% for IGST.

30.s: Under GST 2.0, the 40% rate applies to:
30.x: GST 2.0 has 5% for merit goods, 18% standard, and 40% for sin and ultra-luxury (de-merit) goods.

30.s: In December 2022, the work of the National Anti-Profiteering Authority was first transferred to the:
30.x: NAA's work went to the CCI in December 2022, and only from 1 October 2024 to the GSTAT Principal Bench.

30.s: How many digits does a GSTIN have?
30.x: The GSTIN, issued through the GSTN system, is a 15-digit number.

30.s: An e-way bill is generally valid for one day for every:
30.x: An e-way bill, needed for goods above ₹50,000, is valid one day per 200 km.

30.s: Under the GST Compensation Act, any unutilised balance at the end is split between the Centre and the States in the ratio:
30.x: The unutilised balance is split 50:50 – half to the Centre and half shared among the States.

30.s: The GST compensation cess finally ended on:
30.x: Compensation ended in June 2022, cess was scrapped for all but tobacco on 22 Sep 2025, and it ended on 31 March 2026.

30.s: India's record gross GST collection of ₹2.43 lakh crore came in:
30.x: Gross GST hit a record ₹2.43 lakh crore in April 2026.

30.s: In Q1 2026-27, while GST 2.0 cut revenue, the Centre's gross tax grew by only:
30.x: July 2026 GST rose 15.4%, but the Centre's gross tax grew only 3.7% in Q1 2026-27.

31.s: In which month did monthly gross GST collections first exceed ₹2 lakh crore?
31.x: Monthly gross GST collections crossed ₹2 lakh crore for the first time in April 2024.
31.tq: Test a milestone date using close year alternatives.
xs: Monthly gross GST first exceeded **₹2 lakh crore** in **April 2024** — option **(4)**.
**April 2026** is the later **record** month (**₹2.43 lakh crore**), not the first crossing.
xa: FY 2017-18 average: **₹82,000 cr/month**.
**FY 2024-25**: **₹22.08 lakh crore**, avg **₹1.84 lakh crore**/month.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly represents India’s gross GST collection during FY 2024-25?
o: ₹22.08 lakh crore, with an average of ₹1.84 lakh crore per month
₹24.08 lakh crore, with an average of ₹2.04 lakh crore per month
₹22.08 lakh crore, with an average of ₹2.43 lakh crore per month
₹17.4 lakh crore, with an average of ₹1.82 lakh crore per month
31.x: Gross GST collection in FY 2024-25 was ₹22.08 lakh crore, averaging ₹1.84 lakh crore per month.
31.tq: Separate an annual total from its monthly average using precise numerical matching.
xs: **FY 2024-25** gross GST: **₹22.08 lakh crore**, average **₹1.84 lakh crore** per month — option **(1)**.
**₹2.43 lakh crore** is the **April 2026** record month; **₹17.4 lakh crore** is the **Apr-Dec 2025** total.
xa: Collections **doubled in 4 years**, a **CAGR of 18%**.
FY 2017-18 average was only **₹82,000 cr/month**.

31.s: Which of the following correctly represents the original GST rate structure introduced in 2017, apart from exempt goods and compensation cess?
31.x: The original GST structure contained slabs of 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%, along with exempt goods and compensation cess over 28% for specified goods.
31.tq: Recall the complete original slab sequence.
xs: The **2017** structure had slabs of **5%, 12%, 18%, 28%** + exempt goods — option **(4)**.
A **compensation cess** sat over **28%** on luxury/sin goods.
xa: GST 2.0: **0, 5% (merit), 18% (standard), 40% (demerit)**.
Special rates: **0.25%** rough diamonds; **3%** gold/silver/jewellery.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about GST collections in April 2026?
o: Gross collection reached a record ₹2.43 lakh crore
It was the first month gross collection crossed ₹2 lakh crore
31.x: Gross GST first crossed ₹2 lakh crore in April 2024; April 2026 set the record of ₹2.43 lakh crore (+8.7%) with net ₹2.11 lakh crore.

31.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the GST rate structure from 22 September 2025?
o: 0%, 5% as merit rate, 18% as standard rate and 40% as demerit rate
31.x: GST 2.0 rationalised the principal slabs into 0%, 5%, 18% and 40%, with 5% as the merit rate, 18% as the standard rate and 40% as the demerit rate.
31.tq: Compare the post-rationalisation labels and rates as a complete structure.
xs: From **22 Sep 2025** slabs are **0, 5% (merit), 18% (standard), 40% (demerit)** — option **(3)**.
**5, 12, 18, 28%** was the pre-2.0 structure; the **12%** slab no longer exists.
xa: Old **12%** slab: ~**99%** of items moved to **5%**.
Approved at the **56th Council** (3-4 Sep 2025).

31.s: The GST rate applicable to rough diamonds and gold, silver and jewellery under the special-rate structure is, respectively:
31.x: Rough diamonds attract a special rate of 0.25%, while gold, silver and jewellery attract 3%.
31.tq: Read paired numerical rates in the order in which the commodities are given.
xs: Special rates: **0.25%** on **rough diamonds**, **3%** on **gold/silver/jewellery** — option **(4)**.
Option (2) reverses the two rates.
xa: Main slabs: **0, 5% (merit), 18% (standard), 40% (demerit)**.
**Tractors 12% → 5%**.
**Small cars, bikes ≤350cc, ACs 28% → 18%**.

31.s: The four-slab structure of GST was originally intended to be:
o: A permanent arrangement for all goods and services
A mechanism for distributing IGST among States
A structure applicable only to petroleum products
31.x: The four-slab GST structure was conceived as a transitional arrangement rather than a permanent structure.
31.tq: Test the intended character of a policy arrangement rather than its numerical details.
xs: The four-slab structure was meant to be **transitional**, ahead of simplification — option **(4)**.
It had slabs **5%, 12%, 18%, 28%** (2017) + exempt goods.
xa: GST 2.0 replaced it with **0, 5, 18, 40%** from **22 Sep 2025**.
Multiple rates caused **misclassification** and **classification disputes**.
Further ask: **GST 3.0** simplification (CII AP, **1 Feb 2026**).

31.s: Which of the following pairs about GST 2.0 slab shifts (from 22 September 2025) is correctly matched?
31.x: About 99% of old 12% items moved to 5%; about 90% of old 28% items moved to 18%, and only the rest to 40%.

31.s: Which of the following is the most direct contribution of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) to inter-State commerce?
o: Replacement of input tax credit by a turnover tax
Creation of a common national market through tax harmonisation
Exemption of all inter-State supplies from taxation
Retention of State border check-posts for all goods
31.x: GST created a common national market by harmonising indirect taxation across States. It also helped reduce the cascading effect through input tax credit.
31.tq: Identify the core objective rather than choosing an extreme or reversed consequence.
xs: GST's key contribution: a **common national market** through **tax harmonisation** — option **(2)**.
**ITC at every stage** was kept, not replaced (ending **cascading**); inter-State supplies are taxed under **IGST**.
Border **check-posts were dismantled**, not retained.
xa: **Digital tools**: e-invoicing, e-way bills, auto-generated returns; reduced human interface.
Taxpayer base: **66.5 lakh (2017) → 1.51 crore (2025)**.

31.s: An e-way bill under GST is valid for one day for every:
31.x: Validity is one day per 200 km; the e-way bill is mandatory above ₹50,000.
xa: E-way bills replaced physical checks, so State border **check-posts were dismantled**.
E-way bills with **e-invoicing** and AI scrutiny counter **fake invoicing**.

31.s: The removal of inter-State check-posts after the rollout of e-way bills primarily resulted in:
o: A shift from digital to manual tax reporting
Reduced transit time and logistics costs
The abolition of input tax credit
31.x: The replacement of physical checks and the dismantling of border check-posts reduced truck waiting time, transit time and logistics costs.
31.tq: Link the administrative reform to its practical logistics outcome.
xs: Removing check-posts **cut transit time and logistics costs** — option **(2)**.
It also cut **truck waiting time**, once **entry tax** was subsumed and **e-way bills** replaced physical checks.
It moved reporting **toward digital**, with fewer physical checks — the opposite of options (1) and (3).
xa: E-way bill: needed for goods over **Rs 50,000**; valid **1 day per 200 km**.
E-way bill volumes rose **21%** in Apr-Dec 2025.
**ITC** at every stage ended the **cascading effect**.

31.s: Which of the following best indicates the expansion of formalisation under GST between 2017 and 2025?
o: The taxpayer base remained unchanged at 66.5 lakh
The taxpayer base increased from 1.51 crore to 66.5 lakh
The taxpayer base increased from 66.5 lakh to 1.51 crore
The taxpayer base declined from 1.51 crore to 66.5 lakh
31.x: The taxpayer base expanded from 66.5 lakh in 2017 to 1.51 crore in 2025, indicating greater formalisation.
31.tq: Compare the direction and magnitude of a two-point trend without reversing the figures.
xs: The GST taxpayer base grew **from 66.5 lakh (2017) to 1.51 crore (2025)** — option **(3)**.
This expansion signals **greater formalisation**.
xa: MSME gains: **credit access/eligibility** and **procurement parity** for small firms.
**Composition scheme**: turnover up to **Rs 1.5 crore** (Rs **50 lakh** for services).
Still a burden: **multiple returns + ITC matching**.

31.s: A taxpayer under the GST composition scheme pays a flat rate of ____ on goods.
31.x: The composition scheme levies 1% on goods and 6% on services, and the taxpayer cannot claim ITC.
xa: Taxpayer base grew from **66.5 lakh (2017)** to **1.51 crore (2025)** — greater formalisation.
**E-way bill** is mandatory for goods worth over **Rs 50,000**.
⚠ **Inverted Duty Structure:** input rate > output rate → refund of unutilised ITC allowed.

31.s: The GST 2.0 reforms were approved at which GST Council meeting and became effective from which date?
31.x: The GST 2.0 reforms were approved at the 56th GST Council meeting held on 3–4 September 2025 and became effective on 22 September 2025.
31.tq: Pair the reform package with both its approving meeting and effective date.
xs: GST 2.0 was approved at the **56th GST Council meeting** (3-4 Sep 2025), effective **22 September 2025** — option **(4)**.
The **57th** meeting is fixed for **12 Sep 2026**, a year later.
xa: Also called the **NextGen GST reforms**.
Inverted-duty refunds were flagged for the **57th** meeting.
**ES 2025-26**: GST 2.0 = **third pillar of tax reform**.

31.s: Which practice is characteristic of the ITC fraud involving bogus entities?
o: Paying output tax twice on genuine transactions
Issuing invoices without actual supply of goods or services
Using only government invoices for exports
Claiming refunds on petroleum products outside GST
31.x: Bogus entities issue invoices without any corresponding supply in order to fraudulently claim input tax credit.
31.tq: Identify the fraudulent mechanism from a practical transaction scenario.
xs: In **ITC fraud**, bogus entities **issue invoices without actual supply** — option **(2)**.
An **AP-Telangana-Karnataka** network used **fake registrations + scrap bills** to claim ITC (**3 Jan 2026**).
xa: Countered by **e-invoicing**, **UPI/Aadhaar tracking** and **AI scrutiny**.
AP's **Legal-AI assistant** was trained on ~**22,000 judgments**.
**E-way bills** add to AI-based scrutiny against fake invoicing.

31.s: The destination principle of GST generally favours:
o: States with the highest rates of State excise duty
Producing States because tax is collected at the point of manufacture
Consuming States because taxation follows the place of consumption
31.x: GST follows the destination principle, under which consuming States benefit because revenue is associated with the place of consumption.
31.tq: Distinguish destination-based taxation from origin-based taxation.
xs: The destination principle favours **consuming States**, since taxation follows the **place of consumption** — option **(3)**.
GST revenue goes to the State where goods/services are **consumed, not produced** — so producing States do not gain (option 2).
xa: **IGST** on inter-State supply (**Art. 269A**): levied by the Centre, apportioned; the **destination State** gets the State share.
Manufacturing States (**Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka**) feared loss.
AP, a **consuming State**, benefits via **IGST settlement**.

31.s: Andhra Pradesh, being a consuming State, benefits from GST primarily through:
o: State excise on petroleum under GST
Abolition of its own tax revenue
31.x: As a consuming State, Andhra Pradesh benefits from the destination principle through IGST settlement.
31.tq: Apply the destination principle to the fiscal position of a particular State.
xs: AP, a **consuming State**, benefits mainly through **IGST settlement** — option **(2)**.
Under the destination principle, the **destination State** receives the State share of IGST.
**Petroleum** is still outside GST, so option (3) is impossible.
xa: AP's **Net GST** = **SGST + IGST settlement share**.
GST is AP's largest own-tax source: **38%** = **Rs 36,296 crore** (2024-25 RE).
Up to **Aug 2026**, AP net GST was **₹16,452.62 cr**.

31.s: Under an Inverted Duty Structure, input tax credit accumulates and blocks working capital because:
o: Tax on output exceeds tax on inputs
Tax paid on inputs exceeds tax payable on output
IGST is not apportioned to States
31.x: When the tax on inputs is higher than the tax on output, ITC piles up and blocks the working capital of businesses.

31.s:
Consider the following about an inter-State supply under GST:
1. IGST is levied by the Centre and apportioned.
2. The State share of IGST goes to the producing State.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
31.x: IGST is levied by the Centre and apportioned; the destination (consuming) State receives the State share.
xa: IGST rests on **Art. 269A**.
GST is a **destination-based consumption tax**.
The fear of producing States was a key reason for the **5-year compensation guarantee**.

31.s: Which group of States mainly represents manufacturing or producing States that feared revenue loss under the destination-based GST system?
o: Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka
31.x: Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka were identified as manufacturing States that feared losses because GST revenue follows consumption rather than production. This concern contributed to the five-year compensation guarantee.
31.tq: Match the policy effect with the group of affected producing States.
xs: **Maharashtra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka** — manufacturing States — feared loss — option **(1)**.
Under the destination principle, revenue goes to the **consuming** State, not the producing one.
xa: This fear was a key reason for the **5-year compensation guarantee**.
Today **manufacturing States gain** from concentrated buoyancy; **unorganised-sector States** depend on FC devolution.
AP, a **consuming State**, benefits via IGST settlement.

31.s: For Andhra Pradesh, “Net GST” is defined as:
o: Gross GST collections minus customs revenue
SGST plus the State’s share of IGST settlement
SGST minus the State’s share of IGST settlement
31.x: Andhra Pradesh’s Net GST consists of SGST plus its share received through IGST settlement.
31.tq: Discriminate between a State’s own GST component and its settled IGST share.
xs: AP's **Net GST** = **SGST + the State's share of IGST settlement** — option **(3)**.
IGST settlement is **added**, not subtracted, and **State Excise** is outside GST.
xa: Up to **Aug 2026**: net GST **₹16,452.62 cr**; commercial taxes **₹25,449.80 cr** (+18.05%).
AP benefits as a **consuming State** via IGST settlement.

31.s: In May 2026, the Andhra Pradesh High Court held that where Central and State GST investigations overlap, the authorities must:
o: Abandon the investigation if the entity operates in more than one State
Decide inter se which authority will proceed
Transfer every case automatically to the Union Government
Both proceed simultaneously against the same entity
31.x: The Court held that Central and State GST authorities must decide inter se who will proceed against a common entity, thereby preventing dual action.
31.tq: Identify the precise institutional solution to overlapping jurisdiction.
xs: The **AP High Court** (May **2026**) held that Central and State GST authorities must **decide inter se** who proceeds — option **(2)**.
The aim is to **prevent dual action** against one entity — so option (4) is the very thing ruled out.
xa: **Mohit Minerals (2022)**: Council recommendations **persuasive, not binding**.
Fake invoicing is countered by **e-invoicing** + AI-based scrutiny with e-way bills.

31.s: States were guaranteed GST compensation at an assured annual growth rate of ____ over the 2015-16 base.
31.x: Compensation was assured for five years (July 2017 – June 2022) at 14% annual growth over the 2015-16 base.

31.s: The GST compensation cess was continued after the compensation period primarily to:
o: Repay loans taken to pay compensation during the COVID-19 period
31.x: After the compensation period, the cess was continued to repay loans taken for paying GST compensation during the COVID-19 period.
31.tq: Identify the stated purpose behind continuation of a fiscal instrument.
xs: The cess was continued to **repay COVID back-to-back loans** taken to pay compensation — option **(2)**.
It ran to **March 2026** for that purpose, long after compensation ended in **June 2022**.
xa: Scrapped **22 September 2025** except **tobacco products**.
The **tobacco cess** continues until cess-account **loan obligations are discharged**.
Compensation period: **5 years** at **14%** growth.

31.s: With effect from 22 September 2025, the GST compensation cess was scrapped for all goods except:
31.x: The compensation cess was scrapped on 22 September 2025 except for tobacco products, on which it continues until cess-account loan obligations are discharged.
31.tq: Test the exception to a general abolition of the cess.
xs: From **22 September 2025**, the cess was scrapped for all goods except **tobacco products** — option **(3)**.
The tobacco cess continues until **cess-account loan obligations** are discharged.
**Online gaming** and luxury cars now fall in the **40%** demerit slab; aerated drinks lost the cess.
xa: Original cess goods: **luxury cars, aerated drinks, pan masala, tobacco**.
GST 2.0 took effect on the same date, **22 September 2025**.
Unused balance: **50% to Centre**, **50% to States**.

31.s: How is the unused balance of the GST compensation cess to be shared?
o: Entirely to the States in proportion to their population
50% to the Centre and 50% to the States in proportion to their SGST revenue
As per the Finance Commission's horizontal devolution formula
31.x: The unused balance goes 50% to the Centre and 50% to the States, with the States' half shared in proportion to their SGST revenue. It does not all go to the Centre (A), it is not shared by population (B), and the Finance Commission formula (D) does not apply because cess is outside the divisible pool.
31.tq: Unused compensation cess: 50:50, States' half by SGST share.
xs: The unused cess balance goes **50% to the Centre** and **50% to the States**, in proportion to **SGST revenue** — option **(3)**.
It is not all to the Centre, not by population, and not by the FC formula — cesses sit **outside the divisible pool**.
xa: Cess **scrapped 22 September 2025** except tobacco.
Compensation: **July 2017 - June 2022** at **14%** growth.
Law: **GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017**.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about GST compliance for small businesses?
o: The composition scheme has eased the compliance burden
Automated registration has eased the compliance burden
Multiple returns and ITC matching remain a burden
The reform agenda proposes replacing pre-filled returns with manual filing
31.x: The reform agenda calls for pre-filled returns, time-bound digital registration and automated exporter refunds, not manual filing.
xa: The agenda also seeks **time-bound digital registration** and **automated refunds for exporters** (Aug 2025).
Composition: flat **1%** goods / **6%** services.

31.s: What is identified as the biggest drawback of the multiple-rate structure under GST?
o: Delay in settlement of IGST between the Union and the States
Dependence of States on Finance Commission devolution
Misclassification of goods and services and classification disputes
Complete exclusion of petroleum products from taxation
31.x: The multiple-rate structure creates difficulties in classifying goods and services, resulting in frequent classification disputes.
31.tq: Directly identify the specific weakness associated with a tax structure.
xs: The biggest drawback of multiple rates is **misclassification of goods and services** and **classification disputes** — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 2017).
Near-identical products land in **different slabs** → disputes and **litigation**.
xa: The **four-slab** structure was meant to be **transitional**.
Pending reform (Aug 2025): "**standardise product classification**".
GST 2.0 cut the main slabs to **5%** and **18%** + **40%**.

31.s: Under a multi-rate GST, placing near-identical products in different slabs mainly leads to:
31.x: Differing classification of similar products invites litigation; standardising classification is a pending reform.
xa: Misclassification is the **biggest drawback** of multiple rates (APPSC 2017).
Sector pleas: notebook makers hit by the **Sep 2025** rate revision (9 Sep 2026).

31.s: Which of the following continue to remain outside the GST framework?
31.x: Petroleum and electricity remain outside the GST framework.
31.tq: Use confusable sector exclusions to distinguish items inside and outside a tax regime.
xs: **Petroleum and electricity** are still **outside GST** — option **(1)**.
Petroleum (**crude, petrol, diesel, natural gas, ATF**) is within GST law but taxed only from a date the **GST Council recommends** (**Art. 279A(5)**).
xa: Other asks: **GST 3.0** simplification (CII AP, **1 Feb 2026**).
Criticism: **vertical fiscal imbalance** and loss of **state tax autonomy**.
Cesses remain **outside the divisible pool**.

31.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the GST Appellate Tribunal (GSTAT)?
o: Its Principal Bench is located in Mumbai
It was created through the Finance Act, 2024
It was formally launched in September 2025
31.x: GSTAT's Principal Bench is at New Delhi, not Mumbai.
xa: GSTAT **Procedure Rules 2025**.
First President = **former Chief Justice of Jharkhand HC**.

31.s: As of mid-2025, which problem was associated with the GST Appellate Tribunal?
o: State benches had exclusive jurisdiction over direct taxes
The tribunal had replaced the Supreme Court as the final court of appeal
Only the New Delhi Principal Bench had been abolished
Functional benches were absent in many States despite notification
31.x: Although GSTAT had been notified, functional benches were absent in many States as of mid-2025, causing appeals to accumulate in High Courts.
31.tq: Distinguish notification or legal creation from actual operationalisation.
xs: Mid-2025: GSTAT was **notified**, but **functional benches were absent in many States** — option **(4)**.
As a result, appeals **piled up in High Courts** (Jul **2025**).
xa: It was **formally launched Sep 2025**, with **hearings from Dec 2025**.
Created via **Finance Act 2024**; **Procedure Rules 2025**.
Appeals are to be filed **online within 3 months**.

31.s: With reference to Union of India v. Mohit Minerals (2022), which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: GST Council recommendations – Binding on legislatures
Status of GST Council – Statutory body
Source of simultaneous GST power – Article 279A
31.x: The Court called India a flexible federation; recommendations are persuasive, the simultaneous power flows from Article 246A, and the Council is constitutional.
xa: Other landmark rulings: **Safari Retreats**, **VKC Footsteps** (Jul **2025**).
Council voting: Centre **1/3**, States **2/3**; decisions need **3/4**.

31.s: Why does the Centre have an effective veto in the GST Council?
o: Because the Centre’s one-third vote can prevent a three-fourths majority
Because the Centre has two-thirds of the weighted vote
Because State representatives cannot vote on tax matters
Because the Centre alone nominates all State members
31.x: Since three-fourths weighted support is required and the Centre holds one-third of the vote, the Centre can block a proposal without its support.
31.tq: Infer institutional power from the voting weights and decision threshold.
xs: The **Centre's one-third vote** can **prevent a three-fourths majority** — option **(1)**.
With **2/3** weight, the States alone fall short of **3/4**, so no decision passes without the Centre.
The Centre has **1/3**, not 2/3, so option (2) is wrong.
xa: The weights are of **votes present**.
Debate: **loss of state tax autonomy** and **vertical fiscal imbalance**.

31.s: Which of the following groups of petroleum products is covered by the GST law but remains outside GST taxation until a date recommended by the GST Council?
o: Crude oil, petrol, diesel, natural gas and ATF
Natural gas, electricity, alcohol, tobacco and ATF
Coal, electricity, iron ore, cement and steel
Gold, silver, diamonds, petrol and coal
31.x: Crude oil, petrol, high-speed diesel, natural gas and aviation turbine fuel are within the GST law but are taxed outside GST until the Council recommends a date under Article 279A(5).
31.tq: Test the complete list and distinguish legal inclusion from present tax treatment.
xs: **Crude, petrol, diesel (HSD), natural gas, ATF** are within GST law but taxed only from a date the **GST Council recommends** — option **(1)**.
The power is in **Art. 279A(5)**; until then they remain **outside GST**.
**Electricity**, **alcohol**, **coal** and **gold** are not part of this petroleum group.
xa: Coverage gap: **petroleum and electricity** still outside GST.
**Gold/silver/jewellery** are taxed at a special **3%**.

31.s: Which of the following is a criticism of cesses in the GST framework?
o: They can be imposed only by State legislatures
They are always included in the divisible pool for distribution to States
They remain outside the divisible pool, contributing to concerns over State fiscal autonomy
31.x: Cesses outside the divisible pool reduce the share available for devolution and are therefore linked with concerns about States’ fiscal autonomy and vertical fiscal imbalance.
31.tq: Connect the fiscal instrument with its federal consequence.
xs: **Cesses remain outside the divisible pool**, feeding concerns over **State fiscal autonomy** — option **(3)**.
They are not in the divisible pool (option 2) and do not remove **vertical fiscal imbalance** (option 4).
xa: Other criticism: **loss of state tax autonomy**; vertical fiscal imbalance.
The unused compensation cess balance is split **50:50** between Centre and States.
States' **weak own revenues** mean **dependence on transfers**.

31.s: According to the Economic Survey 2025–26, a cut in GST rates may have what effect on revenue?
o: Volume effects may offset the initial revenue loss
It necessarily eliminates all future GST revenue
It reduces transaction volumes in every sector
It affects only customs revenue and not GST revenue
31.x: The Economic Survey 2025–26 observed that increased volume of transactions following a rate cut may offset the associated revenue loss.
31.tq: Recognise the stated dynamic revenue effect instead of assuming a static tax-base response.
xs: **ES 2025-26**: after a rate cut, **volume effects may offset the revenue loss** — option **(1)**.
The Survey does not say a cut wipes out revenue or shrinks volumes.
xa: ES 2025-26 calls **GST 2.0** the **third pillar of tax reform**, with "**no net tax hike**".
**ES 2019-20**: rationalisation shocks raise collections only for **1-3 months**.
GST revenue growth in **H2 2025-26** was only **4.67%**.

31.s: The Economic Survey 2025–26 described GST 2.0 as the:
31.x: GST 2.0 was described as the third pillar of tax reform, after the 2019 corporate tax cut and the 2025 personal income-tax reform.
31.tq: Use the sequence of reforms rather than identifying GST only by its tax rates.
xs: **ES 2025-26** called **GST 2.0** the **third pillar of tax reform** — option **(3)**.
It follows the **2019 corporate tax cut** (first) and the **April 2025 personal income tax reform** (second).
xa: The Survey stressed "**no net tax hike**".
It also said rate-cut **volume effects may offset revenue loss**.
GST 2.0 took effect on **22 Sep 2025**.

31.s: One major fiscal consequence for States of surrendering independent indirect-tax powers under GST has been:
o: Greater dependence on transfers because of weak own revenues
Automatic equalisation of revenues among all States
Complete elimination of State taxation powers
31.x: The surrender of independent indirect-tax powers, combined with weak own revenues, has increased States’ dependence on transfers.
31.tq: Link the loss of fiscal autonomy with the resulting dependence on transfers.
xs: Surrendering indirect-tax powers left States with **weak own revenues** and **greater dependence on transfers** — option **(1)**.
Taxes given up: **VAT, entry tax, luxury tax, entertainment tax, octroi**.
FC devolution was not abolished — **unorganised-sector States depend on FC devolution**.
xa: Only **16 States/UTs** had post-settlement GST growth above the national average.
Compensation: **5 years** at **14%** growth, under the **GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017**.
Criticism: **vertical fiscal imbalance**.

31.s: Which is the second-largest contributor to Andhra Pradesh's own tax revenue (2024-25 RE)?
31.x: GST is the largest at about 38% (₹36,296 crore) and State Excise second at about 22% (₹21,300 crore).

31.s: GST was introduced in India with effect from 1 July 2017 through which constitutional framework?
o: The 101st Amendment Act, 2016 and Articles 246A, 269A and 279A
The 86th Amendment Act and Articles 243G, 243H and 243I
The 73rd Amendment Act and Articles 280, 281 and 282
The 42nd Amendment Act and Articles 301, 302 and 303
31.x: GST came into force on 1 July 2017 under the 101st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, with Articles 246A, 269A and 279A forming its key constitutional basis.
31.tq: Match the reform with its effective date, amendment and constitutional Articles.
xs: GST came in from **1 July 2017** under the **101st Amendment Act, 2016**, with **Arts. 246A, 269A and 279A** — option **(1)**.
**246A** = GST law-making power; **269A** = inter-State supply/IGST; **279A** = GST Council.
xa: GST is the **biggest indirect tax reform since Independence**.
Taxpayer base: **66.5 lakh (2017) → 1.51 crore (2025)**.
FY 2017-18 average: **₹82,000 cr/month**.

31.s: The collection of 'Goods and Service Tax' in Indian economy in October, 2020 has been :
o: More than Rs. One lakh crore
Less than Rs. One lakh crore
Equal to Rs. One lakh crore
Equal to Rs. Two lakh crore
31.x: The collection of gross 'Goods and Services Tax' (GST) revenue in Indian economy in October, 2020 was Rs. 105,155 crore. In 2025-26, GST recorded its highest-ever gross collection of Rs. 22.27 lakh crore, reflecting a year-onyear growth of 8.3 percent. The average monthly collection stood at approx. Rs. 1.86 lakh crore in 2025-26. In April, 2026 the government has collected the all time highest (till date) monthly gross GST revenue (Rs. 242,702 crore). The gross GST collection for the months of January, February and March, 2026 stands at Rs. 193,384 crore, Rs. 183,609 crore and Rs. 200,064 crore, respectively.

31.s: The highest-ever annual gross GST collection, ₹22.27 lakh crore, was recorded in:
31.x: FY 2025-26 recorded the highest-ever ₹22.27 lakh crore (+8.3%); FY 2024-25 was ₹22.08 lakh crore.
31.tq: one-liner

31.s: Under GST 2.0, which of the following falls in the 40% demerit slab?
o: Most items of the old 12% slab
31.x: Private aircraft, yachts, ultra-luxury cars, tobacco, pan masala and online gaming are at 40%; gold is 3% and rough diamonds 0.25%.
31.tq: one-liner

31.s: The Principal Bench of the GST Appellate Tribunal is located at:
31.x: GSTAT has its Principal Bench in New Delhi, with State benches.
31.tq: one-liner

31.s: The GST Appellate Tribunal was launched in September 2025; its hearings began in:
31.x: GSTAT was launched in September 2025 and hearings began in December 2025.
31.tq: one-liner

31.s: In Mohit Minerals (2022), the power of Parliament and the States to legislate on GST under Article 246A was held to be:
31.x: The Court held that Parliament and the States have simultaneous power under Article 246A and the Council's recommendations are only persuasive.
31.tq: one-liner

31.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about unresolved GST issues?
o: Petroleum and electricity remain outside GST
The date for taxing petroleum is set on Council recommendation under Article 279A(5)
Cesses lie outside the divisible pool
GST Council recommendations are binding on the States
31.x: Mohit Minerals held Council recommendations persuasive, not binding; the other three are correct.
31.tq: NOT

12.s: Which Article requires the President to lay the report of the Finance Commission before each House of Parliament along with an explanatory memorandum on the action taken?
12.x: Article 281 requires the President to lay the Finance Commission’s report before each House of Parliament together with an explanatory memorandum on the action taken.
12.tq: Distinguish the Article dealing with presentation of the report from the Article establishing the Commission and its functions.
xs: **Article 281** requires the President to lay the Finance Commission's report before **Parliament** with an action-taken memorandum — option **(3)** is correct.
**Article 280** is the provision under which the President **constitutes** the Commission, not the one on laying its report.
**Article 270** governs the **divisible pool** of shareable Union taxes; **Art. 243I** links the FC to State funds for **Panchayats**.
xa: The Finance Commission is a **quasi-judicial** body constituted **every 5 years** (5th year) or earlier.
Composition: **Chairman + 4 members**; qualifications under the **Finance Commission (Misc. Provisions) Act, 1951**.
Its recommendations are **advisory**, not binding on the government.

12.s: The Finance Commission’s function of recommending measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State for supplementing the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities was added through the:
12.x: The relevant function was added by the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, 1992, relating respectively to Panchayats and Municipalities.
12.tq: Associate the local-government finance function with the constitutional amendments that strengthened local self-government.
xs: The local-body function was added by the **73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, 1992** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is **Art. 280(3)(bb) and (c)**: measures to augment a State's **Consolidated Fund** to support **Panchayats and Municipalities**.
It is linked to **Art. 243I** (Panchayats) and **Art. 243Y** (Municipalities).
xa: **Art. 280(3)(a)**: distribution of **net proceeds of shareable taxes**, vertical and horizontal.
**Art. 280(3)(b)**: principles for **grants-in-aid** (Art. 275) from the **Consolidated Fund of India**.
The **16th FC** gives only **local body** (**₹7.91 lakh crore**) and **disaster** grants.

12.s: The Finance Commission is constituted by the President every:
12.x: The quasi-judicial FC is constituted every fifth year or earlier; its recommendations are advisory.
xa: Report + action-taken memorandum laid before **Parliament** under **Art. 281**.
Composition: **Chairman + 4 members**; qualifications under the **Finance Commission (Misc. Provisions) Act, 1951**.
"The present Finance Commission" now means the **Sixteenth** (Chairman **Arvind Panagariya**).

12.s: Which of the following is NOT a duty of the Finance Commission under Article 280(3)?
o: Maintaining the income-expenditure accounts of the Union and State Governments
Recommending the distribution of the net proceeds of shareable taxes between the Centre and the States
Recommending principles governing grants-in-aid from the Consolidated Fund of India
Recommending measures to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities
12.x: Maintaining government income-expenditure accounts is not a Finance Commission function. Its duties include tax devolution, grants-in-aid principles and augmentation of State funds for local bodies.
12.tq: Find the administrative accounting function that does not belong to the Finance Commission.
xs: **Maintaining the income-expenditure accounts** of the Union and States is NOT an FC duty — option **(1)** (the **APPSC-G2 2017** key).
Distribution of **net proceeds of shareable taxes** is **Art. 280(3)(a)**.
**Principles for grants-in-aid** from the **Consolidated Fund of India** is **Art. 280(3)(b)**.
Augmenting a State's **Consolidated Fund** for **Panchayats and Municipalities** is **Art. 280(3)(bb), (c)**.
xa: Also outside the FC: **cesses/surcharges**, **GST** revenue sharing (**GST Council**) and plan/discretionary grants.
**Art. 280(3)(d)**: any matter **referred by the President**.
Exam angle: "which is NOT a function" questions are a favourite on this topic.

12.s: Which institution primarily deals with the sharing of GST revenue?
o: Comptroller and Auditor General of India
12.x: GST revenue-sharing recommendations are dealt with through the GST Council, not as a function of the Finance Commission.
12.tq: Use institutional discrimination to separate closely related fiscal bodies.
xs: **GST** revenue sharing is dealt with by the **GST Council** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Finance Commission** does **not** cover GST revenue sharing; it recommends sharing of the **divisible pool** and **grants-in-aid**.
The **CAG** figures only as certifier: the 16th FC recommends annual **CAG-certified** disclosure of net tax proceeds.
xa: The divisible pool includes **CGST** and the **Centre's IGST share** under **Art. 270**.
The FC also does not cover **cesses/surcharges** or plan/discretionary grants.
FC recommendations are **advisory**, not binding.

12.s: In the context of fiscal federalism in India, vertical devolution refers to
o: allocation of grants among local bodies
sharing of net tax proceeds between the Union and the States
distribution of the States' share among individual States
distribution of centrally sponsored schemes among districts
12.x: Vertical devolution means sharing net tax proceeds between the Union and the States. Distribution of the States' share among individual States is horizontal devolution.
12.tq: Distinguish the two closely related terms before considering the options.
xs: **Vertical devolution** = sharing of **net tax proceeds between the Union and the States** — option **(2)** is correct.
Distribution of the States' share **among individual States** is **horizontal devolution** (option 3).
Both are recommended under **Art. 280(3)(a)**.
xa: **Divisible pool**: taxes under **Art. 270** (corporation tax, income tax, **CGST**, Centre's **IGST** share).
**Tax devolution** under Art. 270 is **untied**.
Vertical share now **41%** (15th and 16th FCs).

12.s:
Consider the following about Article 280(3):
1. Clause (b) concerns principles governing grants-in-aid under Article 275.
2. Clause (d) concerns any other matter referred to the Commission by the President.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
12.x: Article 280(3)(b) covers grants-in-aid principles under Article 275, and clause (d) any other matter referred by the President.
xa: Clauses **(bb), (c)** were added by the **73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992**.
Art. 275 grants are paid from the **Consolidated Fund of India** and are **charged** on it.
Example under clause (d): **disaster-management financing** (**Disaster Management Act, 2005**).

12.s: Article 275 grants are NOT generally meant for:
o: Welfare of Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Areas
12.x: Article 275 grants support revenue deficits, local bodies, disasters and tribal welfare, not every CSS.
xa: Art. 275 grants are recommended by the **Finance Commission** and **charged on the CFI**.
The **16th FC** gives only **local body** + **disaster** grants (total **₹9.47 lakh crore**).
The **15th FC** gave RD, sector-specific and State-specific grants totalling **₹10.1 lakh crore**.

12.s: Which approach was associated with the Sixteenth Finance Commission’s treatment of Centrally Sponsored Schemes?
o: Linking them to measurable outcomes and reviewing inefficient schemes
Charging all CSS directly to the Consolidated Fund of India as Article 275 grants
Transferring their administration exclusively to local bodies
12.x: The Sixteenth Finance Commission linked CSS to measurable outcomes and proposed a high-powered committee to close inefficient schemes.
12.tq: Identify the policy reform from its stated objective and institutional mechanism.
xs: The 16th FC linked CSS to **measurable outcomes** and to **reviewing inefficient schemes** — option **(1)** is correct.
It proposed a **high-powered committee** to close inefficient schemes.
CSS are not Art. 275 grants; they keep a **matching share** from States.
xa: The 16th FC shifts transfers from **entitlement to performance**.
States' deficit capped at **3% of GSDP**; off-budget borrowing to be ended.

12.s: What was the principal effect attributed to SASCI in the Economic Survey analysis?
o: It restricted capital expenditure to higher-income States.
It reduced State capital expenditure by replacing grants with revenue loans.
It converted all State borrowings into tax devolution.
It helped prevent pro-cyclical compression of State capital expenditure through 50-year interest-free capex loans.
12.x: SASCI provides 50-year interest-free capital expenditure loans and helped prevent pro-cyclical compression of State capital expenditure.
12.tq: Connect the policy instrument with its stated macroeconomic effect.
xs: **SASCI** gave **50-year interest-free capex loans** that kept State capex from **pro-cyclical compression** — option **(4)** is correct.
It did not restrict capex to richer States: **lower-income States** relied on it more, aiding **convergence**.
These are **capex loans**, not revenue loans, and do not replace tax devolution.
xa: States' capital outlay rose from **2.17% of GDP (FY22) to 2.37% (FY25)**.
⚠ Excluding SASCI, capital outlay **fell from 2.11% to 1.92%**.
Interest-free capex loans in Budget 2026-27: **₹1,85,000 crore**.

12.s: According to the Sixteenth Finance Commission framework, the fiscal deficit of a State should be capped at
12.x: The Sixteenth Finance Commission recommended capping State fiscal deficits at 3% of GSDP.
12.tq: Distinguish the State fiscal-deficit cap from the Union’s corresponding GDP figure.
xs: The 16th FC caps States' deficit at **3% of GSDP** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is part of the shift from **entitlement to performance**.
The same framework says **off-budget borrowing** is to be ended.
xa: The 16th FC also introduced a **GDP criterion** and **conditional grants**.
Extra borrowing: **0.5% of GSDP** for power-sector reforms.
AP: RD grant loss pushes revenue deficit to **1.1%** (Budget 2026-27).

12.s: Which of the following correctly shows the States’ share of central taxes recommended by the 10th to 13th Finance Commissions?
12.x: The respective shares were 29% under the 10th, 29.5% under the 11th, 30.5% under the 12th and 32% under the 13th Finance Commission.
12.tq: Read the sequence across the comparison table without reversing adjacent percentages.
xs: 10th to 13th FCs: **29%, 29.5%, 30.5% and 32%** respectively — option **(2)** is correct.
**12th (C. Rangarajan)** 30.5%; **13th (Vijay Kelkar)** 32%.
xa: **14th (Y.V. Reddy)** jumped to **42%** — the largest-ever jump (+10 points).
**15th (N.K. Singh)** **41%**; **16th (Arvind Panagariya)** **41%** retained.
The 10th FC's 29% was of **gross proceeds** under the **"Alternative Scheme of Devolution"**.

12.s: The reduction in the States’ share from 42% under the 14th Finance Commission to 41% under the 15th Finance Commission was attributed to:
o: The abolition of the divisible pool
The introduction of the GDP criterion
Jammu and Kashmir becoming a Union Territory
12.x: The reduction was attributed to Jammu and Kashmir becoming a Union Territory.
12.tq: Link the change in percentage to the specific institutional change responsible for it.
xs: The cut from **42% to 41%** was due to **Jammu & Kashmir becoming a Union Territory** — option **(4)** is correct.
J&K and **Ladakh** became UTs, so they dropped out of the States' share at the **15th FC (N.K. Singh)**.
The **divisible pool** was not abolished, and the **GDP criterion** belongs to the **16th FC**.
xa: The **16th FC** retained **41%** unchanged.
The **14th FC** (**42%**) was the largest-ever jump (+**10** points).
Shift from tax effort (**2.5%**) to GDP contribution (**10%**) criticised as rewarding size, not need.

12.s: Which of the following Centre-to-State transfers is untied?
12.x: Tax devolution under Article 270 is untied; Article 282 grants are discretionary and CSS generally need a matching State share.
xa: Art. 275 grants are **charged on the CFI**; Art. 282 grants are not.
CSS examples: **MGNREGA/VB-G RAM G, PMAY, NHM**.

12.s: Centrally Sponsored Schemes are best described as schemes which are
o: recommended only by the Finance Commission and funded only from Article 275 grants
designed by States and financed entirely by local bodies
designed by the Centre and require a matching State share
implemented without any State financial contribution
12.x: Centrally Sponsored Schemes are Centre-designed schemes requiring a matching contribution from the States.
12.tq: Apply the funding and design features to identify the scheme category.
xs: **CSS** are schemes **designed by the Centre** that need a **matching State share** — option **(3)** is correct.
Examples: **MGNREGA/VB-G RAM G, PMAY, NHM**.
They are not FC/Art. 275 funded: CSS mostly flow through **Art. 282** grants.
xa: **16th FC**: CSS linked to **measurable outcomes**; **high-powered committee** to close inefficient schemes.
CSS spending routed to States is one reason the share stayed at **41%**.

12.s: Which of the following grants were discontinued by the 16th Finance Commission?
o: Revenue-deficit grants, sector-specific grants and State-specific grants
All grants to rural local bodies
12.x: The 16th Finance Commission discontinued revenue-deficit grants, sector-specific grants and State-specific grants.
12.tq: Identify the complete set of discontinued grants without overextending the word “all”.
xs: The 16th FC dropped **revenue-deficit, sector-specific and State-specific grants** — option **(1)** is correct.
These were **15th FC** grants (total **₹10.1 lakh crore**).
The 16th FC kept **only local body** (**₹7.91 lakh crore**) and **disaster** grants, so options 2–4 are wrong.
xa: 16th FC total grants **₹9.47 lakh crore**; share in FC transfers **19.4% → 8.3%**.
AP angle: **RD grant loss** → AP revenue deficit **1.1%** (Budget 2026-27).
AP's 16th FC local-body grants: **₹16,627 crore** (rural), **₹12,158 crore** (urban).

12.s: The expression “41% illusion” in discussions on tax devolution refers principally to the fact that:
o: cesses and surcharges are outside the divisible pool
the Finance Commission fixes all tax rates at 41%
States receive 41% of total public expenditure
41% of the divisible pool is transferred only through grants
12.x: The expression highlights that the stated share can overstate actual resources available to States because growing cesses and surcharges remain outside the divisible pool.
12.tq: Decode a debate-related phrase by identifying the fiscal mechanism behind it.
xs: The **"41% illusion"**: **cesses and surcharges** lie **outside the divisible pool** — option **(1)** is correct.
As cess/surcharge grows, the States' real share of gross tax revenue shrinks below the headline **41%**.
41% is a share of the **divisible pool**, not a tax rate or a share of expenditure.
xa: Divisible pool fell **89.2% (FC-13) → 82.1% (FC-14) → 78.3% (FC-15)** of gross tax revenue.
Capping cess/surcharge was called "**neither permissible nor desirable**".
16th FC asks for annual **CAG-certified** disclosure of net tax proceeds.

12.s: Which of the following best reflects the equity-efficiency issue in the design of fiscal devolution?
o: All States possess identical fiscal capacity, so devolution automatically equalises them.
Most Finance Commissions relied on income distance and population, while critics argue that fiscal capacity is not uniform.
Efficiency requires replacing all tax devolution with discretionary grants.
Equity is achieved only when every State receives an identical absolute amount.
12.x: Most Finance Commissions relied on income distance and population to pursue equity. Critics argue that fiscal capacity is not uniform, so devolution is not automatically self-equalising.
12.tq: Separate the equity objective from the criticism concerning unequal fiscal capacity.
xs: Most FCs relied on **income distance and population**, while critics say **fiscal capacity is not uniform** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **16th FC view** assumes fiscal discipline suffices.
Critics reply that, as fiscal capacity varies, devolution is **not self-equalising** — so option 1 is the very assumption criticised.
xa: Shift from tax effort (**2.5%**) to GDP contribution (**10%**) is criticised as rewarding **size, not need**.
**Horizontal devolution** = distribution of States' share among States.
The 16th FC shifts transfers from **entitlement to performance**.

12.s: Which one of the following best describes the principal shift associated with the Sixteenth Finance Commission in intergovernmental transfers?
o: From performance-based transfers to unconditional entitlement
From tax devolution to complete abolition of grants
From State transfers to exclusive Central expenditure
From entitlement-based transfers to performance-oriented transfers
12.x: The Sixteenth Finance Commission is associated with a shift from entitlement-based transfers towards performance-oriented transfers.
12.tq: Identify the reversed comparison by focusing on the direction of the policy shift.
xs: The 16th FC shifts transfers from **entitlement to performance** — option **(4)** is correct.
Tools: **GDP criterion** + **conditional grants**; deficit capped at **3% of GSDP**.
Option 1 states the reverse; grants were not abolished — **local body** and **disaster** grants remain.
xa: 16th FC: CSS linked to **measurable outcomes**.
Grants' share in FC transfers fell **19.4% → 8.3%**.
Critics: fiscal capacity is not uniform → devolution **not self-equalising**.

12.s: Under the Gadgil-Mukherjee formula, which pair of criterion and weight is correctly matched?
12.x: Population carried 60%, per capita income 25%, tax effort 7.5% and special problems 7.5%.
xa: Gadgil (**1969**): Population **60%**; per capita income, tax effort, irrigation/power projects and special problems **10%** each.
Highest weight under Gadgil-Mukherjee = **population** (**UPPSC 2008**).
Endorsed by the **National Development Council** in **1968-69**; used from the **4th Plan (1969)**.

12.s: Recommendations of the Finance Commission are:
o: Binding on the Union and the States
Advisory and not binding on the Government
12.x: FC recommendations are not binding on the Government; it may also deal with matters referred by the President.
xa: ⚠ GST revenue sharing is handled by the **GST Council**, not the Finance Commission.
Maintaining **income and expenditure accounts** of Centre and States is not its job (**APPSC-G2 2017** key).
Example of a Presidential reference: **disaster-management financing** under the **Disaster Management Act, 2005**.

12.s: Which of the following is excluded from the divisible pool of Union taxes?
12.x: Cesses and surcharges are excluded from the divisible pool, as is the cost of collection; pool taxes are shared under Article 270.
xa: Divisible pool fell from **89.2% (FC-13)** to **82.1% (FC-14)** to **78.3% (FC-15)** of gross tax revenue.
**80th Amendment, 2000** made all central taxes shareable.

12.s: The largest-ever increase in the States' share of Union taxes occurred under the
12.x: The Fourteenth Finance Commission increased the States' share from 32 per cent to 42 per cent, a rise of 10 percentage points, the largest-ever jump.
12.tq: Use the size of the change, not merely the final percentage, to identify the Commission.
xs: The **Fourteenth Finance Commission** gave the largest-ever jump — option **(2)** is correct.
It raised the States' share from **32%** (13th FC) to **42%**: **+10 points**.
The **15th** cut it to **41%** and the **16th** retained **41%**; the **13th** moved it only from **30.5%** to **32%**.
xa: 14th FC chairman: **Y.V. Reddy**; award period **2015-20**.
Its 42% award was **accepted 24 Feb 2015**.
The notes do not list the 14th FC's own vertical-devolution considerations (asked in **APPSC 2017**).

12.s: The 80th Constitutional Amendment, 2000 gave effect to the 'Alternative Scheme of Devolution' of which Finance Commission?
12.x: The 80th Amendment implemented the 10th FC's Alternative Scheme (29%), making all central taxes shareable with effect from 1 April 1996.

12.s:
Consider the following about the divisible pool of central taxes:
1. It excludes cesses and surcharges.
2. It was about 81% of gross tax revenue in 2025–26.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
12.x: The divisible pool comprises shareable taxes under Article 270, excluding cesses and surcharges, and was about 81% of gross tax revenue in 2025–26.
xa: **80th Amendment, 2000** (from **1 Apr 1996**) made all central taxes shareable.
"**41% illusion**": growing cess/surcharge outside the pool shrinks States' share.

12.s: The 16th Finance Commission retained the States' share in the divisible pool at:
12.x: It retained 41 per cent; the demand of 18 of 28 States for 50 per cent was not accepted.
xa: Reasons: **CSS** spending routed to States anyway; Union needs funds for **defence and infrastructure**.
Capping cess/surcharge was called "**neither permissible nor desirable**".
⚠ The one-point cut (**42 → 41**) came at the **15th FC**, not the 16th.

12.s: Tax devolution from the Centre to the States takes place under which Article?
12.x: Tax devolution is under Article 270; Article 275 covers FC grants, Article 282 CSS and other transfers, and Article 123 is the ordinance power.

12.s: Grants under Article 282 are generally:
o: Statutory grants recommended by the Finance Commission
Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
Discretionary, mostly tied and routed through Union ministries
Untied transfers from the divisible pool
12.x: Article 282 grants are discretionary, mostly tied and scheme-based; Article 275 grants are statutory and charged on the CFI.
xa: Art. 275 grants go to States in need of assistance, as **Parliament** determines; Art. 282 grants for **any public purpose**.
Art. 282 is the route for most **CSS**.
⚠ Exam trap: "Art. 282 needs FC recommendation" is **false**.

12.s: The 15th Finance Commission's revenue-deficit, sector-specific and State-specific grants totalled about:
12.x: The 15th FC's grants totalled about ₹10.1 lakh crore, against ₹9.47 lakh crore under the 16th FC.
xa: 16th FC grants: only **local body** (**₹7.91 lakh crore**) + **disaster** grants.
Budget **2026-27**: **₹1.4 lakh crore** FC grants for FY27.
15th FC gave **RD**, **sector-specific** and **State-specific** grants.

12.s: Which two phenomena were recommended to be notified as disasters under the disaster-grant framework?
12.x: Heatwave and lightning were recommended to be notified as disasters.
12.tq: Test the specific pair of newly proposed disaster categories.
xs: **Heatwave and lightning** were recommended as notified disasters — option **(3)** is correct.
This is part of the **16th FC** disaster-grant framework.
The other pairs are not the new additions the notes record.
xa: **SDRF/SDMF** corpus: **₹2,04,401 crore** (Union share about **₹1.55 lakh crore**).
Cost-sharing: NE/Himalayan **90:10**; others **75:25**.
Disaster financing under the **Disaster Management Act, 2005** came into FC terms of reference.

12.s: The 15th Finance Commission recommended Rs 4,800 crore for 2022-23 to 2025-26 to incentivise States on:
12.x: The 15th FC set aside Rs 4,800 crore (2022-23 to 2025-26) to reward States for better educational outcomes (UPSC 2025). Property tax was an entry condition for local-body grants, power-sector reform was tied to extra borrowing, and disaster funds come through SDRF/SDMF.
xs: The **₹4,800 crore** (**2022-23 to 2025-26**) was to reward better **educational outcomes** — option **(2)** is correct (**UPSC 2025**).
It was part of the **15th FC**'s sector-specific grants.
**Power-sector reforms** were linked instead to extra borrowing of **0.5% of GSDP**.
xa: 15th FC grants totalled **₹10.1 lakh crore** (RD, sector-specific, State-specific).

26.tq: Use the exact target range rather than confusing it with the general government debt ceiling.
