It comes under the **debt-anchor rule** that operates from **2026-27**.
**60%** was the FRBM (2018) general-government ceiling and **40%** the Centre's FRBM ceiling — not the 2031 target.
xa: ⚠ The debt anchor allows a higher debt ratio than FRBM's **40%** (2 Feb 2026 critique).
FD target for 2026-27: **4.3%** of GDP.

26.s: Who was the first to develop a theory linking fiscal policy with economic performance in the modern sense?
26.x: J. M. Keynes developed the theory linking fiscal policy with economic performance. His General Theory was published in 1936 and formed the basis of active demand management.
26.tq: Use the economist-contribution association rather than the similarly named fiscal-policy committee figures.
xs: **J.M. Keynes** first developed a theory linking fiscal policy with economic performance — option **(3)**.
His **General Theory** (**1936**) became the basis of **active demand management**.
**V.P. Singh** presented the Long-Term Fiscal Policy (**1985**); **N.K. Singh** headed the **2016** FRBM review committee.
xa: **Richard Musgrave** gave the three budget functions and popularised **fiscal federalism** (**1959**).
N.K. Singh Committee debt anchor: **60%** = Centre **40%** + States **20%**.
Fiscal policy influences **aggregate demand**, allocation and distribution.

26.s: The Long-Term Fiscal Policy of India, announced in 1985, was presented by
26.x: India's Long-Term Fiscal Policy was presented in 1985 by Finance Minister V. P. Singh.
xs: The Long-Term Fiscal Policy (**1985**) was presented by Finance Minister **V.P. Singh** — option **(1)**.
It is listed among the FIRSTs of Indian fiscal policy.
xa: **J.M. Keynes** (General Theory, **1936**) first linked fiscal policy to economic performance.
**FRBM Act 2003**: FD **3%**, RD zero; amended **2018**.
**N.K. Singh** Committee **2016**, report **2017**.

26.s: The N. K. Singh Committee's debt-anchor framework referred to general government debt of
o: 60% of GDP, comprising Centre 40% and States 20%
70% of GDP, comprising Centre 40% and States 30%
60% of GDP, comprising Centre 50% and States 10%
50% of GDP, comprising Centre 30% and States 20%
26.x: The N. K. Singh Committee recommended a general government debt anchor of 60% of GDP, divided into 40% for the Centre and 20% for the States.
26.tq: Separate the aggregate debt anchor from its Centre-State components.
xs: N.K. Singh Committee debt anchor: **60% of GDP = Centre 40% + States 20%** — option **(1)**.
Committee set up in **2016**, report in **2017**.
The **FRBM (2018)** ceilings adopted this: general govt debt **60%**, **Centre 40%** by **Mar 2025**.
xa: FRBM (2018) also set **FD 3% by Mar 2021**.
New target: central debt **50 ± 1% by March 2031**.
⚠ S&P says general government debt is **above 80% of GDP**.

26.s: The original FRBM Act, 2003 targeted which of the following for the Union Government?
o: Fiscal deficit 3% of GDP and revenue deficit eliminated
Fiscal deficit 4.5% of GDP and revenue deficit 2% of GDP
Fiscal deficit eliminated and revenue deficit 3% of GDP
Debt-GDP ratio of 50% and fiscal deficit 4.3% of GDP
26.x: The FRBM Act, 2003 set the fiscal deficit target at 3% of GDP and revenue deficit at zero; it was amended in 2018. 4.5% was the FY22 glide-path commitment for 2025-26; 50 ± 1% debt by 2031 and FD 4.3% belong to the 2026-27 debt-anchor framework; FD was never targeted at zero.
xs: The **FRBM Act 2003** targeted **fiscal deficit 3%** of GDP and **revenue deficit zero** — option **(1)**.
It was **amended in 2018**.
**4.5%** was the FY 2021-22 commitment for **2025-26**; **50 ± 1%** debt and FD **4.3%** belong to the later debt-anchor phase.
xa: FRBM (2018): **FD 3% by Mar 2021**; general govt debt **60%**; **Centre 40%** by **Mar 2025**.
FRBM bars the RBI from subscribing to **primary issues** of G-Secs from **2006-07**, except under the **escape clause**.
**ERD** was written into FRBM by the **2012 amendment**.

26.s: Which one of the following is NOT an objective of fiscal policy?
o: Management of money supply and liquidity
26.x: Managing liquidity and money supply is an objective of monetary policy, not fiscal policy. Fiscal policy objectives include employment, price stability, growth, redistribution, mobilisation and regional balance.
26.tq: Find the monetary-policy function among the fiscal-policy objectives.
xs: **Management of money supply and liquidity** is NOT a fiscal-policy objective — option **(2)**.
Managing liquidity, money supply and directing interest rates belong to **monetary policy**.
**Full employment**, **price stability** and **balanced regional development** are fiscal-policy objectives.
xa: ⚠ "Directing interest rates" was an APPSC GS **2023** distractor.
Other objectives: **economic growth**, **equitable distribution** of income and wealth, **resource mobilisation**.
Monetary tools: **Repo, CRR, SLR, OMOs, LAF** (RBI / MPC).

26.s: From 2006-07, the FRBM framework bars the RBI, in normal times, from:
o: Subscribing to primary issues of Government securities
Acting as banker to the States
26.x: The RBI cannot subscribe to primary issues of G-Secs except under the escape clause.
xa: **Monetised deficit** = part of the deficit financed by the **RBI** → inflationary.
**Ad hoc T-bills** abolished from **1 April 1997** (**1994** agreement).
**FRBM Act 2003**: FD **3%**, RD zero; amended **2018**.

26.s: Under the national Direct Benefit Transfer system for fertiliser rolled out in 2018, subsidy is released to companies after:
o: Retail sale is recorded through PoS machines with Aadhaar authentication of the buyer
The State Legislature approves each individual transaction
The fertiliser is manufactured, without any retail verification
The buyer submits a post-purchase paper claim to the Finance Ministry
26.x: Under fertiliser DBT, retail sale is recorded on PoS machines and the buyer is authenticated through Aadhaar; the subsidy is then released to the companies.
26.tq: Follow the transaction sequence and identify the point at which the subsidy is released.
xs: Subsidy is paid **after retail sale is recorded through PoS machines with Aadhaar authentication of the buyer** — option **(1)**.
This is the **DBT in fertiliser** system, national rollout **2018**.
xa: **Urea** is the largest fertiliser subsidy item.
Rationalising subsidies via **DBT** is an **expenditure-side** deficit-reduction measure.

26.s: Budget deficit plus borrowings and other liabilities of the Government is equal to:
26.x: Fiscal deficit = budget deficit + borrowings and other liabilities (APPSC 2019). Revenue deficit is revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts; primary deficit is FD minus interest payments; monetised deficit is the part financed by the RBI.
xs: **Budget deficit + borrowings and other liabilities = Fiscal deficit** — option **(3)** (APPSC **2019**).
**Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts; **primary deficit** = FD − interest payments.
**Monetised deficit** = the part financed by the **RBI**.
xa: FD always equals **borrowings and other liabilities**.
FD = **total expenditure − total receipts excluding borrowings**.

26.s: Under the FY 2021-22 glide path, the Union fiscal deficit was to be brought below what share of GDP by 2025-26?
26.x: The commitment was below 4.5% of GDP by 2025-26 (met at 4.4%); from 2026-27 the fiscal deficit is calibrated each year to keep the debt-GDP ratio falling.
xa: Debt target: **50 ± 1% by March 2031**.
FY27 BE fiscal deficit: **4.3%** of GDP (~**₹16.96 lakh crore**).
COVID peak FD in **2020-21**: **9.2%** of GDP.

26.s: Resource mobilisation, equitable distribution and balanced regional development are objectives of:
26.x: Economic growth, equitable distribution, resource mobilisation and balanced regional development are all objectives of fiscal policy.
xa: Also: **full employment** and **price stability**.
NOT fiscal objectives: **directing interest rates**, managing **liquidity and money supply** (monetary policy).
Direct taxes = **58.8%** of total taxes in **FY25** — evidence of progressive taxation.

26.s: Which of the following is NOT an instrument of fiscal policy?
26.x: The repo rate is a monetary policy tool of the RBI/MPC; the others are fiscal tools of the Government.
xa: Other fiscal tools: **public expenditure** (capex as **"pump priming"**), the **budget**, **PLI**.
Monetary tools: **Repo, CRR, SLR, OMOs, LAF**.
Trade policy (Ministry of Commerce): **tariffs, quotas, export incentives**.

26.s: Monetary policy can act relatively quickly because the MPC takes decisions:
26.x: The MPC decides bi-monthly, whereas fiscal policy works through the slower budget cycle.
xa: Fiscal authority: **Govt (MoF)**; monetary authority: **RBI / MPC**.
Fiscal tools: **taxation, public expenditure, public debt, subsidies**, DBT, PLI.
Monetary tools: **Repo, CRR, SLR, OMOs, LAF**.

26.s: If the Fiscal Deficit is ₹4 crore and GDP is ₹400 crore, the Fiscal Deficit as a percentage of GDP will be:
26.x: Fiscal Deficit as a percentage of GDP = (₹4 crore ÷ ₹400 crore) × 100 = 1 percent.
26.tq: Convert the deficit-to-GDP ratio into a percentage by multiplying by 100.
xs: FD as % of GDP = **4 / 400 × 100 = 1 percent** — option **(2)**.
The notes give exactly this example: FD **4** on GDP **400** = **1% of GDP**.
xa: FD target for 2026-27 is ~**₹16.96 lakh crore**.

26.s: From 1 April 1997, ad hoc Treasury Bills were replaced by:
26.x: Ad hoc T-bills, which meant automatic monetisation, were replaced by WMA; an overdraft is only use of WMA beyond the limit.
xa: The phase-out began with the **1994** RBI-Government agreement.
**Budget deficit** stopped being the headline measure after ad hoc T-bills ended.
**FRBM:** RBI barred from **primary issues** from **2006-07**, except under the **escape clause**.

26.s: Use of Ways and Means Advances beyond the permitted limit is called:
26.x: WMA are temporary RBI advances for cash mismatches; using them beyond the limit is an overdraft.
xa: WMA replaced **ad hoc Treasury Bills** from **1 April 1997**.
RBI money creation → **money supply ↑** → **inflation** — the **most inflationary route**.
**Borrowings and other liabilities** = **24 paise** of every rupee of receipts (**2026-27**).

26.s: A fiscal stance that runs deficits in recessions and consolidates in booms is called:
26.x: Counter-cyclical policy runs deficits in slumps (e.g. Atma Nirbhar Bharat, 2020); pro-cyclical policy deepens volatility.
xa: Recession response: **more spending on public projects** (UPSC PYQ).
**Neutral** stance: balanced effect on demand → stable equilibrium.
Related terms: **fiscal drag**, **pump priming**, **fiscal neutrality**.

26.s: With reference to Union Government deficits, which one of the following correctly represents the fiscal deficit in 2020-21 and 2026-27 (BE), respectively?
26.x: The fiscal deficit was 9.2% of GDP in 2020-21, the peak shown in the series, and is estimated at 4.3% in 2026-27 (BE).
26.tq: Split the options by the two years and match the fiscal-deficit column precisely.
xs: **4.8%** was FY25 actual; **7.3%** and **1.5%** are RD figures; **8.4%** was **1990-91** gross FD.
xa: Consolidation **9.2% → 4.4%** brought **three sovereign rating upgrades in 2025**.
FD target 2026-27: ~**₹16.96 lakh crore**.

26.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Contractionary fiscal stance – Used during recession
Neutral fiscal stance – Used to address overheating
Expansionary fiscal stance – Used during recession
Expansionary fiscal stance – Balanced effect on demand
26.x: Expansionary policy supports the economy in recession; contractionary policy addresses overheating and a neutral stance has a balanced effect on demand.
xa: Expansionary risk: **inflation**; contractionary risk: growth and jobs.
**Counter-cyclical** example: **Atma Nirbhar Bharat, 2020**.

26.s: The gross fiscal deficit of the Union Government reached the earlier peak of 8.4% of GDP in:
26.x: The earlier gross fiscal-deficit peak was 8.4% of GDP in 1990-91.
26.tq: Discriminate between adjacent crisis-period years using the exact benchmark year.
xs: Gross fiscal deficit was **8.4% of GDP** in **1990-91** — option **(1)**.
This was the historical peak before the COVID year.

26.s: Tax concessions and cheap credit are examples of:
26.x: Tax concessions and cheap credit can constitute hidden subsidies.
xa: Explicit subsidies: **food, fertiliser, export** and **interest** subsidies.
Implicit subsidies: under-pricing of **education, health** and other public services.

26.s: India's fiscal deficit declined from 9.2 per cent to ____ per cent during its fiscal consolidation.
26.x: The decline from 9.2 to 4.4 per cent was linked to three sovereign rating upgrades in 2025 by Morningstar DBRS, S&P and R&I.
xa: ⚠ The marginal **4.4% → 4.3%** step is criticised for slowing rating upgrades.
**9.2%** was the COVID peak FD in **2020-21**.

26.s: If primary deficit is zero, then the amount of borrowing will be :
o: just equal to the interest payment
26.x: If the primary deficit is zero, the fiscal deficit becomes equivalent to the interest liabilities. This implies that the government has resorted to borrowings just to pay off the interest payments and the amount of borrowing will be just equal to the interest payments.

26.s: Public borrowing used to finance the Fiscal Deficit may be classified as:
o: Only external borrowing through multilateral institutions
26.x: Public borrowing may be internal, such as bonds, Treasury Bills and small savings, or external, such as multilateral borrowing and sovereign bonds. It finances the Fiscal Deficit.
26.tq: Identify the complete classification and reject the ‘only’ alternatives.
xs: Public borrowing is **internal** and **external** — option **(2)**.
**Internal** = bonds, T-bills, small savings; **External** = multilateral loans, sovereign bonds.
Public borrowing **finances the fiscal deficit**; taxation is not borrowing.
xa: Other sources: **market borrowings** (dated G-Secs), **small savings / NSSF**, provident funds.
Net home borrowing includes indirect borrowing from banks via **SLR**.
Budget 2026-27: **borrowings and other liabilities = 24 paise** of every rupee of receipts.

26.s: A zero primary deficit means the government borrows only to:
26.x: Zero PD means FD equals interest payments, so borrowing only services past debt, a debt-trap signal.
xa: **Debt trap** = borrowing to make interest payments.
**FD** always equals **borrowings and other liabilities**.

26.s: Which way of financing a deficit may expose the economy to currency risk?
26.x: External borrowing creates currency risk; RBI financing creates money and public borrowing absorbs liquidity.
xa: Money-printing = the **most inflationary route**.
**Crowding out**: heavy govt borrowing pushes up interest rates → **private investment falls**.
Ad hoc T-bills (automatic monetisation) abolished from **1 April 1997**.

26.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the most desirable source for financing a current account deficit?
26.x: Foreign direct investment is identified as the most desirable source of CAD financing. FPI is volatile, while other sources include ECBs, NRI deposits, reserve drawdown and multilateral loans.
26.tq: Compare external financing sources by stability and desirability rather than merely identifying a foreign source.
xs: **Foreign direct investment** is the **most desirable** CAD financing source — option **(1)**.
**FPI** is **volatile**; forex reserve drawdown and **ECBs** are other, less preferred, sources.
xa: Other sources: **NRI deposits**, **IMF/World Bank** loans.
**Twin deficit** = fiscal deficit + current account deficit.

26.s: The fiscal multiplier is defined as:
o: Fiscal Deficit divided by Primary Deficit
Change in government spending divided by change in GDP
Change in GDP divided by change in government spending or taxes
Total tax revenue divided by total expenditure
26.x: The fiscal multiplier measures the change in GDP resulting from a change in government spending or taxes. It is expressed as change in GDP divided by the change in government spending or taxes.
26.tq: Recall the direction of the multiplier formula carefully.
xs: **Fiscal multiplier = change in GDP / change in government spending or taxes** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) inverts the ratio.
xa: **Capex multiplier** in India estimated at **2.5-3**.
It is larger for **capital expenditure** than for revenue spending or transfers.
**Crowding in**: public capex draws private investment.

26.s: 'Crowding out' in fiscal policy refers to a situation in which:
o: Heavy government borrowing pushes up interest rates and private investment falls
Public capital expenditure creates infrastructure that draws in private investment
Government cuts spending in a slump and raises it in a boom
Rising incomes push taxpayers into higher tax brackets and slow demand
26.x: Crowding out: heavy government borrowing absorbs loanable funds, pushes up interest rates and reduces private investment (UPSC 2026). Public capex attracting private investment is crowding in; cutting in slumps and spending in booms is pro-cyclical policy; bracket creep slowing demand is fiscal drag.
26.tq: Crowding out = govt borrowing up, rates up, private investment down.
xs: **Crowding out**: **heavy government borrowing pushes up interest rates and private investment falls** — option **(1)** (UPSC **2026** key).
Public capex drawing private investment is **crowding in**.
Cutting in a slump and spending in a boom is **pro-cyclical** policy.
xa: Borrowing from the public **absorbs liquidity** and can slow private activity.
**Capex multiplier** estimated at **2.5-3** in India.

26.s:
Statement (A) : A big source of deficit in the Government’s budget is the financial subsidy.
Reason (R) : The level of financial subsidy is much higher in Indian agriculture than in developed countries.
Select the correct answer with the help of following code:
o: A and R both are true and R is the correct explanation
A and R both are true, but R is not the correct expla-
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
26.x: Statement (A) is correct, because during the question period India was providing about 12 percent of its expenditure as financial subsidy (in Union Budget 2026-27 total subsidies are about 8.5% of total expenditure), which was a major source of budget deficit. Reason (R) is incorrect, because western countries provide much higher financial aid to their agriculture sector than India.

26.s:
Consider the following statements about the Union Budget:
1. It is prepared by the Department of Economic Affairs.
2. Article 112 of the Constitution uses the word 'Budget' for it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
26.x: Statement 1 is correct: the Department of Economic Affairs prepares the Union Budget. Statement 2 is wrong: the word 'Budget' does not appear in the Constitution; Article 112 calls it the 'Annual Financial Statement'. So only 1 is correct; 'Both' and '2 only' accept the false statement and 'Neither' rejects the true one.
26.tq: Art. 112 = Annual Financial Statement; the word Budget is not in the Constitution.
xs: Only statement **1** is correct — option **(1) 1 only**.
Statement 1 — correct: the Union Budget is prepared by the **Department of Economic Affairs (DEA)**.
Statement 2 — wrong: **Art. 112** calls it the **"Annual Financial Statement"**; the word **"Budget"** does not appear in the Constitution.
xa: Fiscal policy is made by the **Ministry of Finance**, with legislative backing.
**Long-Term Fiscal Policy** was presented in **1985** by Finance Minister **V.P. Singh**.
Budget 2026-27: **borrowings and other liabilities = 24 paise** of every rupee of receipts — the largest single item.

26.s: Which one of the following is a part of fiscal policy?
26.x: Taxation, public expenditure and public debt are the important instruments of Fiscal policy. In other words, a policy related to public expenditure, taxation and public debt is called fiscal policy.

26.s: Long-term fiscal policy was announced by which finance minister of India?
26.x: Long-term fiscal policy in India was announced by the then Finance Minister Vishwanath Pratap Singh in his Budget Speech 1985-86. Through this policy, government revenue and expenditure was framed with a long-term framework.

26.s: Which among the following is a tool of Fiscal Policy?
26.x: The main tools of fiscal policy are government spending and taxation, with transfer payments also playing a significant role. Government use these instruments to influence economic activity by adjusting the amount of money in the economy. Expansionary fiscal policy involves increasing spending or cutting taxes to stimulate growth, while contractionary policy reduces spending or raises taxes to cool an overheating economy. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer. Other three options are tools of monetary policy.

26.s: What is the fiscal deficit target of India for the financial year 2016-17?
26.x: In Union Budget 2016-17, the fiscal deficit target for the financial year 2016-17 was at 3.5% of GDP. The government’s fiscal deficit target in the Union Budget 2026-27 is pegged at Rs. 1695768 crore or 4.3% of the GDP.

26.s: Which of the following is NOT a tool of fiscal policy?
26.x: Among the given options, public expenditure, deficit financing and taxation are tools of fiscal policy, while interest rate is an instrument of monetary policy.

26.s: Which one of the following is not an objective of Monetary Policy ?
o: Equitable Distribution of Income and Assets
26.x: Equitable distribution of income and assets is not an objective of monetary policy. Rest three are the objectives of monetary policy.

26.s: Which one of the following is not an objective of fiscal policy of Government of India?
o: Equitable distribution of wealth and income
26.x: Fiscal policy, as a prime lever of economic stabilisation policy, seeks to influence the level of aggregate demand in the economy in pursuit of the larger societal goals of higher economic growth, full employment, equitable distribution of wealth and income and price stability. Regulation of inter-state trade is not an objective of fiscal policy in India.

26.s: The difference between the government’s total expenditure and its total receipts excluding borrowing is called _____.
26.src: APPSC 2023 Lecturers in Government Degree Colleges

26.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Assertion (A): Fiscal deficit is greater than budgetary deficit.
2. Reason (R): Fiscal deficit is the borrowings from the Reserve Bank of India plus other liabilities of the Government to meet its expenditure. Options:
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not a correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
26.x: Budgetary deficit refers only to the gap between total receipts and total expenditure of the government. Fiscal deficit is a broader concept and represents the total borrowing requirements of the government, including borrowings from the Reserve Bank of India and other liabilities. Hence, fiscal deficit is generally greater than budgetary deficit, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion.

26.s:
Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the Lists:
List I (Term)
I. Fiscal deficit
II. Budget deficit
III. Revenue deficit
IV. Primary deficit
List II (Explanation)
A. Excess of Total Expenditure over Total Receipts
B. Excess of Revenue Expenditure over Revenue Receipts
C. Excess of Total Expenditure over Total Receipts less borrowings
D. Excess of Total Expenditure over Total Receipts less borrowings and Interest Payments
26.x: Fiscal deficit refers to the excess of total expenditure over total receipts excluding borrowings, hence I-C. Budget deficit means the excess of total expenditure over total receipts, so II-A. Revenue deficit occurs when revenue expenditure exceeds revenue receipts, making III-B correct. Primary deficit is fiscal deficit minus interest payments, that is, excess of total expenditure over total receipts excluding borrowings and interest payments, therefore IV-D.

26.s: Ad hoc Treasury bill system of meeting budget deficit in India was abolished on :
26.x: The Ad hoc Treasury Bills emerged as a mode of financing Central Government's deficit in the mid-1950s. It was initiated as an administrative arrangement between the Central Government and the Reserve Bank of India. It was issued on the name of RBI for the short term lending requirements of the Government. It directly become monetize because with the issuance of it, the assets of RBI increases and hence liabilities also getting increased. The system of Ad hoc Treasury Bills to finance budget deficit was abolished on 31 March, 1997 (discontinued with effect from 1st April, 1997). The Union Budget for 1997-98 had announced the decision to introduce a new system called 'Ways and Means Advances (WMA)' in place of Ad hoc T-Bills.

26.s: After deducting grants for the creation of capital assets from revenue deficit, we arrive at :
26.x: Effective revenue deficit is defined as the difference between revenue deficit and grants for creation of capital assets. Effective revenue deficit signifies that amount of capital receipts that are being used for actual consumption expenditure of the Government. The concept of effective revenue deficit has been initiated from Union Budget for the financial year 2011-12. The main objective to introduce this type of deficit concept is to denote constructive imbalances of revenue account. It included in the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 through an amendment in 2012. In Union Budget Estimates 2026-27, the effective Revenue deficit is estimated at 0.3 percent of GDP whereas in revised estimates of 2025-26 it was at 0.6 percent of GDP.

26.s: 'Budget' is an instrument of :
26.x: Budget is an instrument of fiscal policy of the government. Under Article 112 of the Constitution, a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India has to be laid before both the Houses of Parliament in respect of every financial year. This statement titled 'Annual Financial Statement' is the main budget document.

26.s: Fiscal deficit/GDP ratio has been maximum in the financial year :
26.x: Among the given financial years, fiscal deficit/GDP ratio had been maximum in the year 2011-12 (5.9%). Fiscal deficit was at 9.2 percent of the GDP in 2020-21 which is the highest level of fiscal deficit for the Centre since 8.4 percent reported in financial year 1990-91. From 2021-22 to 2026-27 (B.E.), it was highest in 2021-22 (6.7%).

26.s:
Assertion (A): The Government is resorting to disinvestment of some of the public sector units (PSUs).
Reason (R): PSUs have not generated enough employment opportunities.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct expla-
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
26.x: The Government is resorting to disinvestment of some of the PSUs as part of economic reforms policy of liberalization and privatization, mainly due to reduce the fiscal burden and bridge the revenue shortfall of the Government. Hence, the assertion is true but the reason given is incorrect, as it cannot be said that PSUs have not generated enough employment opportunities. In fact, PSUs have an important role in generating employment in the country. Studies have shown that PSUs have beaten the private sector in terms of employment growth in recent years.

26.s: Fiscal deficit implies :
26.x: Fiscal deficit is the difference between the government's total expenditure and its total receipts excluding borrowings. Gross fiscal deficit = Total expenditure – (Revenue receipts + non-debt creating capital receipts) Non-debt creating capital receipts include recovery of loans and the proceeds from the sale of PSUs (receipts from disinvestment).

26.s: If interest payments are subtracted from gross fiscal deficit, the remainder will be :
26.x: The borrowing requirment of the government includes interest obligations on accumulated debt. The goal of measuring primary deficit is to focus on present fiscal imbalances. To obtain an estimate of borrowing on account of current expenditure exceeding revenues, we need to determine what has been called the primary deficit. Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit – Interest payments or, Primary deficit = Fiscal deficit – Net interest liabilities Net interest liabilities consist of interest payments minus interest receipts by the government on net domestic lending.

26.s:
Assertion (A) : Fiscal deficit is greater than budgetary deficit.
Reason (R) : Fiscal deficit is the borrowing from the Reserve Bank of India plus other liabilities of Government to meet its expenditure.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
26.x: Fiscal deficit is greater than budgetary deficit, because where budgetary deficit is a difference between total receipts and total expenditure of the Government, the fiscal deficit has been the difference between total income and total expenditure of the Government. Public debt and other liabilities are the receipts of Government but they are not income, because the government have responsibility to return them. Hence, fiscal deficit is greater than budgetary deficit.

26.s: Effective Revenue deficit was introduced in the Union Budget of :
Which of the following expression shows the formula of Gross Fiscal Deficit?
o: Gross Fiscal Deficit = Primary Deficit + Net borrowing
Gross Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure – Revenue
Gross Fiscal Deficit = Revenue Deficit + Capital
Gross Fiscal Deficit = Net borrowing at home +
26.x: The Gross Fiscal Deficit is the excess of total government expenditure over revenue receipts and capital receipts that do not create debt. The fiscal deficit will have to be financed through borrowing. Thus, it indicates the total borrowing requirements of the government. Hence, from the financing side Gross Fiscal Deficit = Net borrowing at home + Borrowing from RBI + Borrowing from abroad

26.s: A country's fiscal deficit stands at ₹50,000 crores. It is receiving ₹10,000 crores through non-debt creating capital receipts. The country's interest liabilities are ₹1,500 crores. What is the gross primary deficit?
26.x: Use the formula: Gross primary deficit = Fiscal deficit - Interest liabilities. Substitute the given values: Gross primary deficit = ₹50,000-₹1,500 = ₹ 48,500 crores.

26.s: A country's fiscal deficit stands at ₹ 50,000 crores. It is receiving ₹ 10,000 crores through non-debt creating capital receipts. The country's interest liabilities are ₹ 1,500 crores. What is the gross primary deficit?
26.x: Primary Deficit is simply the Fiscal Deficit after deducting interest payments. Given that, Fiscal Deficit = ₹50,000 crore and Interest payments = ₹1,500 crore. Therefore, the difference between the two is the correct answer, i.e., ₹48,500 crore.

Suppose the revenue expenditure is ₹ 80,000 crores and the revenue receipts of the Government are ₹ 60,000 crores. The Government budget also shows borrowings of ₹ 10,000 crores and interest payments of ₹ 6,000 crores. Which of the following statements are correct?
I. Revenue deficit is ₹ 20,000 crores.
II. Fiscal deficit is ₹ 10,000 crores.
III. Primary deficit is ₹ 4,000 crores.
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
26.x: Revenue Deficit– When the government’s revenue expenditure is more than its revenue receipts. Fiscal Deficit– When the government’s total expenditure is more than its total non-debt receipts; this gap represents the government’s borrowing requirement. Primary Deficit– Fiscal deficit excluding interest payments on past debt (i.e., fiscal deficit minus interest payments). Hence all three statements I, II and III are correct as per calculations and official definitions. Therefore, the correct answer is option (d).

In the context of governance, consider the following:
1. Encouraging Foreign Direct Investment inflows
2. Privatization of higher educational institutions
3. Down-sizing of bureaucracy
4. Selling or offloading the shares of Public Sector Undertakings
Which of the above can be used as measures to control the fiscal deficit in India?
26.x: Statement 1 is incorrect: FDI flows primarily into the private sector, not directly into government accounts. Does not automatically increase government revenue or reduce expenditure. Hence, not a direct fiscal deficit control measure. Statement 2 is incorrect: Privatisation of higher educational institutions is a structural reform, not a budgetary or fiscal instrument. It may marginally reduce future public spending, but is not treated as a direct fiscal deficit control tool. Statement 3 is correct: Downsizing of bureaucracy reduces recurring expenditure such as salaries and pensions. Lower recurring expenditure reduces the fiscal deficit. Statement 4 is correct: Selling or offloading shares of Public Sector Undertakings generates non-debt capital receipts, directly lowering the fiscal deficit, without increasing government liabilities.

Consider the following actions by the Government:
1. Cutting the tax rates
2. Increasing the government spending
3. Abolishing the subsidies Indian Economy: Public Finance PMF IAS IE – 120 In the context of economic recession, which of the above actions can be considered as part of the fiscal stimulus package?
26.x: Fiscal stimulus refers to expansionary fiscal policy used during economic recessions to boost aggregate demand. Cutting tax rates increases disposable income and consumption. Increasing government spending directly injects demand into the economy. Abolishing subsidies is a contractionary measure. Removing subsidies reduces financial support, potentially increasing costs for consumers and businesses, which can further dampen demand during a recession.

26.s: Which among the following steps is most likely to be taken at the time of an economic recession?
o: Cut in tax rates accompanied by increase in interest rate
Increase in expenditure on public projects
Increase in tax rates accompanied by reduction of interest rate
Reduction of expenditure on public projects
26.x: During an economic recession, the economy experiences a slowdown in growth, reduced consumer spending, lower business investments, and rising unemployment. To counter these effects, governments typically adopt expansionary fiscal policies to stimulate economic activity. Technically (there is no official definition of recession), a recession means that the total output in the economy — measured by the Gross Domestic Product or GDP — contracts for two consecutive quarters. A quarter is a period of three months. An increase in public project expenditure is the most likely step to be taken during an economic recession. Indian Economy: Public Finance PMF IAS IE – 115 • Stimulating Demand: Increasing expenditure on public projects, such as infrastructure development, directly injects money into the economy. It leads to increased government spending, which creates jobs, boosts income, and increases consumer spending power. • Addressing Unemployment: Public projects, like building roads, schools, and hospitals, typically require a large workforce, thus helping to reduce unemployment levels. • Boosting Private Sector Confidence: Increased government expenditure can also instil confidence in the private sector. 26.s: Which one of the following best describes the Crowding Out Effect in fiscal policy?
o: Increased private investment due to higher Government spending
Government borrowing leads to higher interest rates, reducing private investment
Taxation leads to increased private investment
Government borrowing has no impact on aggregate demand
26.x: The Crowding Out Effect happens when the government borrows heavily to finance its spending. Since both the government and private businesses borrow money from the same financial market, greater government borrowing increases competition for available funds. As demand for loans rises, interest rates usually increase. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for companies, so businesses may postpone or reduce investments such as expansion, new projects, or purchasing machinery. So, more government borrowing → higher interest rates → lower private investment

Consider the following statements : The ‘Stability and Growth Pact’ of the European Union is a treaty that :
1. limits the levels of the budgetary deficit of the countries of the European Union
2. makes the countries of the European Union to share their infrastructure facilities
3. enables the countries of the European Union to share their technologies
How many of the above statements are correct?
26.x: Described as the Eurozone's fiscal rulebook, the 'Stability and Growth Pact (SGP)' is a set of fiscal rules designed to prevent EU countries from spending beyond their means. Since 1997, member States have agreed that they should keep GDP ratios of deficit and debt below 3% and 60% respectively. Countries that break the rules for three consecutive years are fined a maximum of 0.5% of their GDP. These guidelines are intended to ensure sound management of public finances, in order to prevent one Member State’s irresponsible budgetary policies from spilling over and undermining the economic stability of the entire euro area. The SGP does not make or enable the countries of the European Union to share their infrastructure facilities or technologies. Hence, only statement 1 is correct and option (a) is the correct answer.

27.s: Which one of the following is NOT an objective of the FRBM Act, 2003?
27.x: The FRBM Act aims at inter-generational equity, long-run macroeconomic stability, elimination of the revenue deficit and reduction of the fiscal deficit, fiscal discipline, transparency and a balanced budget over time. 27.tq: FRBM objectives: equity across generations, RD elimination, transparency.

FRBM objectives: **inter-generational equity**, long-run macroeconomic stability, **elimination of the revenue deficit**, reduction of FD.
It also seeks to institutionalise fiscal discipline, **transparency** and a **balanced budget** over time — so options (1), (2) and (3) are objectives.
xa: The Act was introduced by **Yashwant Sinha** and enacted in **2003** for **fiscal discipline** (APPSC 2019).
FRBM Rules notified **2004**, in force from **5 July 2004**.
Original annual reduction under the Rules: **FD by 0.3%** and **RD by 0.5%** of GDP each year.

The Act does **not provide penal provisions** for missing targets (APPSC-G2 2017) — the favourite exam trap.
It does prescribe **deficit limits**, **statements laid with the Budget** and **disclosure of borrowings and contingent liabilities** — options (2), (3), (4).
xa: Additional guarantees against the **Consolidated Fund** are capped at **0.5% of GDP** a year.
FRBM does not make the Centre answerable for **States' failures**; States have their own Acts.

xa: The committee made **debt** the principal anchor: general govt **60% of GDP by 2023** (Centre **40%** + States **20%**).

Another design gap critics cite: **no penalty clause**.

27.s: Through the FRBM deviation statement, the Government has formally acknowledged deviation from which targets of the Act?
27.x: The Government has acknowledged deviation from the Act's 3% fiscal-deficit and 40% Central-debt targets.
xa: New rule from **2026-27**: Central debt **50 ± 1% of GDP by 31 March 2031** — above FRBM's **40%**.
The halving commitment was met: **9.2%** (2020-21) to **4.4%** (2025-26), not a legislative target.

27.s: The FRBM Review Committee, formed in May 2016 and reporting in January 2017, was chaired by:
27.x: N.K. Singh chaired the FRBM Review Committee, set up in May 2016, which reported in January 2017.
n: The FRBM Review Committee was formed in May 2016. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 30-32]
N.K. Singh was the chairman of the FRBM Review Committee. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 30-32]
The FRBM Review Committee submitted its report in January 2017. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 30-32]
The N.K. Singh Committee is the FRBM Review Committee. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 30-32]

27.s: With regard to fiscal discipline, States generally operate under:
o: The Union FRBM Act, applied identically
Rules framed by the Finance Commission
27.x: States have their own fiscal responsibility Acts; the Union FRBM framework does not automatically apply to them.
xa: States enacted their laws mostly after the **12th FC** tied debt relief (**Debt Consolidation and Relief Facility**) to it.
AP's law: **Andhra Pradesh FRBM Act, 2005** — eliminate RD, FD at **3% of GSDP**.
The FRBM Act also provides **no penal provisions** for missing targets.

27.s: The N.K. Singh FRBM Review Committee recommended which indicator as the principal fiscal anchor?
27.x: Debt-to-GDP was the principal anchor and fiscal deficit the operational target, with general government debt at 60% by 2023.
xa: Other recommendations: **FD 3% of GDP** for three years; **RD 0.8% of GDP by 2023**; an independent advisory **Fiscal Council**.
⚠ The new 2026-27 debt rule targets Central debt of **50 ± 1%** by **2031** — above FRBM's **40%**.
The **2018 amendment** set general govt **60%**, Centre **40%** by **31 March 2025**.

27.s: The debt anchor and escape-clause recommendations of the N.K. Singh Committee were incorporated into the FRBM Act through which amendment?
27.x: The committee's debt anchor and escape clause were written into the FRBM Act through the 2018 amendment.
27.tq: Match the substantive institutional change with the later amendment, not the amendment that added expenditure projections.
xs: The debt anchor and escape clause were written into the Act by the **2018 amendment** — option **(1)**.
2018 also set **FD 3% by 31 March 2021**, dropped RD/ERD targets and added a **buoyancy clause**.
**2012** added ERD and the MTEFS; **2015** deferred target dates — neither brought the debt anchor.
xa: 2018 debt anchor: general govt **60%**, Centre **40%** by **31 March 2025**.
The escape-clause deviation is capped at **0.5% of GDP**.
The Act is now cited as "**FRBM Act, 2003 (amended 2018)**".

27.s: The Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement sets ____ rolling targets.
27.x: It sets three-year rolling targets for revenue deficit, fiscal deficit, a tax-GDP indicator and total outstanding liabilities.
xa: MTFPS rolling targets have been **suspended since 2021-22** for post-pandemic flexibility.
**Budget 2026-27** laid a combined **MTFPS cum FPSS** with the **MEFS**.
The **Macro-Economic Framework Statement** covers growth, inflation, external balance and risks.

27.s: The 2018 amendment to the FRBM framework envisaged which combination of targets?
o: Fiscal deficit of 3% by 31 March 2021, general government debt of 60% and Central debt of 40% by 31 March 2025
Fiscal deficit of 3% by 31 March 2018 and Central debt of 50% by 2025
Fiscal deficit of 4.5% by 31 March 2025, general government debt of 50% and Central debt of 30% by 2031
Revenue deficit of zero and Central debt of 60% by 31 March 2021
27.x: The 2018 amendment set a 3% fiscal-deficit target by 31 March 2021 and debt anchors of 60% for general government and 40% for the Centre by 31 March 2025.
27.tq: Combine the year, date and multiple numerical targets without swapping their deadlines.
xs: The 2018 amendment set **FD 3% by 31 March 2021**, general govt debt **60%** and Central debt **40% by 31 March 2025** — option **(1)**.
It also dropped RD/ERD targets and added an **escape clause** (**0.5%** cap) and a **buoyancy clause**.
The **50%** Central debt by **2031** figure belongs to the new **2026-27** debt rule, not the 2018 amendment.
xa: The Government has acknowledged **deviation** from the Act's **3% FD** and **40% Central debt** targets.
COVID **2020-21**: FD **9.2%**; escape clause used, no amendment.

27.s: During COVID-19 in 2020–21, India's fiscal deficit was recorded at:
27.x: The fiscal deficit reached 9.2 per cent of GDP in 2020–21, after which targets were recalibrated with a gradual return path.
xa: The commitment to halve the 2020-21 FD in five years was met: **4.4% in 2025-26**.
In **2020-21** the escape clause was used with no amendment, to keep flexibility.

27.s: Which one of the following is a ground for invoking the FRBM escape clause?
o: Routine tax shortfall due to administrative delay
Sharp rise in real output growth
27.x: Escape-clause grounds include national security, war, national calamity, agricultural collapse, structural reforms and a sharp fall in output; a routine tax shortfall is not one, and a sharp rise in growth triggers the buoyancy clause instead.

27.s: FRBM targets were suspended after the global financial crisis in:
27.x: After the 2004 Rules, the targets were suspended in 2008-09 following the global financial crisis; 2012 added new targets and 2018 brought the debt anchor.

27.s: When the FRBM escape clause is invoked, the Government must place before Parliament:
o: An RBI approval for the deviation
A justification and a path back to the target
27.x: The Government must justify the deviation (capped at 0.5% of GDP) and lay a path back to the target before Parliament.
xa: Grounds: **national security, war, national calamity**, collapse of agriculture, **structural reforms**, severe slowdown.
Slowdown test: real output growth **3 percentage points** below the average of the previous four quarters.
⚠ **Buoyancy clause:** FD must fall by **at least 0.25%** if growth rises sharply.

27.s: The commitment to halve the 2020-21 fiscal deficit within five years was fulfilled when the fiscal deficit reached:
27.x: The 2020-21 fiscal deficit of 9.2% was more than halved to 4.4% in 2025-26. This was a commitment, not a legislative target.
27.tq: Calculate the direction of change while retaining the distinction between a commitment and a statutory target.
xs: The halving commitment was met when FD reached **4.4% of GDP in 2025-26** — option **(3)**.
**2020-21** FD was **9.2%**; halving it in five years was a commitment, **not a legislative target**.
xa: The **2025-26** target "below **4.5%**" (set in FY 2021-22) was met.
The **16th FC** path: Centre FD **3.5% of GDP by 2030-31**.

27.s: The Sixteenth Finance Commission described State fiscal rules as:
27.x: It called State fiscal rules 'effectively unenforced' and sought a wider deficit definition covering off-budget borrowing.
xa: **AP FRBM Act, 2005**: eliminate the revenue deficit; FD at **3% of GSDP**.

27.s: The FRBM escape clause can be triggered when real output growth falls ____ percentage points below the average of the previous four quarters.
27.x: One escape-clause trigger is a fall in real output growth by 3 percentage points below the average of the previous four quarters.
xa: Deviation under the escape clause: **not more than 0.5% of GDP** in a year.
Buoyancy clause: if growth rises sharply, FD must fall by **at least 0.25% of GDP**.

27.s: Under the buoyancy clause of the 2018 FRBM amendment, a sharp rise in real output growth requires the fiscal deficit to fall by at least:
27.x: The buoyancy clause requires at least a 0.25% of GDP cut in the fiscal deficit; it never permits an automatic increase.
xa: ⚠ Escape clause = deviation up to **0.5%**; buoyancy clause = FD cut of at least **0.25%**.
2018 also set the **debt anchor**: general govt **60%**, Centre **40%** by **31 March 2025**.

27.s: Under the Fifteenth Finance Commission, the net borrowing limit for States in 2022-23 was:
27.x: The limits were 4% in 2021-22, 3.5% in 2022-23, and 3% from 2023-24 to 2025-26 plus 0.5% for power-sector reforms.
xa: FRBM limits restrain AP's **open-market borrowing**.
AP slippage: FD **5.05%** vs mandated **4%** ceiling (7 Mar 2026).
**16th FC**: States **3% of GSDP** by **2030-31**.

27.s: Which one of the following correctly states the fiscal-deficit recommendations associated with the Sixteenth Finance Commission?
o: Centre 3.5% of GDP and States 3% of GSDP by 2030-31
Centre 4.3% of GDP and States 3% of GSDP by 2026-27
Centre 3.5% of GDP and States 4% of GSDP by 2030-31
Centre 3% of GDP and States 3.5% of GSDP by 2030-31
27.x: The Sixteenth Finance Commission recommended that the Centre reach a fiscal deficit of 3.5% of GDP and States reach 3% of GSDP by 2030-31.
27.tq: Keep the Centre and State limits separate before comparing the two figures.
xs: The **16th FC**: Centre FD **3.5% of GDP** and States **3% of GSDP** by **2030-31** — option **(1)**.
**4.3%** is the Centre's FD in **2026-27 BE**, not an FC recommendation.
**4%** of GSDP was the **15th FC** State borrowing limit for **2021-22**.
xa: The 16th FC also asked for State fiscal-rule reform and a wider deficit definition covering **off-budget borrowing**.
It found State fiscal rules "**effectively unenforced**".
⚠ FRBM 2018 target for the Centre was **3%**; the 16th FC path is **3.5%** by 2030-31.

27.s: In which year was the Andhra Pradesh Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act enacted?
27.x: The AP FRBM Act was enacted in 2005; it aims to eliminate the revenue deficit and limit the fiscal deficit to 3% of GSDP.
xa: It has been amended from time to time to match **Finance Commission** borrowing limits.
**AP BE 2026-27**: FD **3.84%**, RD **1.11%** of GSDP — above the **3%** norm.
Slippage: FD **5.05%** vs mandated **4%** ceiling; borrowings **₹81,071 crore**.

27.s: State fiscal responsibility legislation was promoted after the Twelfth Finance Commission because debt relief was linked to:
o: The Debt Consolidation and Relief Facility
The Goods and Services Tax Compensation Fund
27.x: The Twelfth Finance Commission linked debt relief for States to the enactment of fiscal responsibility legislation through the Debt Consolidation and Relief Facility.
27.tq: Identify the specific facility associated with the debt-relief incentive.
xs: The **12th FC** tied debt relief to the **Debt Consolidation and Relief Facility** — option **(1)**.
States enacted Fiscal Responsibility Legislation mostly after this link.
Several States passed FRBM Acts on the **central model**; AP's came in **2005**.
xa: AP FRBM Act targets: eliminate RD, **FD 3% of GSDP**.
The central FRBM Act does **not apply to States**.
**16th FC** found State fiscal rules "**effectively unenforced**".

27.s: The main significance of the FRBM framework is that it:
o: Made fiscal discipline a legal duty and added disclosure statements to the Budget
Gave the Finance Commission control over Union borrowing
27.x: The FRBM framework gave fiscal discipline a legal basis and made disclosure statements part of the Budget process.
xa: Criticism: frequent **escape-clause** use and repeated target deferrals.
Design gaps: **no penalty clause**; no independent **fiscal council** yet.
Current relevance: Budget 2026-27 switched to a debt-GDP rule (**50 ± 1% by 2031**).

27.s: Which one of the following statements is correct regarding the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (FRBM Act)?
o: It concerns both fiscal and revenue deficit
It concerns neither fiscal deficit nor revenue deficit
27.x: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 is a landmark Indian legislation aimed at institutionalizing financial discipline, reducing the fiscal deficit, eliminating the revenue deficit, and managing public debt. It compels the government to adopt transparent budgetary practices to ensure long-term macroeconomic stability and inter-generational equity.

27.s: Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act was enacted in India in the year :
27.x: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 was enacted in August, 2003. It became effective from 5 July, 2004 (date of commencement). The FRBM Act, 2003 sets a target for the Government to establish financial discipline in the economy, improve the management of public funds, reduce the fiscal deficit and improved macroeconomic management by moving towards a balanced budget and strengthen financial prudence. The FRBM Act, 2003 requires the Central Government to progressively reduce its outstanding debt, revenue deficit and fiscal deficit. The Central Government has to give threeyear rolling targets for these indicators when it presents the Union Budget each year. The Government was supposed to achieve fiscal deficit of 3% of GDP by 31 March, 2021. In Budget Estimates 2020-21, the fiscal deficit target was relaxed to 3.5% (as permitted by the FRBM Act) and it was estimated that fiscal deficit of 3.1% will be achieved by 2022-23, but as per actual figures of 2020-21, the fiscal deficit was zoomed to 9.2% of GDP (due to COVID-19 pandemic impact). It is to be noted that the Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement has not provided rolling targets for budget deficits since 2021-22. The Union Government in Budget Speech of FY 2024-25 has outlined a medium term policy stance. It seeks to keep the central Government fiscal deficit to GDP ratio such that the debt to GDP ratio is on a declining path from 2026-27 onwards.

27.s: Along with the budget, the Finance Minister also places other documents before the parliament which include "The Macro Economic Framework Statement" The aforesaid document is presented because this is mandated by
o: Article 112 and Article 110(1) of the constitution of India
Article 113 of the Constitution of India
Provisions of the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003
27.x: The documents that the government is required to present along with the budget as per the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, 2003 are: Macroeconomic Framework Statement: This statement provides an overview of the economy, including GDP growth, inflation, receipts and expenditure.  Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement: This statement sets out the government's fiscal policy goals for the medium term.  Fiscal Policy Strategy Statement: This statement explains how the government plans for fiscal policy goals.  Medium-Term Expenditure Framework: This framework sets out the government's spending plans for the medium term.

27.s: Along with the Budget, the Finance Minister also places other documents before the Parliament which include 'The Macro Economic Framework Statement'. The aforesaid document is presented because this is mandated by :
o: Article 112 and Article 110 (1) of the Constitution of
Article 113 of the Constitution of India
Provisions of the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget
27.x: Every year, along with the budget, the 'Macro-Economic Framework Statement' is presented before the Parliament by the Finance Minister. This is mandated under provisions of section 3 of the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003. The statement contains an overview of the economy. This includes an assessment regarding the GDP growth, fiscal balance of the central government and the external sector balance of the economy.

27.s:
Consider the following statements :
Assertion (A) : There is a history of fiscal deficit in Central Government budgets in India.
Reason (R) : Indian agriculture has enjoyed large amount of subsidies compared to Western countries.
Select the correct answer using the code given below :
o: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not a correct
27.x: There is a history of fiscal deficit in Central Government budgets in India. Hence, Assertion (A) is correct.While Reason (R) is wrong because India's subsidies to its agriculture sector are quite low as compared to Western countries. So option (c) is correct answer.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about the FRBM Act, 2003:
1. It has no penal provisions for missing its targets.
2. It applies automatically to the States.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: The Act has no penal provisions; it does not apply to States, which have their own fiscal responsibility Acts.

27.s: The FRBM Rules came into force on:
27.x: The Act was enacted in August 2003 and its Rules came into force on 5 July 2004.

27.s: Under the FRBM framework, the tax-GDP ratio is:
o: A trigger for the escape clause
A target fixed by the Fiscal Council
An indicator in the Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement
27.x: Tax-GDP is not a legal target; it is one of four indicators in the MTFP Statement.

27.s: Under the original FRBM Rules, the revenue deficit was to be cut each year by:
27.x: The Rules required annual cuts of 0.5% of GDP in RD and 0.3% in FD.

27.s: The Kelkar Task Force (2004) recommended meeting FRBM targets mainly through:
o: Tax reform including a comprehensive GST
27.x: Kelkar's route was tax reform with a wider base and a comprehensive GST; the debt anchor and Fiscal Council came from the N.K. Singh Committee.

27.s: Vijay Kelkar later headed which Finance Commission?
27.x: Vijay Kelkar headed the 13th Finance Commission (2010-15).

27.s: The N.K. Singh Committee's 60% general government debt target included a Central share of:
27.x: General government debt of 60% by 2023 was split as Centre 40% and States 20%.

27.s: The N.K. Singh Committee recommended a revenue deficit target of ____ of GDP by 2023.
27.x: The committee recommended RD of 0.8% of GDP by 2023 along with FD of 3%.

27.s: The effective revenue deficit target and the Medium-Term Expenditure Framework Statement were added to the FRBM framework in:
27.x: The 2012 amendment added the ERD target and the MTEF Statement.

27.s: In 2015, the target of a 3% fiscal deficit was deferred to:
27.x: The 2015 change deferred the dates, with FD 3% to be reached by 2017-18.

27.s:
Consider the following statements about the FRBM escape clause:
1. It allows the fiscal deficit to exceed the target by up to 0.5% of GDP in a year.
2. A routine tax shortfall is a valid ground for invoking it.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
27.x: Escape-clause deviation is capped at 0.5% of GDP in a year; a routine tax shortfall is not a ground for it.

27.s: The Andhra Pradesh FRBM Act, 2005 set a fiscal deficit target of:
27.x: The AP FRBM Act, 2005 aimed to eliminate RD and hold FD at 3% of GSDP.

27.s: Which amendment of the AP FRBM Act raised the revenue deficit limits?
27.x: The AP FRBM Act was amended in 2010, 2011, 2020 and 2021; the 2020 amendment raised RD limits.

27.s: From 2023-24 to 2025-26, the 15th Finance Commission allowed States extra borrowing for power-sector reforms of:
27.x: States' net borrowing limit was 3% of GSDP plus 0.5% for power-sector reforms in 2023-26.

27.s: The Medium-Term Expenditure Framework Statement sets:
o: Growth, inflation and external balance assumptions
27.x: The MTEF Statement, added in 2012, sets 3-year expenditure ceilings; rolling targets belong to the MTFP Statement.

32.s: Along with the end of the Plan/non-Plan classification, the Union Budget began to be presented on:
32.x: The Railway Budget was merged with the Union Budget and the Budget was presented on 1 February.
xa: ⚠ **2017** = three changes together: **Railway merger** + **1 February** date + **plan/non-plan** ended.
The separate Railway Budget had run from **1924** (**Acworth Committee**, 1921) — a **92-year** practice ended.
The plan/non-plan split was removed on the advice of the **Expenditure Management Commission**.

32.s: The separate Railway Budget was introduced in 1924 on the recommendation of the:
32.x: The separate Railway Budget began in 1924 following the recommendations of the Acworth Committee constituted in 1921.
32.tq: Match the reform with the committee that recommended it.
xs: The separate Railway Budget began in **1924** on the **Acworth Committee** (**1921**) recommendation — option **(2)**.
It was merged with the Union Budget in **2017** (Budget 2017-18), ending a **92-year** practice.
The **Expenditure Management Commission** is linked to ending the plan/non-plan split, not the Railway Budget.
xa: The Budget date also moved to **1 February** in **2017**.
**Outcome Budget / Gender Budget** came in **2005-06**; the Budget went **paperless** in **2021**.

32.s: India's Budget has been presented in paperless or digital form since:
32.x: The Budget has been presented in paperless or digital form since 2021.
32.tq: Recall the starting year of the digital reform.
xs: The Budget has been **paperless (digital)** since **2021** — option **(4)**.
**2017** is the year the Budget moved to **1 February** and the Railway Budget merged.
**2019** is when **Nirmala Sitharaman** began presenting every Budget.
xa: Printing begins with the **Halwa ceremony** at **North Block**.
The word "Budget" comes from French **bougette** ("little bag") and is **not in the Constitution**.

32.s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
o: Liaquat Ali Khan – Presented the most budgets (10)
James Wilson – First budget of India, 7 April 1860
R.K. Shanmukham Chetty – First budget of independent India, 26 November 1947
32.x: Liaquat Ali Khan presented the 1947-48 Interim Government budget; Morarji Desai presented the most budgets (10).
xa: **Nirmala Sitharaman** has presented every Budget since **2019**.
The Budget date moved to **1 February** in **2017**.
**1973-74** = "Black Budget"; **1997-98** = "Dream Budget".

32.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Receipt Budget — output-outcome framework for schemes
Expenditure Profile — detailed estimates of tax receipts
Outcome Budget — output-outcome framework for schemes
32.x: The Outcome Budget presents the output-outcome framework for schemes. The Receipt Budget deals with receipts, while the Expenditure Budget or Expenditure Profile deals with spending.
32.tq: Start from the sure document-function pair and eliminate swapped descriptions.
xs: **Outcome Budget — output-outcome framework for schemes** is correct — option **(3)**.
The **Receipt Budget** gives estimates and trends of tax, non-tax and capital receipts — so option (1) is wrong.
The **Expenditure Profile** is scheme- and ministry-wise **spending**; the **Finance Bill** carries **tax proposals**.
xa: **Appropriation Bill**: **Art. 114(3)** — authorises withdrawal from the CFI.
**Finance Bill** is under **Art. 110(1)(a)**, with an explanatory **Memorandum**.
Other documents: **Budget at a Glance**; FRBM statements (**MEFS**; **MTFPS cum FPSS**).

32.s: The word 'Budget' comes from the French word 'bougette', meaning:
32.x: 'Bougette' means 'little bag'; Budget printing begins with the Halwa ceremony at North Block.
xa: The **Budget circular** is issued in **September**.
The Budget is prepared by the **Budget Division, Department of Economic Affairs**, Ministry of Finance.

32.s: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the Appropriation Bill?
32.x: Article 114 covers the Appropriation Bill; 112 is the Annual Financial Statement, 113 the estimates, 115 supplementary grants.
xa: **Art. 116** = **vote on account**, vote of credit, exceptional grants; **Art. 117** = special provisions on financial bills.

32.s: Who prepares the Union Budget through the Budget Division?
o: NITI Aayog independently of the Ministry of Finance
Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance
Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance
32.x: The Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs in the Ministry of Finance prepares the Union Budget, in coordination with NITI Aayog and spending ministries.
32.tq: Apply the ‘who performs this job?’ test to distinguish adjoining financial institutions.
xs: The Budget is prepared by the **Budget Division, Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance** — option **(2)**.
It works with **NITI Aayog** and the spending ministries — NITI does not prepare it independently.
The **Department of Revenue** (**CBDT/CBIC**) only furnishes revenue estimates.
xa: The DEA also prepares budgets of **States under President's Rule** and **UTs**.
The **Budget circular** is issued in **September**; printing begins with the **Halwa ceremony** at **North Block**.

32.s: The Annual Financial Statement is provided for under Article:
32.x: Article 112 provides for the Annual Financial Statement; the Constitution does not use the word 'Budget'.
xa: The AFS is presented on the "**first working day of February**" — in practice **1 February**, even on a Sunday (**2026**).
The **Contingency Fund of India** (Art. 267) corpus was raised to **₹30,000 crore** from **2021-22**.

32.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Demands for Grants?
o: They include capital expenditure and loans
Charged expenditure is not shown separately in them
32.x: Demands for Grants (Article 113) cover revenue, capital and loan components; charged items are shown separately, so the last statement is false.

32.s: A Finance Bill is treated as a Money Bill under which constitutional provision?
32.x: A Finance Bill comes within the scope of a Money Bill under Article 110(1)(a), insofar as it contains provisions dealing with taxation.
32.tq: Distinguish the constitutional provision governing taxation-related Money Bills.
xs: The Finance Bill is a **Money Bill** under **Article 110(1)(a)** — option **(2)**.
It gives effect to the **tax proposals** and comes with an explanatory **Memorandum**.
**Art. 112** is the **Annual Financial Statement**, not the Finance Bill.
xa: The Finance Bill must be enacted within **75 days** (**Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931**).
It is the **sixth** and last stage of the budget process, after the **Appropriation Bill**.

32.s: The Public Account of India is provided for under Article:
32.x: The Public Account is under Article 266(2); withdrawals need no appropriation since the government acts only as banker.
xa: **Art. 266** = Consolidated Fund; **Art. 267** = Contingency Fund.
The **Contingency Fund** corpus was raised to **₹30,000 crore** from **2021-22**.

32.s: The list of expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India is laid down in:
32.x: Article 112(3) lists charged expenditure (President's emoluments, debt charges, judges' salaries, CAG etc.). Art 114(3) bars withdrawal from the CFI without an Appropriation Act, Art 266(2) is the Public Account, and Art 110(1)(a) brings tax provisions within a Money Bill.
32.tq: Charged list = 112(3); discussable but not votable = 113(1).
xs: Charged expenditure is listed in **Article 112(3)** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 114(3)** bars withdrawal from the CFI without an **Appropriation Act**.
**Art. 266(2)** is the **Public Account**; **Art. 110(1)(a)** is the **Finance Bill**.
xa: Charged items include the **President**'s emoluments, **debt charges**, **SC judges**' salaries, the **CAG**.
Charged expenditure is **not voted**, only **discussed** (**Art. 113(1)**).

32.s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with its budget-account characteristic?
o: Capital account — current-year routine transactions only
Capital account — no transactions involving liabilities
Revenue account — creation of long-term assets only
32.x: The revenue account records current-year transactions, while the capital account relates to assets and liabilities.
32.tq: Use the running-versus-asset-creation distinction to reject reversed descriptions.
xs: **Revenue account — current-year transactions** is correct — option **(3)**.
The **capital account** records **assets and liabilities**, so options (1) and (2) are wrong.
Revenue spending **creates no asset** — it maintains assets (salaries, pensions, interest, subsidies).
xa: Capital spending creates assets or reduces liabilities: capex, roads, **defence equipment**, loans given, debt repayment.
Mnemonic: "Revenue = Running the government; Capital = Creating assets".

32.s: Which of the following gives effect to the tax proposals of the Union Budget?
32.x: The Finance Bill gives effect to tax proposals; the Appropriation Bill authorises withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund.
xa: The Finance Bill must be enacted within **75 days** (**Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931**).
The **Public Account** needs no appropriation — the government acts as banker.

32.s: Under the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931, the Finance Bill must be enacted within:
32.x: The Finance Bill must be enacted within 75 days under the stated provision of the Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931.
32.tq: Recall the statutory time limit using closely spaced numerical options.
xs: The Finance Bill must be enacted within **75 days** — option **(3)**.
This comes from the **Provisional Collection of Taxes Act, 1931**.
The Finance Bill is a **Money Bill** under **Art. 110(1)(a)** and gives effect to tax proposals.
xa: Budget = estimate statement; **Finance Bill** = the legal instrument for taxes.
The Finance Bill comes with an explanatory **Memorandum**.

32.s: No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India without:
32.x: Withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund (Article 266) needs an Appropriation Act; a vote on account authorises advance spending.

32.s: A full statement of receipts and expenditure presented by an outgoing government in an election year is called:
32.x: An interim budget is a full statement of receipts and expenditure by an outgoing government; a vote on account only authorises expenditure for part of the year.
xa: In election years a vote on account covers **3-5 months**.
⚠ Vote on account is rarely needed since **1 February**, except in **interim budget** years.

32.s: A government has a fiscal deficit of Rs 80,000 crore and interest payments of Rs 25,000 crore. Its primary deficit is:

A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

Revenue receipts do not reduce government assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #32 · pp 47-49]
Capital receipts create a liability or reduce financial assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #32 · pp 47-49]

**Capital receipts** **create a liability or reduce financial assets** (R) — a fact about a different class, so it does not explain A.
xa: **Borrowings create a liability**; **disinvestment reduces assets**.

32.s: In which of the following countries, zero-based budgeting was first adopted?
32.x: Zero-based budgeting (ZBB) is a method of budgeting in which all expenses must be justified for each new period. Zero-base budget technique involves a critical review of every scheme before a budgetary provision is made. Developed by Peter Pyhrr in the 1970s, zero-based budgeting starts from a ‘zero base’ at the beginning of every budget period, and every function within an organization is analyzed for its needs and costs. Jimmy Carter, then Governor of Georgia (U.S.), was the first to adopt the process of zero-base into the government in 1973 budget. Three years later, the U.S. federal government for the first time implemented zero-based budgeting in ‘The Government Economy and Spending Reform Act, 1976’. In India, the Department of Science and Technology was the first to introduce zero-based budgeting in 1983 and in 1986, the Indian Government adopted zero-based budgeting for determining expenditure budget.

Identify the correct sequence in the classification of government receipts:
A. Revenue Receipts
B. Capital Receipts
C. Tax Revenue
D. Non-tax Revenue Note: For this question, discrepancy is found in question/answer. So,this question is ignored for all candidates.

Consider the following statements :
I. Capital receipts create a liability or cause a reduction in the assets of the Government.
II. Borrowings and disinvestment are capital receipts.
III. Interest received on loans creates a liability of the Government.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
32.x: Government receipts are divided into two main categories– Revenue Receipts and Capital Receipts. Th ose government receipts which create a liability for the government or reduce its fi nancial assets are called Capital Receipts. On the other hand, Revenue Receipts, are those which neither create any additional liability on the government nor reduce its assets; these include tax revenue and non-tax revenue (such as interest, dividend, fees, etc.). When the government borrows from the market, RBI, or other financial institutions, it creates an obligation to repay the principal and interest in the future; therefore, these receipts create a new liability for the government and are treated as Capital Receipts. Under Disinvestment, the government sells its equity stake in public sector enterprises. This reduces the government’s financial assets, and in official accounting such receipts are also treated as Capital Receipts (especially as non-debt capital receipts). Thus, both borrowings and disinvestment are capital receipts. The interest received by the Central Government on loans given to states, public sector enterprises, etc., is classified officially as non-tax revenue and included under Revenue Receipts, not under Capital Receipts. Revenue receipts neither create any new liability nor reduce the government’s financial assets. Thus, only Statements I and II are correct, while Statement III is incorrect; therefore, the correct answer is option (a).

56.s: Which one of the following correctly explains the difference between the Centre’s and Andhra Pradesh’s estimates of the post-bifurcation resource gap?

56.s: In the context of Andhra Pradesh's bifurcation, the 'resource gap' for the first post-bifurcation year refers to:
o: The fiscal deficit of the State for the full financial year 2014-15

The shortfall in capital outlay compared with the 13th Finance Commission projection
The difference between borrowings and repayments for 2014-15

xs: Resource gap = **the revenue deficit (revenue expenditure − revenue receipts) for the first ten months** — option **(2)**.
